At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.
The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.
Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.
Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".
The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.
The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.
Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.
The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.
The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.
Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.
Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains.
The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.
The train continued for around nine kilometres (5.6 miles) before coming to a halt.
In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.
Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.
There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.

71f298312da2.text: By — Wufei Yu, Associated Press Wufei Yu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/floods-bring-rare-relief-to-u-s-southwest-reservoirs-as-lake-powell-rises-20-feet Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Floods bring rare relief to U.S. Southwest reservoirs as Lake Powell rises 20 feet Nation Nov 8, 2026 12:31 PM EST PHOENIX (AP) — Recent flooding across the U.S. Southwest is providing rare relief to thirsty reservoirs that had fallen to record lows amid a yearslong megadrought. WATCH: How the West is preparing for a drier future as water supplies hit lows Storms in late October and early November sent torrents of water through normally small or dry creeks that overflowed their banks and flooded local communities. Hundreds of people were told to evacuate, and the flooding cut off access to some areas. Yet most of that water will end up feeding depleted lakes and underground aquifers, said Martin Hoerling, a climate scientist and hydrologist at the University of Colorado, Boulder. "That's somewhat of an unexpected boost from Mother Nature," Hoerling said. Last winter's lackluster snowfall did little to recharge water bodies when it melted in the spring and summer, when they typically get their biggest bump of the year. Then came the chaotic climate phenomenon, El Niño, that has intensified heavy rain and floods. Experts say its impacts will last several more months, potentially further boosting water supplies across the West where water primarily is stored in lakes, aquifers and snowpack. READ MORE: Colorado River plan to cut water amid drought brings uncertainty for cities and farmers Lake Powell, the second-largest reservoir in the U.S., rose more than 20 feet (6.1 meters) from its mid-September low — dwarfing its gains from this year's snowmelt, Hoerling said. Still, the lake remained just over a quarter full, and 15 of its 17 boat launches remained unusable as of Friday. The floodwaters and additional rain could raise the lake along the Arizona-Utah border further, for a total of over 1.2 million acre-feet — enough to support around 4 million average families for a year, Hoerling estimated. Rain brings temporary relief to regional and local water supplies Cities in the region reported some of their wettest weather in decades. Before storms began dumping about 7 inches (17.78 centimeters) of rain around Pagosa Springs, Colorado, in October, more than 10,000 people in the town and surrounding communities were under water restrictions. Restaurants were encouraged to serve water only on request, town manager David Harris said. Those restrictions are now lifted. "While the storm was destructive, I think there is a silver lining," Harris said. "You're getting a good start to the winter snowpack in the higher elevations." WATCH: Tipping Point — The Colorado River Reimagined | A PBS News Special Upper Lake Mary, which captures spring snowmelt in Northern Arizona and supplies Flagstaff, Arizona, with up to 40% of its water, received more than 3 billion gallons of water since early October, said Flagstaff water production manager Brian Huntzinger. Storms last weekend dumped the equivalent of more than two years of water into the town's surface water supply and provided a buffer for an operation that depends heavily on underground aquifers, Huntzinger said. "It's just a great, great thing to see," Huntzinger said. "We might be overflowing at this rate before we see any snow fly." In central Arizona, heavy floodwaters that trapped people in their homes gushed into streams that feed the Verde River. That prompted water officials to release water from two nearly full dams into the Verde's normally dry stretch in metro Phoenix, said Bo Svoma, the principal meteorologist at the Salt River Project that manages reservoirs on the Salt and Verde rivers. Wet weather is unlikely to change decisions on the Colorado River The region remains in drought despite the intense rains. And decisions already have been made to divvy up water in the Colorado River basin. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, which manages reservoirs in the West, is unlikely to change its water releases from Lake Powell or other areas until it knows when snowpack has peaked, typically around April, said Jack Schmidt, a Utah State University professor who studies the Colorado River. READ MORE: Lake Powell hits record low, threatening key water and electricity supply for millions Reclamation spokesperson Mary Carlson acknowledged conditions have improved but added "considerable uncertainty remains." Under the federal plan for managing the Colorado River's Lower Basin, California, Nevada and Arizona will collectively reduce water use by 1.25 million acre-feet (about 1.54 billion cubic meters) annually in the next two years. That is enough to fill over 600,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools, with the possibility of larger cuts depending on conditions. Nevada and Arizona are challenging the plan in court. Some Arizona cities have agreed to fund preliminary work to reduce reliance on the Colorado River by expanding an existing dam on the Verde River to capture runoff from storms, Svoma said. "We need to figure out how to be resilient in a drier future. And we're not quite there yet," Hoerling said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Wufei Yu, Associated Press Wufei Yu, Associated Press

ab20afc74f55.text: Attorney General Todd Blanche refused Sunday to rule out prosecuting Democratic lawmakers who say they'll investigate Trump officials, a day after President Trump ordered the Justice Department to probe lawmakers. Why it matters: The confrontation threatens a constitutional crisis over the separation of powers: Trump is ordering prosecutors to go after lawmakers in a potential effort to hamper Congress' power to hold the executive branch accountable. Driving the news: In a Truth Social post Saturday, Trump accused Democrats of threatening administration officials and Republican donors with investigations and impeachment. "This is extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable for this," Trump wrote. He singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), accusing her of threatening young people who hold Republican views. "The imprisonment should be against these EXTORTIONISTS," Trump wrote. "By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!" he added. The latest: On CNN's "State of the Union," Blanche acknowledged Congress' constitutional oversight authority but argued that Democrats' rhetoric had crossed a line. Asked whether DOJ would investigate Democratic lawmakers, Blanche did not identify a criminal statute or confirm that an investigation had begun. Asked whether lawmakers could face imprisonment, Blanche said it depended on what crimes they had committed. On Fox News, he said the possibility of criminal charges depended on what Democrats had said. The White House and Justice Department have not responded to requests for comment. What they're saying: Blanche singled out incoming House Oversight Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who warned officials, including incoming White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, to "lawyer up." "I would be very worried if I was a member on that committee," Blanche told CNN. He also said the department would provide legal defense for administration officials facing congressional scrutiny, including incoming White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. The other side: Garcia accused Blanche of trying to intimidate Congress and said Democrats would not back down. "They can come after us however they want. We're not going to be intimidated," Garcia told CNN. Garcia said his committee would pursue alleged wrongdoing involving Trump's administration, family and corporate allies. Flashback: In February, a federal grand jury rejected DOJ's attempt to indict Slotkin and five other Democratic lawmakers over a video urging service members to refuse unlawful military orders. What's next: It remains unclear whether DOJ has opened an investigation in response to Trump's order, which lawmakers it might examine or what conduct it believes could constitute a crime.

f32bb7044351.text: By — Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Melanie Lidman, Associated Press By — Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israels-president-formally-gives-eisenkot-the-first-chance-to-form-the-next-government Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israel's president formally gives Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government World Updated on Nov 8, 2026 1:13 PM EST — Published on Nov 8, 2026 11:32 AM EST JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog formally gave opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government Sunday evening. Complex coalition negotiations still lie ahead, but it marked a significant step in the former military chief's effort to oust Israel's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, after elections held in a deeply divided country. Israel remains scarred by the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, and the multifront wars they triggered. READ MORE: Israel's president taps opposition candidate Eisenkot to form a government, in setback for Netanyahu "I hope with all my heart that whatever government is formed will lead to unity, connection and healing among all segments of our people — for our very existence depends on it, and we have only one country," Herzog said at the ceremony at the presidential residence in Jerusalem. The announcement doesn't guarantee that Eisenkot, a former army chief, will become the next prime minister. He has up to six weeks to form a coalition government by securing alliances, a daunting challenge because the Oct. 27 election gave neither his bloc nor Netanyahu's a clear majority in parliament. Herzog said that in consultations with the parties, a majority of members of parliament, known as the Knesset, supported giving Eisenkot this task. At Sunday's ceremony, Eisenkot promised to give the country leadership that people can trust, that will act in the interests of the public and that represents all parts of society. "An absolute majority of Knesset members representing the Israeli public support change," he said. "I intend to navigate the situation with patience, humility, composure and a deep commitment to a Jewish, equal, liberal, and secure Israel." Politically fraught coalition choices lie ahead Among the possible kingmakers — and most politically fraught potential allies — are the Arab-led parties. They made historic gains in the election thanks to high voter turnout among Israel's Arab citizens. Only one Arab party, Ra'am, has ever joined a governing coalition, in 2021. Ra'am has said it will support Eisenkot, but the party does not have enough seats on its own to give Eisenkot a parliamentary majority. Breaking with decades of precedent, the second Arab-led party, the Joint List, has offered to support Eisenkot from outside the coalition to end Netanyahu's grip on power. But that cooperation is fraught for both sides. For the Joint List, it would mean backing a government unlikely to end Israel's wars or curb settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. For Eisenkot and other opposition parties, it would mean aligning with parties that not only criticize Israel's policies but reject its identity as a Jewish state. READ MORE: Israel's president takes first steps on building new government after accepting election results One of Eisenkot's partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beytenu party, already has said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties. Eisenkot has laid out four conditions for parties that want to join him. They must recognize Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept its declaration of independence, support military, national or civil service for all citizens, and declare the Hamas militant group a terrorist group. It remains unclear whether his would-be Arab partners are ready to accept these conditions. Furthermore, Netanyahu has repeatedly asserted unsubstantiated claims that the election was "stolen" by Arab parties. In a pressure tactic on Eisenkot, he says any alliance with these parties would be an act of betrayal. Israel's Shin Bet security agency has launched an investigation into possible foreign interference in the vote, but the country's Central Elections Committee — and Herzog — say the vote was valid and even if wrongdoing is found, it did not have a significant impact on the electoral results. Eisenkot faces significant challenges on the road to becoming prime minister Eisenkot has vowed to form a government as quickly as possible. But each likely scenario appears to entail compromises or broken promises. Aside from seeking the support of the Arab-led parties, Eisenkot has two options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community. Eisenkot and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the long-standing draft exemptions. WATCH: What Israel's election deadlock means for Netanyahu and the region The religious parties, which were part of Netanyahu's outgoing coalition, want to preserve them, calling them essential to their devout lifestyle. But the exemptions have grown especially controversial among the broader public during the past three years of war. Anticipating its position as a swing vote, the ultra-Orthodox party United Torah Judaism has left the door open to cooperating with Eisenkot. Eisenkot has 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible two-week extension from the president. If he is unable to form a government, Netanyahu could then be given a chance to put together a coalition. If Netanyahu is also unable to do so, the country would return to elections early next spring. Israel's new members of Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday evening. Footage shows derailed carriages after fatal train crash in Egypt
A train collision has killed at least seven people and injured dozens in northern Egypt.
Footage showed multiple overturned carriages and dozens of people surrounding them.
One train was travelling from Giza to the Fayoum oasis, south west of Cairo, while the other was heading from Cairo to Aswan in the south.

- Published
Millions across India are celebrating Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.
The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.
Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.
But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.
Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.
Air pollution in the Indian capital Delhi has reached such hazardous levels that it is the most polluted Diwali festival in a decade. New measures to improve air quality do not seem to have been successful.
India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks.
In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.
These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are at reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.
Despite the debate over fireworks, Diwali is about much more than firecrackers.
The festival celebrates the return of Lord Ram to Ayodhya after his victory over Ravan, the main antagonist in the Hindu epic Ramayana, and symbolises the triumph of good over evil, light over darkness, and knowledge over ignorance.
In the days leading up to the festival, families clean and decorate their homes with flowers, colourful lights and traditional oil lamps known as diyas.
The celebrations also bring families and friends together for prayers, elaborate feasts and the exchange of gifts, and lots of traditional Indian sweets.
Colourful patterns known as rangoli are created at entrances to homes, while markets bustle with shoppers buying festive essentials beneath brightly lit decorations.
The celebrations began on 6 November with Dhanteras, when buying gold, silver or new utensils is considered auspicious and believed to bring good fortune.
The second day, known as Chhoti Diwali, or small Diwali, is marked by the lighting of oil lamps and, in some households, setting off firecrackers.
The third day is the main celebration, when families offer evening prayers to Lakshmi, the Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity, before gathering for festive meals and fireworks.
The fourth day is celebrated differently across India, with family gatherings and New Year festivities in some communities. The fifth and final day, known as Bhai Dooj, celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters.
The festival is also celebrated by Sikhs and Jains along with other important religious observances.
Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas, or Prisoner Release Day, commemorating the release of their sixth guru, Guru Hargobind, from imprisonment at Gwalior Fort in the early 17th Century.
For Jains, Diwali marks the attainment of moksha, or liberation from the cycle of rebirth, by Lord Mahavira, the 24th and last Tirthankara, or spiritual teacher, of the current era.
With Indian communities spread across the world, Diwali is also celebrated internationally, with families and friends coming together for festive gatherings and exchanging gifts.
The festival is considered an auspicious time to make new purchases, which many believe bring prosperity and good fortune. India's stock exchanges even hold a special one-hour trading session for investors who consider buying and selling shares on Diwali favourable. Known as Muhurat trading, it will take place on 8 November this year.
Although rooted in Hindu traditions, Diwali is celebrated by people across different faiths and communities.

Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media.
Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused of throwing Molotov cocktails and grenades, using bladed weapons and firearms, and setting fire to public facilities in the city of Karaj, west of Tehran, Iran's state news agency Tasnim, external reported.
The executions are the latest in a series linked to the protests, including those of people accused of having ties to Israel and the United States.
The number of executions in Iran has increased since US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic began in late February.
The protest movement initially sparked in December last year by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 of January.
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, and blamed the violence on "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the US and Israel.
However foreign-based NGOs gave higher figures and the BBC received multiple accounts from Iranians of security forces opening fire on unarmed protesters.
Tasnim reported that the three men were executed after the Supreme Court upheld their convictions and found them guilty of "participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups".
The damage allegedly included an electricity substation in Karaj which caused power outages in some areas.
Dioband was arrested on 11 January after investigations identified him as a suspect in attacks on public property and incitement to violence.
Ten others accused of taking part in the unrest under his supervision were later arrested.
Reuters news agency reports that they received prison terms of 5 to 10 years.
The latest executions in Iran come after the UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said he was alarmed by the rise in death penalties.
In August, TÃ¼rk said at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests.
Iran is thought to be the world's second-most prolific executioner after China. Last year, it put to death at least 2,159 people, according to Amnesty International.
The human rights group said that was the highest figure on record since 1981 and included 45 executions of suspected dissidents on national security-related charges.

362b11a3bad3.text: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani can't be president, so he's trying to be the next best thing: a progressive kingmaker for 2028. Mamdani has been meeting privately with union leaders, urgently talking up the need for a labor-aligned or leftist candidate to run for the White House, four people familiar with the talks told Axios. He's arguing that progressives can't afford to squander their midterm momentum. Why it matters: Behind closed doors, Mamdani has made a striking admission that helps explain why he's so eager to huddle with allies about 2028: He's uncertain whether New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, his close political partner, will launch a White House run, the sources said. If Ocasio-Cortez stays out of the 2028 race, it would upend the Democratic primary — and potentially leave the party's insurgent left without a candidate. Zoom in: Mamdani — who's ineligible to be president because he was born in Uganda — wants to coordinate with progressive leaders partly to prepare to unite against any leading centrist presidential contender they aren't happy with, according to one of the sources who has spoken with the mayor. Mamdani "wants the progressive ecosystem to mobilize quickly, strategically and efficiently if a moderate candidate is clearly on the rise," the person said, pointing to how former President Barack Obama appeared to help Joe Biden consolidate support against Bernie Sanders in 2020. Last month, Mamdani summoned the president of the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades, Jimmy Williams Jr., to Gracie Mansion to talk about 2028. Mamdani asked Williams which potential presidential candidates he liked and how his union's endorsement process would unfold. He also asked Williams whether he'd ever considered running for office, the sources said. The source who has spoken with Mamdani noted that the mayor recruited — and helped elect — several left-wing congressional candidates in New York this year. Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants-C.W.A, also met with Mamdani recently to discuss 2028 and other issues. The mayor plans to get together soon with yet another labor leader — Shawn Fain, president of the United Automobile Workers. Zoom out: Mamdani's efforts to influence the 2028 contest come as many progressives are growing anxious about the prospect of a presidential race without a left-wing contender. Many think Ocasio-Cortez is leaning toward a Senate bid in 2028 instead of a White House run. She's said she's considering both options. Some allies hope that progressives' success in battleground states in the midterms will encourage her to go for the White House. But Democrats of all political stripes won races in last week's nationwide rebuke of the Trump administration, so the postelection case for left-wingers in 2028 isn't necessarily stronger than it is for centrist Democrats. What they're saying: Williams, the IUPAT president, told Axios he's "absolutely supportive" of people from the labor movement running for office up and down the ballot. "We put a freaking ironworker in Congress. We put a IUPAT member in the Senate," he said, referring to Democrats who won in the midterms. But Williams said he's not interested in running for elected office. Spokespeople for Mamdani, Fain and Nelson did not comment. Asked by WNYC last month if he wants to see Ocasio-Cortez run for president, Mamdani said, "I want to see AOC do whatever it is that AOC wants to do" and called her "an inspiration." Between the lines: With Ocasio-Cortez's future a question mark, some progressives are beginning to look elsewhere for a presidential candidate. Some on the left hope Abdul El-Sayed, the incoming senator in Michigan, will take a look at 2028. Others are lining up behind California Rep. Ro Khanna, who's widely expected to run. Bhaskar Sunkara, a 2020 Sanders surrogate and president of the liberal publication The Nation, wrote an op-ed last summer calling for Ocasio-Cortez to run for president. More recently , he's been talking up the idea of a labor candidate. "Progressive ideas only win when working-class voters see themselves in the fight," he told Axios. "There's no better way to do that than to run an actual worker for president, not a professional politician." Williams, Nelson and Fain are widely seen as some of the most progressive labor leaders in the country. Fain is known for railing against billionaires, and Nelson joined Sanders' "Fighting Oligarchy" tour. Williams wrote in 2025 that he "was proud that my union was among the first to call for a ceasefire in Gaza." Some left-wing activists have encouraged Fain, whose union helped elect El-Sayed, to consider a presidential bid. But he told the Detroit News last month he has "no plans" to run.

Paraguayâs president was removed from office and detained after the countryâs largest digital bank melted down, leaving half the populace without access to funds and plunging the country into a political crisis.
A youth-friendly banking app, Ueno collapsed amid allegations of insider lending and proximity to the countryâs longtime ruling party, which is closely aligned with Washington.
The app was credited with expanding access in a region where as many as one in four adults does not have a bank account; its implosion was a âkind of tsunami in the end,â a political scientist said, and puts at stake âthe credibility of a country that has spent years trying to establish itself as a stable, reliable destination for international investment,â a regional analyst wrote in Americas Quarterly.

f9b91d609f86.text: By — Isabel DeBre, Associated Press Isabel DeBre, Associated Press By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-arrives-in-argentina-and-tells-milei-that-people-not-the-economy-should-come-first Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Leo arrives in Argentina and tells Milei that people, not the economy, should come first World Nov 8, 2026 5:42 PM EST BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV delivered a diplomatic but subtly strong critique of Argentine President Javier Milei's austerity measures and libertarian agenda as he arrived Sunday in Argentina, insisting that political leaders must put people, not the economy, first. Leo used his first public speech in Argentina to lay out a vision of governance, democracy and society sharply at odds with Milei's, exposing differences over spending cuts, social justice and artificial intelligence that the government had sought to play down ahead of the visit. "The economy must serve the person, not the person the economy," Leo told officials, diplomats and civic leaders upon his arrival in Buenos Aires from Uruguay. READ MORE: With an ode to mate, Pope Leo urges faithful in Uruguay to build bridges of fraternity and faith Leo's visit to Argentina is by far the most politically delicate of his three-nation South American tour, and a place where Leo will also confront the complicated legacy of Argentine Pope Francis, who never returned home during his 12-year pontificate. Milei, a self-described anarcho-capitalist, has staked his presidency on slashing public spending to tame inflation, while describing the notion of social justice as "a horror," a "moral aberration" and "theft" in recent speeches. Much like its allies in the Trump administration, Milei's government has portrayed the cuts as part of a necessary reform process to remake Argentina's troubled economy and eliminate fraud and waste in the federal bureaucracy. Ahead of Leo's arrival in Argentina, the first by a pope in nearly 40 years, Milei's officials had dismissed the prospect of a political clash. "There's no way the pope is coming here to comment on local politics," Human Capital Minister Sandra Pettovello said in an interview with a Buenos Aires radio station last week. In a message welcoming Leo, Milei said he hoped the trip would "strengthen the faith, renew hope and bring a message of peace to all Argentines." A call for civility in politics People hold a banner depicting Pope Leo as they await his visit to the Monument to General San Martin at Plaza San Martin during his 12-day trip to South America, on the first papal visit to Argentina since 1987, in Buenos Aires on Nov. 8, 2026. Photo by Matias Baglietto/Reuters Leo took up that message of peace, opening with a call for gentler politics in deeply polarized Argentina. Democracy depends on "careful use of words" and "the ability to see those who think differently as fellow citizens with whom we share a common future," he said. Milei's style is far more combative, costing him allies in Congress and public support. He posts dozens of times a day on social media, branding critics "traitors" and "human trash" and tagging posts #NOLSALP, a Spanish acronym for "We don't hate journalists enough." Milei, who once called Francis the "representative of evil on Earth," paid homage to the late pope in welcoming Leo on Sunday. Interrupted by applause, he called Francis an "exceptional figure" and "undoubtedly the most important Argentine in history" whose teachings continue to resonate. He also struck a rare conciliatory tone in welcoming politicians, diplomats and civil society representatives from across Argentina's ideological spectrum to Leo's ceremony. "There are causes and occasions that transcend our differences," he said. On the economy, Leo nodded to Milei's free-market instincts, urging Argentina to encourage "whatever creates opportunities" and "stimulates private initiative." But growth must also benefit "those who are disadvantaged," he said, including the unemployed, retirees and "all those who, despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household's needs." READ MORE: What to know about Pope Leo XIV's trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru Milei's austerity drive has produced a rare budget surplus and slashed annual inflation from 200% to about 32%. But real wages remain below where they were when he took office in late 2023, and roughly 300,000 formal jobs have vanished. Retirees who say they can't afford medicine on an average monthly pension of $510 have protested outside Congress every Wednesday for more than two years. Milei has mocked the widespread complaint that families can't make it to the end of the month as "huge stupidity." A missionary priest in Peru for two decades, Leo has embraced a pastoral style reminiscent of Francis, who as archbishop of Buenos Aires expanded the ranks of priests serving in the city's crime-ridden informal settlements. Leo laid out a Christian vision of democracy, authority and economic progress that ran counter to Milei's. But he couched the implicit rebuke by referencing the church's social doctrine and papal pronouncements spanning more than six decades, invoking St. John Paul II, the last pope to visit Argentina, in 1987, among others. That tradition also ran through Francis' papacy. His 2020 encyclical "Fratelli Tutti" criticized laissez-faire economics and defended social justice and workers' rights. Argentina's bishops, many of them appointed by Francis, have become some of Milei's most persistent critics. Of the 44 documents on public policy published by the country's bishops' conference between January 2024 and September 2026, 42 criticized Milei's administration, on issues from poverty to migration, according to an analysis by sociologist Sol Prieto from Argentina's national research council. Speaking to reporters after a Mass last month

- Published
US tech giant Nvidia has opened an independent investigation following reports its CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
The company, one of the most valuable in the world, said its board had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, adding that the CEO was committed to continuing to lead the company.
Separately, Jensen Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.
US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.
Jensen Huang said he took "full responsibility" for what he did, adding that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to Nvidia's employees, board and shareholders.
Nvidia is one of the world's largest companies and seen as central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, and Jensen Huang has been in charge of it for more than 30 years.
He said: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
His statement continued: "Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, Nvidia's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."
A separate statement issued by Nvidia's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
It continued: "The Board prioritises US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."
Jensen Huang rescued Nvidia from almost going broke on more than one occasion, and he took a punt on AI a long time before the rest of the world did.
His decision to make Nvidia chips, originally designed for gaming, become the best in the business for AI development, has now paid off in spades and the company is worth trillions.
This is a big blow for a man who is renowned for being a workaholic, a perfectionist and someone who expects incredibly high standards from his staff.
Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, is linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed.
The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation.
Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, providing chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.
The microchip manufacturer is worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever.
China has previously rejected allegations of an espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".
US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang â who is also known as Huang Le â allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
Last week, members of Congress wrote to Jensen Huang, asking him to appear before them in the light of the reported relationship.
Three House Republican committee leaders asked the CEO to appear later in the month, to talk about Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage" given his reported relationship with Alice Huang.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information.
"The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the letter said.
Nvidia's AI chips have been a major focus of the rivalry between the US and China, and Washington has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

bc3fd0826983.text:
Israelâs president tapped Gadi Eisenkot to try to form the countryâs next government, kicking off a tortuous negotiating process that could oust long-serving Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
While Eisenkot and Netanyahu differ in style and substance, both men reflect the âmonolithically anti-Palestinian stance that dominates Israeli politics,â an International Crisis Group expert told Le Monde.
There is also little âreal differenceâ between the two on Iran, an Israeli analyst said, though recent elections in the US and Israel have created further uncertainty around the simmering conflict: President Donald Trump said on Sunday that further US strikes were âhighly unlikely,â while Iran â which has taken credit for Republicansâ poor midterm showing â said negotiations were paused following the âshockâ election result.

5aae36239c40.text: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is positioning himself for a presidential run. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is running away from the idea of his own campaign for the White House. Why it matters: The political posturing of the two Florida Republicans — or the efforts to draft either for 2028 — underscores the sudden volatility of the way-too-early GOP preprimary campaign to succeed President Trump . Before Tuesday's midterm Republican wipeout, the party's 2028 primary looked like a relatively easy coronation for Vice President Vance (if he runs, as expected). Now there's a nascent movement to kneecap Vance and promote other possible opponents. Zoom in: As Trump's home base, Florida was bound to take center stage in the conversation. But two things distinguish Florida from other states: DeSantis and Rubio have national profiles rooted in their own prior presidential campaigns, in 2024 and 20216, respectively. Florida was the lone red-wall state that the national blue wave couldn't top, which DeSantis has been happy to emphasize repeatedly since Tuesday. "The alligator people are stirring," said one national Republican consultant with extensive Florida experience, referring to the Sunshine State's official reptile. Zoom out: The differences between DeSantis and Rubio are vast when it comes to their political futures and styles. DeSantis is hungry. Rubio isn't. DeSantis terms-out of the governor's office in January and is looking for work. He hasn't made an official decision on whether to run for president — but he has stoked speculation with a media blitz that began with an Election Day appearance on Stephen A. Smith's podcast. Rubio repeatedly has said he plans to stay put in the Trump administration and serve out the rest of his term, until January 2029. He also said in May that he wouldn't run against Vance, and hasn't changed his position publicly. The intrigue: During the somber election watch party at the White House on Tuesday night, Rubio's phone "blew up" with supporters urging him to reconsider running for president, according to a source familiar with the scene. "There was this sense of 'We lost the Latino vote , you can get it back, etc.,'" said the source. "To some people, Rubio seemed to entertain the idea for the first time. Or he didn't shut it down fast enough." Two days later, two publications reported that Rubio was actively considering resigning to lay the groundwork to run for president. Rubio denied it to the New York Times, and longtime associates of Rubio's told Axios that the reporting was bogus. "Now if Vance doesn't run or if POTUS tells him to step aside so Marco can run, does he? Maybe. I don't see that. But maybe," said one insider. That same night, Vance got feedback from one supporter who said he shouldn't run. And some GOP donors said they would back DeSantis, according to The Wall Street Journal. What's next: There's no debate about whether DeSantis is considering a bid. He is. DeSantis's postelection appearance on CNN with Jake Tapper was a sign he learned a lesson from his 2024 presidential campaign : Earning free media by sitting for more podcast and TV interviews is crucial. Asked whether he plans to run again, DeSantis wouldn't say. But he emphasized that "I haven't planned anything because I just think this is a very uncertain time. But last night should be a wakeup call for our party." "We really got blasted into oblivion," DeSantis added. "And Florida is kind of the last one standing."

13129d88ae3a.text: An unusual coalition wants to recruit outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie as the Libertarian Party's 2028 presidential nominee, betting that MAGA fractures can turn a third-party candidacy into a spoiler for the Republican nominee. Why it matters: Organizers see a fighter in Massie, a frequent critic of President Trump who pushed hard on releasing the Epstein files and lost a bitter primary rather than quietly walking away. Massie raised almost $10 million in the process and has a large online donor list and base. For his parting act in Congress, Massie is pushing an impeachment vote against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth . Driving the news: For months, Libertarian Party operatives and MAGA defectors have been privately and publicly encouraging Massie to run under a rebranded party. "Libertarian Jesus is Ron Paul, and one of our saints is Thomas Massie," Larry Sharpe, a perennial Libertarian candidate and longtime third-party operative, told Axios. Sharpe has spoken with Massie several times about a potential presidential run. Aside from playing GOP spoiler, organizers believe the Libertarian Party's existing ballot access and infrastructure could help them win 5% of the national vote — which would qualify its next presidential nominee for federal funding. Massie didn't respond to several requests for comment. The big picture: The plan is for libertarians to claim dibs on the "America First" agenda, mainly focusing on anti-war sentiment. Organizers believe they can build consensus among supporters of the MAGA wing that's closer to Tucker Carlson, former Trump official Joe Kent and former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.), as well as disillusioned "Make America Healthy Again" activists and populist-inclined voters on the right and left. "A party that would speak clearly about the disaster of the war in Iran, that would speak clearly about the mistake to continue to give military aid, taxpayer-funded military aid, to Israel — that would perk up a lot of ears among young people," said James Fishback, a former GOP gubernatorial candidate in Florida who met with the organizers in October. "The idea is if one can take 5, 10, 15% of the vote from one of these parties, then that party has to listen and cave to interest of the people," Bret Weinstein, a lead organizer of this effort, said on his podcast last week. Zoom in: LP operative Michael Heise, a leader and founder of the Mises Caucus, is a main organizer for this rebranded party. Heise's caucus took over the LP in 2022. The LP picks its presidential nominee at conventions by delegates voting on the floor. Those who bring the most delegates can take over a convention. Heise is also a skilled fundraiser — by third party standards. The Mises PAC, which is bankrolling this "draft Massie" operation, according to the website, raised $394,000 in 2024's election cycle. The PAC has previously received donations from Kimbal and Christina Musk, Elon's brother and sister-in-law; Abigail Rockefeller, a former Robert F. Kennedy Jr. campaign and Democratic-leaning donor; and Patricia Duggan, a MAGA Inc mega-donor and longtime LP contributor, according to FEC records. Heise declined to comment.

92ce6f25a384.text: By — Josh Boak, Associated Press Josh Boak, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/voters-demanded-economic-relief-trump-and-democrats-face-tough-choices-on-how-to-deliver Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Voters demanded economic relief. Trump and Democrats face tough choices on how to deliver Economy Nov 8, 2026 4:59 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Voters have sent a strong election-year message to the new Democratic congressional majority and President Donald Trump: Repair the damage inflation has done to the economy. Trump, who campaigned on the idea that a Democratic victory in the midterms would trigger a 1929-style economic depression, has maintained that the economy is booming. Since his party lost in Tuesday's voting, he has claimed he is willing to work with Democrats in the House and Senate, though that's not something he has done much of in the past. "I'll get along, probably, with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive," Trump told reporters last week. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. After Friday's strong jobs report showed employers adding 165,000 jobs and the unemployment rate dipping to 4.1%, Trump was defiant. "Democrats may control Congress, but I will NEVER stop fighting for you, and I will VETO anything that hurts America," he said in a text message to his supporters. Democrats are seeking to check Trump's power and are preparing for early fights on government spending. Other challenges include chronic budget deficits, tariffs, artificial intelligence and difficult choices about a Social Security system that could run short of money in as little as six years. But as long as rising prices keep making middle-class lives less affordable, Democrats and Republicans alike face the risk of angering and alienating voters in the next election cycle. "Until inflation and interest rates are under control, the likelihood of change elections is going to be high on an ongoing basis," said Marc Goldwein, senior vice president at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. Americans want lower prices Trump's tariffs and the war against Iran that he launched in February contributed to the consumer price index climbing to 3.7% annually. The president also tried to bully the Federal Reserve, an independent body tasked with keeping inflation low, to slash its benchmark interest rate in ways that could have worsened inflation. The gridlock of a Republican White House and Democratic Congress gives the Fed more room to maneuver, possibly smoothing the central bank's ability to return inflation to the 2% target it has failed to reach for nearly six years. "I think that one of the surprise winners Tuesday was the Fed," said Douglas Holtz-Eakin, an economist and president of the center-right American Action Forum. READ MORE: AP Voter Poll: The economy and the state of democracy are voters' top issues The Democratic Senate could block Trump's ability to fill potentially open spots on the Fed board, Holtz-Eakin said, removing "Trump's incentives to meddle with the Fed" and clearing a path for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh "to follow his instincts and aggressively reduce inflation." Trump has maintained that the costs of oil, gasoline and diesel will all plummet once the Iran war ends. The problem is he refuses to say when or how the war will come to a conclusion. John Cochrane, an economist at Stanford University's Hoover Institution, stressed that the Fed's efforts to combat inflation would be helped if the federal government reduced budget deficits. "It takes monetary and fiscal restraint," he said. The federal government keeps borrowing about $2 trillion annually The U.S. government keeps amassing debt as tax revenues fall short of burgeoning spending on Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security and other programs. Paying the interest on the national debt now tops $1 trillion annually and exceeds spending on the military. The problem could spiral because investors have pushed up the interest rates charged on government debt over the past year. Neither the White House nor Democrats ran on spending cuts. The president wants an additional $500 billion a year for the military, while some Democratic candidates have pushed for restoring Affordable Care Act subsidies that lapsed under Trump. WATCH: What to know about a better-than-expected jobs report amid AI bubble concerns Since August, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has repeatedly said the administration would put forward a plan to trim the roughly $2 trillion annual budget deficit. Bessent is working with White House budget director Russell Vought on cuts they're branding as a "fiscal consolidation plan," to be released after the election. Deficit reduction would likely require some combination of tax increases and spending cuts, Goldwein said. But he said that the lowest hanging fruit would be to trim Medicare expenditures in ways that save money for both the government and patients. "It's not rocket science," he said. "The most important thing you can do is reduce healthcare costs and find policies that lower the costs of Medicare, which will reduce deficits and interest rates." AI could power stronger growth, but voters have concerns about the technology When Harvard University economist Jason Furman thinks about the most important economic issues facing the United States, AI is at the top of his list. "It's the most screamingly obvious investment boom this country has ever had, or, possibly, second to railroads" in the late 19th century, Furman said. Using AI, Furman has built an economic analysis tool called Econvitals that replicates some of the work done when he was chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers in Democratic President Barack Obama's administrat

1c2c792f9e67.text: By — Savannah Peters, Associated Press Savannah Peters, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/native-american-women-made-history-in-tribal-state-and-federal-elections Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Native American women made history in tribal, state and federal elections Politics Nov 8, 2026 4:15 PM EST ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — A third-grade field trip to the Navajo Nation Council sparked Crystalyne Curley's political ambition when she witnessed a fiery debate erupt between two tribal lawmakers. "I thought to myself at a very young age, that's where I want to be," Curley said. On Election Day, Curley surpassed that childhood dream and broke a barrier she says she never imagined as a nine-year-old: She was elected the first woman president of the Navajo Nation. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. This week's elections brought a wave of milestone victories, from the nation's first Black female governor to the first openly gay man and first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. It also marked a turning point for Native American women, whose leadership in their families and communities has rarely translated to formal political power. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the Senate, Deb Haaland the first to win a state governorship, and Curley the first to lead one of the largest tribes. "This is a win for all Navajo women," Curley told The Associated Press. Jordan James Harvill, a Cherokee Nation citizen and strategist with the advocacy group Advance Native Political Leadership, said decades of political organizing are bearing fruit as more Native women run for and win office. "This is a seismic shift that is happening in our communities," he said. The Navajo Nation elects its first woman president Lene Bitsui supported Curley in the Navajo Nation election because she felt she was best positioned to restore order to the tribal government after what she sees as a period of dysfunction. But when Bitsui cast her ballot, she felt pessimistic. "I thought our people weren't ready for a female president," Bitsui said. "I was wrong, and I feel so happy to have been wrong." The modern, centralized Navajo government has been led by men since its establishment under federal pressure over a century ago. Navajo has the largest land base of any federally recognized tribe, spanning 27,000 square miles (70,000 square kilometers) in Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, and is second in population to the Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma. Some Navajo people believe traditional teachings prohibit women from holding top government positions. Others say women's absence from the presidency stands in contrast to the matrilineal structure of Diné society. READ MORE: The election brought a wave of historic firsts. Here are some groundbreaking winners "You see the language of tradition used to both deride the possibility of a woman being president and to say that women's leadership is needed now," said Jennifer Nez Denetdale, a professor of Diné studies at the University of New Mexico. Curley, who narrowly defeated attorney Justin Jones, according to unofficial results, told the AP she faced sexist rhetoric while campaigning and expects to be held to a higher standard as the first woman president. "As women, we have to work twice or triple as hard, especially within Navajo politics," said Curley, who also was the first female to lead the tribe's legislative branch as speaker of the tribal council. After Curley and her running mate Chris Deschene take office in January, they plan to transition the Navajo Nation away from coal development, historically a major economic engine for the tribe, and reassert its leading role in national discussions around federal Indian policy. The Seneca Nation of Indians in western New York also elected its first woman president, longtime council member Tina Abrams, on Tuesday. Native women make gains in U.S. Congress At her Senate victory celebration in St. Paul, Minnesota, Democrat Flanagan, a citizen of the White Earth Nation and the state's outgoing lieutenant governor, credited supporters from her community. "I could not run for the U. S. Senate without Native women. I could not exist in the way that I do without Native women," Flanagan said. More than 230 years after the U.S. Senate was established, only four Native people have served in the chamber, all men. "This is a win that shows we can break every single glass ceiling," Harvill said. Live Results: Peggy Flanagan wins Senate election in Minnesota Flanagan will join Oklahoma Republican Sen. Tom Cole, a citizen of the Chickasaw Nation. A victory for Democrat Mary Peltola, a Yup'ik woman, in Alaska's still unsettled Senate race, would mark the first time three Native people have served in the chamber simultaneously. In the House, Kansas Democrat Sharice Davids, Ho-Chunk, and Oklahoma Republican Josh Brecheen, Choctaw, won reelection. New York Democrat Claire Valdez, a citizen of Ysleta del Sur Pueblo, and Michigan Democrat Sean McCann, a citizen of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, became the first Native Americans elected to represent their states in Congress. Deb Haaland notches another first in New Mexico Haaland's political career has been defined by historic milestones. She was one of the first two Native women elected to Congress in 2018 before becoming the first Native American to lead a U.S. Cabinet agency, the Interior Department. Now, in her home state of New Mexico, the Laguna Pueblo citizen, will break ground as the first female Native governor of a U.S. state. "I think it's a long time coming," said Haaland, who traces her ancestry in what is now New Mexico back 800 years. WATCH: New Mexico's Deb Haaland on making history as first Native

008e2f0c0e07.text: Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday dismissed former Trump health adviser Calley Means' corruption allegations against senior White House officials, even as a former FDA commissioner described pressure from tobacco lobbyists and a Republican congressman called for scrutiny. Why it matters: The feud inside President Trump's coalition raises a central question about Trump's health agenda: Were his advisers undermining it, as Means alleges, or were they carrying out the president's wishes? The latest: Asked on CNN's "State of the Union" whether the DOJ would investigate Means' allegations, Blanche responded: "Something that someone says on a podcast? No, I do not listen to that. Absolutely not." Blanche called Means a "disgruntled former administration official" and praised former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles , who Trump announced Friday would be replaced by Stephen Miller . On "Fox News Sunday," Blanche said allegations about Wiles' financial dealings did not concern him. But Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) told CNN that "any allegation of any impropriety like this should be looked at." Driving the news: Means, who alleged widespread corruption in a Friday interview with Joe Rogan, told CBS' "Face the Nation" that he had wanted Wiles removed. Means accused Wiles of blocking an initiative to examine children's sugar consumption because she wanted sugar-industry donations for the midterms. He also alleged that Wiles' deputies pushed policies favorable to the flavored-vaping and kratom industries over the objections of officials working on the Make America Healthy Again agenda. Means accused Trump pollster Tony Fabrizio of advising against defining ultra-processed foods while receiving money from PepsiCo. The White House and the Justice Department did not respond to Axios' request for comment. What they're saying: Former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary backed up part of Means' account in a statement to CBS. "Big tobacco exploited their connections to administration and HHS officials," Makary said, alleging repeated pressure to approve fruit-flavored vapes. Makary said kratom lobbyists similarly tried to undermine his attempts to restrict the substances. He did not identify which officials pressured him. The other side: Former White House adviser James Blair, one of Wiles' allies that Means has accused of wrongdoing, disputed Means' allegations in messages to Axios. "I didn't promote flavored vaping specifically at all," Blair said, adding that he never weighed in on individual applications or which flavors should be approved. Blair said he was following Trump's instructions to ensure the FDA made timely decisions on applications, whether approving or denying them. "The voters elected President Trump. Not me, and not Calley Means," Blair told Axios. He said he never dealt with kratom policy and is reviewing his legal options. When speaking to Axios, Fabrizio called Means' allegation that he was "in the pocket of Big Pharma" "ridiculous" and "demonstrably false," citing his firm's polling showing support for lower prescription drug prices and policies that would cut into pharmaceutical profits. Fabrizio also said he encouraged Republican lawmakers to campaign on Trump's "most favored nation" drug-pricing proposal. In a statement on X, the lobbying firm Ballard Partners took exception to Means' "false" accusations about its interactions with Wiles, who had worked at the company seven years ago. Ballard Partners said it did not lobby Wiles or anyone in the White House on fruit-flavored vapes or another issue Means mentioned, glyphosate, the active ingredient in the weedkiller Roundup, owned by Bayer. In February, Trump outraged MAHA activists by signing an executive order to grant "immunity" to glyphosate producers as Bayer struggled under the weight of lawsuits over roundup. In June, the Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that federal law preempts state lawsuits concerning pesticide sales, thereby making it tougher for people to sue for cancer claims regarding Roundup use. Between the lines: Means has portrayed Trump as unaware of decisions his advisers made. But the Wall Street Journal reported in May that Trump personally pressured Makary to approve flavored vaping products. Pressed by CBS' Margaret Brennan, Means said he did not know whether Trump had called Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. after meeting with tobacco-industry representatives. Means argued advisers manipulated what reached the president and invoked Trump's authority to advance their own priorities. Blair rejected that characterization, telling Axios: "In the White House, I implemented the President's agenda always." Editor's note: This story has been updated with a statement from Ballard Partners.

Jeffries also said he supports a pending resolution from Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Hegseth in a video dismissed the impeachment push as "all about the politics of personal destruction." He said it "won't work with me." New senators express skepticism about Schumer At least two new incoming Democratic senators expressed some reservations Sunday about Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who's expected to be reelected to his post after leading his party back to the majority. US President Donald Trump's administration has vowed not to change course on its mass deportation plans after last week's midterm elections defeat.
"This administration will not slow down its efforts to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens who terrorise our communities," the White House said in a statement to the BBC.
Trump's promotion on Friday of immigration hawk Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff had signalled no climbdown from the administration on border security.
Exit polls indicate immigration was the third most important issue for midterm voters, after the economy and the state of democracy.
In historically conservative states like Texas, a swing of Latino voters towards Democrats helped seal the party's landslide congressional majorities.
But multiple US officials sources told the BBC's US partner CBS that the administration had put the midterm losses down to concerns about the economy, affordability and the war with Iran, rather than its immigration crackdown.
The White House maintained on Sunday there would be no change of direction.
"There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) also said it would forge ahead.
"ICE is NOT backing away or slowing down," a DHS spokesperson told CBS.
"Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS will continue to enforce our nation's laws and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets."
Following Tuesday's results, Vice-President JD Vance had appeared receptive to adjusting their immigration strategy.
"I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement - by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labour, for instance," Vance wrote in a lengthy online post reflecting on the results.
But the White House's posture appears to have hardened after Trump promoted Stephen Miller on Friday to become his new chief of staff.
Miller is widely seen as the architect of the administration's hardline immigration policy during the first and second Trump presidencies.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sources told CBS that in recent weeks officials have been instructed to aim for about 2,700 arrests of illegal immigrants per day, an increase from an earlier 2,000 daily arrest target.
Enforcement sweeps this year spurred anti-ICE demonstrations in cities including Chicago, Minneapolis and Los Angeles.
In Minneapolis, two US protesters, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were fatally shot by immigration agents.

49d818d3e602.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy in a message to his company. The big picture: The company's board launched an independent investigation into reports that he was targeted by Chinese intelligence. Driving the news: "I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang wrote in a draft email to Nvidia employees obtained by Axios. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did." Huang said he took "full responsibility" for his actions, adding that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to Nvidia's employees, board and shareholders. "Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life," Huang wrote. "I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence." Meanwhile: Nvidia's board said an independent committee, assisted by outside counsel, will investigate the matter. The board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised and expressed confidence in Huang's leadership. Flashback: Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned top Trump officials about Huang's relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believed was a Chinese spy, The New York Times reported Friday. The woman, Alice Huang, was recruited to seek information and potentially push for Nvidia's advanced chips to be made available in China, countering existing restrictions, the Times reported. What they're saying: "Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," John Rizzo, head of public policy communications at Nvidia said in a statement.

ff03caaaf5f2.text: By — Rafal Niedzielski, Associated Press Rafal Niedzielski, Associated Press By — Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press By — Beata Zawrzel, Associated Press Beata Zawrzel, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/poles-mourn-rare-mass-killing-as-authorities-say-attacker-had-far-right-views Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Poles mourn rare mass killing as authorities say attacker had far-right views World Updated on Nov 8, 2026 5:14 PM EST — Published on Nov 8, 2026 3:02 PM EST KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — Mourners on Sunday laid candles and flowers alongside bullet holes in Krakow, Poland, after the city's central square turned into a site of bloodshed and grief. A 24-year-old man with far-right views opened fire a day earlier, killing six people and wounding 15 before police shot and wounded him. Poland on Sunday began two days of national mourning following the attack the day before, which Poland's defense minister described as an "act of terror." The violence began Saturday at around 3 p.m. when the assailant drove through the Main Square, in the heart of Krakow's Old Town. The square is a major tourist hub in the country's second-largest city. READ MORE: Gunman opens fire in Polish city of Krakow, killing 6 people and wounding 16 St. Mary's Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody played every hour from the highest tower of St. Mary's Basilica on the Main Square, was paused overnight, the first time the call had been missed since World War II. On Sunday afternoon, St. Anne's Church in Krakow filled with mourners attending a memorial service. The square reopened soon after and locals and visitors alike showed up to reclaim it after the tragedy. "I come here so as not to get caught up in a spiral of fear and anxiety," Krakow local Maciej Sikorski told The Associated Press from the square. "In a situation like this, it's all too easy to stop living — to start being afraid instead, and just vegetate. That is something I really want to avoid." Authorities also found the bodies of the assailant's sister, mother and father at the man's family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds. Woman injured by shrapnel while saving another Witness Andy Hill told the BBC that he'd felt as though he was in a movie scene. "It doesn't feel real," the British tourist said. "And the trouble is, you have such an instantaneous moment to make a decision: Run. Stand still. There's an element of shock. But I just thought the easiest thing to do is dive through a doorway and just take refuge behind the windows." Warsaw native Magdalena Frączak, meanwhile, was visiting Krakow with her friend when shots rang out and the gunman drew closer. "I threw an elderly woman behind the flower planter because she had become tangled in the blanket she had on her lap. I covered her with my body," Frączak told the AP. "I also saw him out of the corner of my eye — he passed just one meter behind my back. That's why I have shrapnel wounds in six places on my back. Only after he had passed did I pull the woman up, and we ran into a café." People gather by a makeshift memorial in the Main Market Square as authorities reopen the area to the public following the Saturday mass shooting in Krakow, Poland, on Nov. 8, 2026. Photo by Jakub Porzycki/Reuters On Sunday, she forced herself to return to the Main Square to grieve among other mourners. "I can't put it into words. Because I knew that I would never come back to Krakow if I didn't come in here," she said. "When I found out that they had reopened the Main Market Square, I told my friend that I had to come here." American tourist Marylin Green mourned the losses in the "beautiful city" during her first trip to Poland that also included the capital. "I'm Polish, my parents were from here," she said. "I loved Warsaw. So I was really looking forward to coming here, too." Police officers described as heroes Prosecutors said Sunday they opened an investigation into the murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, with the act "constituting a terrorist offense." Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday. A man from the U.K. and a woman from Austria were also among the dead. A video posted on social media showed a police officer repeatedly shooting the attacker, who was lying on the street. The officer later slowly collapsed to the ground. The two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities hailed as heroic, remain in the hospital. They were both conscious by Sunday afternoon. "If it weren't for the efficient and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher," Klęczar said. Michał Pędziwiatr and Mateusz Wierdak, two local surgeons who were having a bite to eat nearby, also stepped in. WATCH: Ukrainian refugees face growing hostility in Poland Wierdak "took care of the officer who subdued the attacker because he truly needed urgent help," Pędziwiatr told the Polish news website onet. "Without protection, without gloves, he simply focused on the officer, stopping the bleeding in his chest. This probably saved his life." Five foreigners are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria. The suspect is also in critical condition after undergoing multiple surgeries. There was confusion on Saturday about his age, with authorities first saying 24 and later 25. On Sunday they confirmed that he is 24. The suspect's dead sibling was a young artist studying at the Krakow Academy of Fine Arts. "Nothing will ever be like before. A print by a Yorkshire artist commissioned by Nasa in the early days of space travel will go on show as part of a pop art exhibition.
Komtek I by Michael Fossick, who studied at Bradford School of Art, was created in 1962 to celebrate a Hong Kong company that produced microcomputers in the early days of space travel.
The print was part of a Nasa project to document the effort of sending the first humans to the moon and is on display as part of the Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition.
The display tells the story of the British International Print Biennale, which took place at the Bradford gallery on 11 occasions between 1968 and 1990, and runs until March 2027.
While the exhibition also includes work by Andy Warhol and David Hockney, there is "definitely stuff that people won't have seen before", said curator Jill Iredale.
"It's a completely bizarre sort of connection somehow that an artist born in Sheffield that went to Bradford School of Art was somehow commissioned by Nasa," said Iredale.
"It was actually a screen print, but it was made from a very early computerised image," she said.
In March 1962, Nasa administrator James Webb awarded commissions to 38 artists, including Fossick, to document the space agency's achievements.
John H. Glenn became the first American to orbit the earth on 20 February 1962 and in the following decade Nasa's Mercury programme led to the Apollo missions, and eventually to Neil Armstrong setting foot on the moon in 1969.
Fossick chose to honour Komtek I, a microcomputer produced by Komtek Technologies Ltd in Hong Kong that was significant in the early years of the space programme.
He submitted the print to the First British International Print Biennale held at Cartwright Hall in 1968 where it won a prize.
Created by a group of local print makers and artists, at its height the British International Print Biennale included more than 500 works selected from more than 3,000 entries.
It received work by artists such as Andy Warhol, Roy Licthenstein and David Hockney, which remain in the gallery today.
Hockney was invited to be a judge on the first biennial in 1968 and created the poster for the show, which is on display in the exhibition.
Iredale said the pop art explosion in Bradford was a reaction to the seriousness of the World War Two and the boost in commercial print culture.
"Bradford had quite a strong, experimental kind of light, pretty kind of DIY aesthetic with artists and with the college as well," she explained.
"There was simply loads more young people around, post-baby boom, and an increase in opportunities for working-class youth."
