House Republicans will see a post-election reshuffling this week, with every senior rung of their leadership facing competition â and President Donald Trump is staying out of it.
Reps. Jim Jordan of Ohio and current Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana are vying for minority leader. Current Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota and Rep. August Pfluger of Texas are competing for next Congressâ GOP minority whip spot, while current Conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan faces challenges from Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida.
After their massive Election Day losses, some GOP lawmakers are inclined to fully overhaul their leadership. Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., whoâs backing Jordan, told Semafor: âI think we need to tell the American people, âWe heard you loud and clear. Youâre frustrated, and we need new leadership.ââ
As Republicans look for ways to claw their way out of the hole that the midterms left them in, theyâll also be deciding on a new campaign chief.
Reps. Rudy Yakym of Indiana and Brian Jack of Georgia are running to chair the National Republican Congressional Committee. Notably, neither are seen as interested in carving out distance from Trump.
Democrats will start their leadership elections next week, though Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries isnât expected to face any serious challenges to becoming speaker.
Thereâs not much legislative action yet in the lame-duck session, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will be impeached by the House this week. Though his conviction in the Senate is unlikely, it will be a critical moment for House Democrats to show unity heading into their takeover of the chamber.
Jeffries said he was a âhard yesâ on Hegseth impeachment on ABCâs This Week. With House Republicans looking for a scapegoat after their midterm losses, the impeachment vote could pick up votes on the right, too.
Rep. French Hill, R-Ark., said on CBSâ Face the Nation that he would âwant to hear the debate on it, to see if it merits impeachment or some other disciplinary action or some other action by the president,â adding that he was dissatisfied with how the Iran war has been handled.
House Republican leaders will also face attendance problems post-midterms that are likely to complicate prospects for any other lame-duck legislative action.

Congressâ lame-duck session starts with a bang on Monday, as Senate Republicans debate their future after last weekâs shellacking and Democrats face their first vote on a permitting reform bill that is cleaving them.
On the first front, Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., is expected to deliver Senate Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark., a letter on Monday with the requisite five signatures needed to force a special conference meeting. That wonât delay Majority Leader John Thuneâs leadership election, nor will it block Thuneâs bid to helm the conference in the minority, but it will force a debate about party leadership â and there may eventually be a vote on whether to delay the leadership election.
Meanwhile, the Senate will take a procedural vote on the permitting reform bill this evening, and itâs looking likely to advance despite opposition from some environmental groups. Democrats are seeking more changes to the bill, but many in the party think itâs the right time to move permitting legislation that has now stalled for multiple Congresses.
Two climate hawks, Sens. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., are both publicly pushing to pass the bill in the lame duck, and Democrats often trust their ranking members to cut a good deal. The bill will take probably a couple weeks to pass in the Senate if it advances.
Barring a delay, Senate Republican leadership elections are scheduled to take place at 9 am on Tuesday; in 2022, Republicans squashed a similar delay tactic.
This time around, some Republicans, like Utah Sen. Mike Lee, say they need a plan on how the lame duck will play out before deciding on their leadership votes. Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who has run twice for leader, wants a commitment to pass the GOPâs voter ID legislation. Even swing-state Sen. David McCormick, R-Pa., endorsed a pause to digest and debate what happened.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumerâs day in the spotlight will come, but not for a few weeks: Democratic leadership elections will happen in early December.

Ambily Banerjee moved to Langley, in the borough of Slough, 18 miles west of London, for its good schools and green spaces.
Now, Microsoft is planning to move in nearby. Its proposed 140-megawatt data center, the company promises, will be a good neighbor.
It is the latest operator drawn to Slough for its fast fiber-optic connections to London and to major transatlantic subsea cables farther west, as well as its proximity to, but geographic separation from, the capital, offering security should London’s data infrastructure be compromised.
The borough is home to 40-plus data centers, with more in the pipeline, earning it a reputation as Europe’s data-center capital and placing its cluster among the largest in the world.
Recently, residents like Banerjee have begun to push back, questioning not only what the data-center boom has brought to the borough, but what its longer-term costs might be.
“Where is this supposed investment? Slough has not become Silicon Valley,” said Banerjee, a scientist and mother. “Residents shoulder all the risk, while developers sit in their ivory towers.”
Those questions are being asked far beyond Slough, and have increasingly found their way into electoral politics. In the 2026 U.S. midterms, opposition to the facilities helped Democrats make massive gains. Some 56 percent of voters said data centers were a major or crucial factor in their congressional choices, according to polling by The Wall Street Journal, even as the industry poured mammoth sums into defending its interests.
The British government has played a more direct coordinating role in data center development than its U.S. federal counterpart, giving projects greater weight in the planning system, incentivizing development in designated areas and accelerating planning decisions and grid access for developers that demonstrate specific public benefits.
It remains to be seen what electoral consequences the incumbent Labour Party’s approach will carry. The party, characterized as center-left and sharing similarities with the Democrats, has set out to triple its data center capacity by the decade’s end, dismissing the Green Party’s proposed moratorium, warning it “would be a disaster for jobs and national security.”
Its efforts to manage the industry’s expansion have also been accompanied by significant gaps in oversight, particularly around energy demand and environmental issues.
An investigation by Spotlight on Corruption, a nonprofit that advocates for government transparency, found that ministers and officials had consulted 137 businesses on data center expansion, but just two community groups and no environmental organizations. Government estimates of the sector’s energy demands have also differed by as much as tenfold, according to The Guardian.
Public confidence in how that expansion will be managed appears fragile. With 84 percent of Britons believing the government will “prioritize its partnerships with large technology companies over the public interest” when regulating AI, and sizable campaigns opposing development emerging in Devon, Scotland, Essex and London’s Brick Lane, the prospect of opposition derailing the industry’s expansion is not merely theoretical.
A report by the Sovereign AI Leadership (SAIL) taskforce, drawing on input from the likes of Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco, warned that organized local opposition in the U.S. has already halted fully permitted data center projects, prompting moratoriums even in states otherwise supportive of development.
“Britain has a window—we think of roughly 12 months—to build a compact that earns public consent before that pattern takes hold,” the report said.
Britain’s Plan to Power the AI Boom
The U.K. is the third-largest AI market in the world after the U.S. and China. There are around 500 data centers across the U.K. Up to the end of 2025, around 90 percent were sited in England, with London alone accounting for nearly two-thirds of the national total.
The question of who benefits and who bears the cost took on new significance in Chancellor John Healey’s Oct. 28 budget, which announced a new British Data Centre Covenant. For developers, it set out a clear offer: faster, more certain access to grid connection in exchange for a “credible” commitment that they will not over-reserve, but will use and pay for the grid capacity they request, invest in clean power and net zero, deliver benefits for local residents and businesses and adhere to the “highest” environmental standards.
This comes amid Britain’s growing grid-connectivity problems, which have left some developers waiting years for access, and others forced to abandon projects altogether.
The connections queue, historically operated on a first-come, first-served basis, has become choked with speculative or unviable projects. Microsoft recently withdrew from a flagship data center project in Essex, developed by British startup Nscale, after it became clear it would not be connected to the grid until the 2030s.
There are 315 hyperscale data center projects awaiting access to the national grid, accounting for 73 GW of Britain’s demand connection queue, according to Ofgem, the U.K.’s energy regulator. Peak national demand in 2025 was around 45 GW.
The government is also trying to steer where facilities are built through its AI Growth Zones program, designed to attract investment to locations where data centers can more readily access power. In the past year, five such zones have been announced.
At times, regions generate more power than the grid can transmit elsewhere. Scotland, for example, can produce more wind power than its transmission lines can carry south. The government argues that locating data centers in such areas would allow them to absorb this otherwise-wasted generation, reducing costs across the electricity system. - Published
US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.
"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.
Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
The revelations knocked about $250bn (Â£190bn) off the value of Nvidia during trading on Monday as the firm's share price fell by more than 4%.
Trump later told reporters at the White House that the FBI was now looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the probe or when it was launched. The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia, the company at the centre at the development of AI worldwide through its microchips. She is not related to the Nvidia chief.
Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.
The American firm, co-founded by Huang, is also a major focus in the AI rivalry between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating the company's exports to Beijing as a matter of national security.
Huang and Nvidia were also sued on Monday in a proposed class action lawsuit in California accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing the chief executive's ties with a suspected Chinese spy.
The lawsuit alleges that the firm lied to the media about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.
'He said he had no idea she was a spy'
At the White House, Trump was asked multiple times, including by the BBC, when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.
Trump said he thought Huang was an "honorable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.
"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president said.
He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".
Nvidia designs advanced computer chips that power AI models and is at the centre of the US and China's technology race - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked national security fears.
Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.
The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.
Huang has admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.
He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched.
Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.
In the letter, the chairmen of the committees said they were seeking a briefing "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".
It is unclear whether Huang will appear. Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees.
Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.
It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today.
Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.
But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.
Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”
For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.
By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.
If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.
The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.
It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

The News
Fresh off what one senator called a âgood old-fashioned shellacking,â Republicans are now turning to a more painful phase of their post-election soul-searching: the airing of grievances.
Several senators are unhappy about a rush to reelect the GOPâs Senate leadership team after voters repudiated the partyâs reign in Washington. A small but vocal minority is pushing to delay leadership elections beyond Tuesday, giving more time for a potential challenger to emerge against Majority Leader John Thune and his team.
Thuneâs allies say the move is unnecessary, wonât change the result, and will only lead to more intraparty fighting after an election that could cost the Senate GOP as many as nine seats. Either way, the partyâs second-guessing of Thune and President Donald Trump â not to mention its uncertainty about its own agenda â will come to a head on Tuesday morning in the Old Senate Chamber.
âI saw five signatures on a letter,â Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., told Semafor of his colleagues advocating for a delay. âI think we have to talk, but I donât see why weâd need to change the leadership to do that.â
Beneath the procedural battle are huge debates within the Republican Party about where to turn next. A party that did little to defy Trumpâs unpopular war with Iran and his tariffs now must figure out what strategic adjustments to make â or, perhaps, whether to make none at all.
Cramer blamed the stunning losses on âbad negotiations with Canada, tariffs, not supporting Ukraine enough to end the warâ and allowing more foreign beef into the US. He said âpeople who are overly surprisedâ by the election result âprobably arenât being honest with themselves.â
Retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, who dubbed it a âshellacking,â said the âwar in Iran is extremely unpopular. I donât know what the secretary is briefing the president [on], but itâs not working.â
âWe need to have a tough, family conversation. We just lost seven Senate seats. And there may be more,â said Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo. âI see a lot of blame shifting going on in all of these postmortems. I think itâs probably time for people in Congress to take responsibility for what Congress did.â
Hawley cited Medicaid cuts, the GOPâs closeness to data centers, its turn away from anti-abortion priorities, and its move to âabandonâ poor people and the working class. He said he couldnât pledge his vote to Thune or the rest of the leadership team right now.
Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the effort to delay the leadership election, was even more harsh: âAfter that stunning defeat, we just canât continue on business as usual. I mean â¦ that kind of defeat demands change.â
âYou canât come off a defeat like that and just ram through elections and just elect that leadership team by acclamation,â Johnson said. âItâs obnoxious, particularly at this moment.â
Trump said on Monday that itâs up to the GOP senators to make a call on Thune, calling him a âvery fine manâ but lamenting that he wishes âthey could get more produced.â Thune said he didnât see how delaying the election âsolves anythingâ but agreed the GOP needs to discuss its future.
âJust move forwardâ
Johnsonâs bid to delay the leadership elections means that before taking any votes on them, the GOP will have a special conference meeting beginning at 9 a.m. on Tuesday.
They will then vote on whether to delay the elections of Thune and the rest of the leadership team, which includes Whip John Barrasso of Wyoming; Conference Chair Tom Cotton of Arkansas; Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., the policy chair; and Conference Vice Chair James Lankford of Oklahoma. The GOP is also expected to select Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, a top ally of Trump, as its new campaign chair.
A similar delay bid failed in 2022 after the GOP lost one Senate seat. Though the losses this month are several magnitudes greater, several Republican senators said they donât expect the vote to prevail. Some think the effort to delay is merely a smokescreen to undercut Thune.
âThis is a question that will come up tomorrow: If thereâs a desire for a leadership change, then letâs make the leadership change. I donât sense that, and so I think we ought to just move forward as planned. Weâll have a vote, the majority will rule,â Capito told Semafor.
She said the election was a wakeup call for Republicans to take Americansâ concerns about rising prices more seriously: âMessage received.â
That doesnât mean it will necessarily translate into a binding bipartisan effort to end Trumpâs tariffs or wind down the Iran war. And for either idea to clear the Senate, the GOPâs votes will be required â even with what could be a brawny 56-seat Democratic majority in the Senate and a House majority in the 250s, Trump can still wield the veto pen.
âUltimately, I think the lesson is: We needed senators to act in a more independent fashion. But even Susan Collins â who was very independent â didnât survive it because the whole election became about Donald Trump and whether he was concerned about gas prices,â said Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky.
Voters, Paul concluded, âwere just mad.â
Paul said he was probably OK with a leadership vote on Tuesday after a âfrank discussion.â He added that his hope coming out of the election would be more Republicans joining him in voting against the Iran war and tariffs.
The View From The House
Change may not come for the Senate GOP. But across the Capitol, House Republicans will see a big shakeup as they choose a new minority leader in a race between Reps. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, and Steve Scalise, R-La.
Burgessâs view
Thune doesnât even have a challenger, itâs hard to see a scenario where he isnât reelected as leader on Tuesday. But the anger within the Republican Party is real, and perhaps a bit misdirected.
Few senators beyond Paul want to blame Trump for the partyâs crushing losses, but midterms are as much a referendum on the president as they are on the Congress.

COLUMBIANA, Ala.—Attorneys for Alabama Power didn’t mince words about Fenn Church in a Shelby County courthouse Monday afternoon.
“Mr. Church—over and over again—has said he wants to be arrested,” Alabama Power attorney Jim Byram told Circuit Court Judge Jonathan Spann. “He wants to be run over by a bulldozer. All this kind of ridiculous stuff.”
Fenn Church, a local property owner who runs a trucking company, has fought for months against Alabama Power’s effort to lay a major transmission line across his rural property.
Church, 60, has said that while he understands the need for eminent domain for public use, Alabama Power’s construction of a transmission line across his property—a supply line he believes will support data center infrastructure—should be routed through locations where property owners have agreed to the construction. The enjoyment of his property, Church has said, shouldn’t be trumped by what Spann previously ruled was Alabama Power’s likely arbitrary and capricious location of the line across his wooded land.
“I’m going to stand in front of that gate and say, ‘This is my home, and I’m not letting you drive through that gate,’” Church told Inside Climate News in October. “And then if they want to arrest me, they can handcuff me and take me to jail or run me over. But this is where I take my stand.”
But Church, the man’s lawyers argued during Monday’s hearing, has no desire to defy a court order or be run over by a bulldozer. He simply feels he’s entitled to stand on his property’s edge and protect his property.
“Mr. Church has stood on the property line and said he’s ‘not going to let Alabama Power come onto my property,’” Church’s lawyer, Martin Evans, told the judge. “That’s a fact.”
Byram, the company’s lawyer, refused to comment after Monday’s hearing, but Alabama Power provided the following statement via email.
“As a result of Mr. Church’s refusal to maintain a safe distance while crews are working, Alabama Power is seeking a temporary restraining order to keep him and others out of the work zone to ensure Mr. Church, visitors and our crews remain safe as work continues,” a company spokesperson wrote. “We will continue to respect the legal process as we responsibly pursue the infrastructure investments necessary to provide reliable service to customers across the state.”
Spann, the judge who presided over Monday’s hearing, had previously ruled in Church’s favor in the case, issuing a preliminary injunction last month preventing Alabama Power from accessing Church’s property.
In his ruling, Spann found that Alabama Power had failed to follow the necessary procedures for condemnation of Church’s land outlined in state law. Church was likely to succeed on the merits of his case, and without a preliminary injunction, he would be irreparably harmed, the judge wrote.
Then, on Oct. 21, the Alabama Supreme Court stayed Spann’s preliminary injunction without providing any written reasoning.
By Nov. 3, Alabama Power crews had cleared the land up to Church’s property line. There, under what remained of the Alabama pines, an Alabama Power worker confronted Church.
“Mr. Church, the crews are ready to proceed with the clearing,” the worker told him. “If you and your group could step back 300 feet.”
“I’m not stepping past my line right here,” Church told the Alabama Power representative. “Y’all can have me arrested. “
“That’s all I needed to know,” the worker replied. “Thank you.”
Lawyers for Alabama Power described the incident in its filing requesting the restraining order against Church.
During Monday’s hearing, Church’s lawyers stipulated that without a court order, Church doesn’t plan to allow Alabama Power workers access to his property. The state Supreme Court’s stay “doesn’t give Alabama Power the right of entry” to Church’s property, Evans argued.
Evans said Spann should also dismiss Alabama Power’s lawsuit on procedural grounds: The issues at hand should have been part of his previous cause of action, not a new lawsuit altogether. Evans suggested that the utility’s filing of an additional suit may have been an effort to be assigned a different judge.

Donate Now
Byram said Alabama Power’s suit was a proper mechanism for enforcing the Alabama Supreme Court’s decision in the case, citing case law as he argued that the suit should not be dismissed.
“You can find a case saying Pontius Pilate was a Jew if you try hard enough,” Church’s lawyer replied.
At one point, the judge pushed back on Alabama Power lawyers, who had argued that the Alabama Supreme Court effectively settled the issue at hand by lifting his preliminary injunction.
“How am I to enter a restraining order against the defendant when the underlying issue in the condemnation case is still being litigated in the Supreme Court?” Spann asked.
Issuing a restraining order against Church in the case would be engaging in “speculation and surmise” about how the Alabama Supreme Court may ultimately decide on the merits of the case, the judge said.
“If the Supreme Court was willing to wait and see what happened, they wouldn’t have stayed the preliminary injunction,” Byram told the judge.
“He’s asking you to overrule the Supreme Court and stay the stay,” Byram said of Church. “It’s ridiculous.”
“It sounds like he’s asking me to wait on the Supreme Court to issue a ruling in this case,” the judge said.
The meeting became contentious when lawyers for Church asked to enter into evidence a memo from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers related to the project. Alabama Power’s lawyers objected, arguing that the letter amounted to inadmissible hearsay.
Spann did not admit the memo into evidence, but a copy provided to Inside Climate News by Church is signed by D. Lee Forsgren, a “senior official performing

A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house.
At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home.
"My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service.
Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models.
"My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza.
She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house.
She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women.
Roza says Epstein went on to systematically rape her.
Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused.
We discovered through the Epstein-related documents released by the US Department of Justice [DOJ] that 10 models from MC2 met, or were in communication with, Epstein after his conviction.
The files also show Epstein gave $1m (Â£742,000) to MC2 in 2005 - despite the agency owners telling a US publication two years later that Epstein had no involvement in their company.
Testimony shared with BBC Eye also raises questions about the role played by two other individuals who were active in the model industry, and whom the DOJ files show had close relationships with Epstein - former agent Ramsey Elkholy and agency director Faith Kates.
A DOJ statement from last year, that no evidence has been uncovered which would warrant further investigation against "uncharged third parties", is now being challenged by New York State senator, Zellnor Myrie.
He has proposed a new sex trafficking bill to give police greater power to investigate Epstein's alleged enablers.
Sara Ziff, founder of the Model Alliance, which campaigns for stronger protections for models in the US, approves.
"Often, [model agencies] are the problem. They are the link between the model and these predatory men."
Roza says the person behind the camera at the photoshoots MC2 sent her to was not a professional photographer, but Epstein's girlfriend at the time, Nadia Marcinko.
Roza describes the set-up as "strange - there was no stylist" and the photos were never used. She has since become convinced the shoots were stage-managed by Epstein and MC2.
The Model Trap

"Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says.
A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency.
We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply.
Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims.
"Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked."

The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse.

We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse.
Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kindâ¦ At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed."
He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activityâ¦ my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual."

Moscow and Kyiv are privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would controls Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario, US officials have said.
The comments came on the eve of the first trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine since February.
Senior officials from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington will meet in Abu Dhabi as the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches.
Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.
"An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X.
But Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict in the first place remain far apart.
A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia.
Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security.
While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".
However, he acknowledged that the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".
"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."
For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it's attacked again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from eastern Europe â which would be alarming to Europeans.
The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.
The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.
Since then, European leaders - who have been largely excluded from peace talks â have pushed to be involved in the process amid concerns that decisions about the security of their continent would be made without them.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged on Monday to include Nato allies and EU members into any "meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture". President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly stated Kyiv wanted Europe to be part of the talks.
The US official said the Americans would propose moving into a multilateral format bringing the Europeans into the discussion. "Hopefully we'll get the Russians on board," the official said, while acknowledging that "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans."
Since the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump â who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day â has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.
Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union.
After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine which "might involve all of Europe".
Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result into a fair peace.
Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believes Trump wants "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv.
The only way to make Putin start real negotiations is by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said.
"While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war".
Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi will include Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky.
Kyiv is sending several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya.
Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms.
On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations."
"This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism."

A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.
In January, it could jump by more than a quarter â around Â£460 extra a year for the typical UK household â according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.
For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.
Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.
Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.
And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard â and not just for the UK.
As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.
America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.
Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.
The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?
Two decisions
On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil.
Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a Â£1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security.
Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas.
Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra Â£63bn â around Â£2,200 each â according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations.
Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable.
At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama.
But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."
"We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy."
There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it.
The case for drilling
Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!"
Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field.
Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks.
The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills".
"If we use our own gasâ¦ that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice.
Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress.
But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets."
Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had."
Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year â even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead.

5838f625fd05.text: Lawmakers, investors and tech leaders are assessing bombshell revelations about Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang. Huang admitted to an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia designs chips and processors that power artificial intelligence and underpin much of the enormous investment in the industry. William Brangham reports. Amna Nawaz: Lawmakers, investors, and tech leaders around the world spent part of this day assessing the bombshell revelations about Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, and its founder and CEO, Jensen Huang. Geoff Bennett: Nvidia designs the chips and processors that power artificial intelligence, and now its CEO faces mounting scrutiny inside the company on Capitol Hill and in the courts. Following media reports, Huang admitted he was having an affair. The woman is said to be a suspected Chinese spy, raising questions about Huang, President Trump's relationship with him, and Huang's dealings with China on critical technology. President Trump spoke about it at the White House a short time ago. And that's where William Brangham begins our coverage. William Brangham: President Trump tonight defended Jensen Huang, saying he'd learned about the allegations some time ago. President Donald Trump: He's an amazing guy. I just hope it's -- I hope there's no problem. If there is a problem, we will let you know about it, but I hope there's no problem. I believe he's suffering greatly. William Brangham: The president also said the FBI is involved and that he reached out to Huang today. President Donald Trump: I asked him that question. Did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said: "I had no idea that she was a spy." And I really believe him. William Brangham: The president's comments came in the wake of this shocking revelation from Silicon Valley. Jensen Huang, CEO, Nvidia: Blackwell architecture. William Brangham: The head of one of the companies' most critical to the development of artificial intelligence, Jensen Huang, admitted to having an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive and suspected spy in the pink dress. There's no relation. She's an executive at another computing and AI giant, the Singapore-based firm Megaspeed, which is also one of Nvidia's largest customers. According to reporting by The Financial Times and other news organizations, the Trump administration had intelligence reports indicating Alice Huang had been recruited by the Chinese Ministry of Security, known as the MSS, to gather information on Nvidia. The Chinese government has categorically denied the accusations. Guo Jiakun, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson (through interpreter): We have previously responded to this matter. The so-called claims of a Chinese spy narrative are purely a groundless accusation. William Brangham: Jensen Huang, in a statement yesterday, admitted to the affair in a company-wide statement -- quote -- "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." Two of Huang's children work at Nvidia. The company's board of directors launched an independent probe, saying -- quote -- "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information." Separately, on Capitol Hill, three Republican chairmen of different House committees have requested a closed-door briefing with Huang to determine -- quote -- "the extent to which U.S. national security has been put at risk." Last night, President Trump defended Jensen Huang. President Donald Trump: I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it. I think he's an honorable guy. William Brangham: Huang founded Nvidia in 1993, but he first rose to prominence in late 2023, when Nvidia's computer processors and hardware helped usher in the boom in artificial intelligence. Since then, Huang has developed a close relationship with President Trump. Jensen Huang: Mr. President. William Brangham: Even taking a personal call from the president while on stage at an AI summit. President Donald Trump: It's all a hoax. The data centers are great. William Brangham: On that call, Trump reiterated his opposition to any legislation that would restrict the growth of artificial intelligence, a view that Huang himself shares. Jensen Huang: Market forces are already there. We don't need any new laws. We don't need new regulations. William Brangham: Huang's relationship with the Trump administration also helped his successful lobbying campaign to allow Nvidia to sell some of its AI chips to Beijing earlier this year. Minority House Leader Hakeem Jeffries today said he supported greater regulation of AI exports to China. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY): There are provisions currently in the Senate that will restrict chip access to China that I strongly support. William Brangham: Now this accusation of possible espionage inside one of the most critical tech firms in the world will be a center of attention as the lame-duck Congress returns to work this week. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm William Brangham.

He spent 20 years in the U.S. intelligence community focusing on China. He now runs his own consulting firm, China Strategies Group. Amna Nawaz: For more on the national security risks of Nvidia's CEO having an affair with a possible foreign intelligence agent, we turn to Christopher Johnson. He had a 20-year career in the U.S. intelligence community where he focused on China. He now runs his own consulting firm, the China Strategies Group. Welcome, and thanks for being with us. So, Jensen Huang has admitted to this affair. Alice Huang is accused of being a spy. What does China have to gain from one of their alleged assets having an affair with the head of Nvidia? What possible information could that yield? Christopher Johnson: Well, that's a key question in all this is -- I think first some background. When China sets a national strategic priority or a whole-of-country effort like this, they will do anything they can to achieve the objective, and that includes working their way, buying their way, and often stealing their way to a capability, whether it's a technology or something else they need. So, in this case, we need to look at, what was the sort of motivation, if you will, behind the operation? I see two possibilities. One is that they wanted to place someone physically close to Mr. Huang in order to have access to his electronic equipment, his phones, his computer, things like that. The reporting we have seen so far suggests a broader influence operation, however, where the goal seemed to be to encourage Mr. Huang to use his access to President Trump, probably not to rescind existing export controls, but to prevent him from issuing new ones that would limit Nvidia sales to China. And so, in that case, that tells us pretty clearly that the Chinese, despite their public rhetoric about making great strides in AI and so on and so forth, are still very, very worried about this fundamental choke hold that faces them, which is the U.S. control over the export of these advanced chips. Amna Nawaz: And from what you know about Chinese intelligence operations and techniques, how typical is it for them to do this kind of thing, recruit an agent, someone to have an intimate relationship with a potential U.S. target? Christopher Johnson: Well, it's somewhat odd in their history. They're not above it, of course, but you see this a lot more with the Russian services, I would argue, and so on. Oftentimes, we do see the Chinese Ministry of State Security, however, engaging in access agent operations, where they find someone who is close to an individual that they're targeting and use that person in order to gain influence with the person who's their ultimate target. Amna Nawaz: So, for U.S. lawmakers who now say they want to get some answers, try to determine the extent to which U.S. national security may have been put at risk, I heard you mention that one of the aims here could be proximity to Huang's personal devices, his phone and laptop and such. What kinds of questions should lawmakers be asking right now to determine that potential national security risk? Christopher Johnson: Well, I think they're going to be asking a lot of questions, one of which will be, based on some of the reporting we have seen, there seems to be some lack of clarity with regard to the process inside the Trump administration for how this issue came to light. In a typical investigation, a counterintelligence investigation like this, we would expect to see activity by the Department of Justice's National Security Division, the FBI, and, of course, the CIA's counterintelligence function. In some ways, it sounds like Secretary Rubio was running this process this time, which is somewhat unusual. So, if I'm a lawmaker, I want to know what was happening in terms of the process. We certainly want to know, did Mr. Huang have any awareness of this person's affiliation with Chinese intelligence? My guess is, he probably did not. Also they will be asking serious questions about concerns about diversion of Chinese -- Nvidia chips to Chinese companies through these companies like Ms. Huang's in Southeast Asia. Amna Nawaz: The reporting so far that President Donald Trump, other Trump administration officials were briefed about the affair roughly a year before these public revelations, and as The New York Times has reported that they chose not to do anything with that information, what is your reaction to that? Does that say to you in any way that there's already been a determination that there was no national security risk here? Christopher Johnson: I don't think so. I think what it reflects -- and we saw it in President Trump's interview on "60 Minutes" last night. When asked about artificial intelligence, or, as he calls it, superintelligence, his answer was very clear, which is, we're in a competition with China, we're in a war, if you will, with China to lead in artificial intelligence, and I don't want to do anything that slows us down in that competition. Nvidia is critical, right, to that competition. And I think the president probably thought there may not be enough here to pursue. Now, I think, with all this scrutiny, obviously, he said today that the FBI is investigating and looking into the situation, so he's showing provisional backing for Mr. Huang, but we will see what comes out of the investigation. Amna Nawaz: Meanwhile, we should remind folks Jensen Huang did fly with President Trump on Air Force One to China earlier in this year in May. He's one of a number of tech CEOs to join him on that trip. President Trump could be meeting with Xi Jinping again later this month on the sidelines of the APEC summit, and it's reported that he wants Jensen Huang to come with him again. Christopher Johnson: Yes. Amna Nawaz: In your view, is that appropriate? Is that a smart mov

381f30fb9f00.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman suspected of spying for China echoes past controversies involving prominent Americans whose romantic relationships raised national security concerns. Why it matters: Foreign intelligence operatives can use romantic relationships to gain access to political intelligence, corporate secrets and classified information — posing serious national security risks. Driving the news: Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a message to employees Sunday, following reports that he had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Per The New York Times , U.S. authorities suspected China's Ministry of State Security of recruiting Alice Huang to seek information about Jensen Huang and influence his feelings about selling AI chips to Chinese firms. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. China has also denied the allegations. Zoom out: The evidence of foreign intelligence involvement varies, with some cases involving actual security breaches, while others raised concerns about possible foreign spying. Read more below. Jensen Huang State of play: Reports about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang have raised questions about whether Chinese intelligence gained access to Nvidia's secrets or sought to influence its business decisions. AFP and Reuters photos showed them together in 2024 and 2025. Employees reported seeing Jensen Huang at Megaspeed's offices, where Alice Huang worked as an executive, according to Culper Research, a short-seller that published a report on Nvidia's China business in May 2026. An employee told Culper that Jensen and Alice had a "very close" relationship. What's next: Three Republican House committee chairs have requested a briefing with Huang about his relationship with Alice Huang and Nvidia's safeguards against foreign threats. James J. Smith and Katrina Leung A 2006 DOJ report found that counterintelligence agent James J. Smith had a secret 18-year affair with Katrina Leung, an FBI informant who was suspected of passing information onto China. The investigation found that Leung had provided classified U.S. government information to China without FBI authorization, exposing major failures in the bureau's oversight of informants. A DOJ inspector general investigation also found that Leung had an affair with another FBI agent, William Cleveland. Smith and Leung were arrested in 2003. Both ultimately pleaded guilty to making false statements, rather than espionage charges. Maria Butina and Paul Erickson Russian activist-turned-politician Maria Butina pleaded guilty in 2018 to conspiring to act as an unregistered agent of the Russian government after becoming romantically involved with Republican operative Paul Erickson. Federal prosecutors withdrew the allegation that she traded sex for political access, saying they misinterpreted the evidence, per ABC News . Prosecutors maintained that Butina used her relationship with Erickson to conceal activities intended to advance Russian interests, according to ABC News. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang FBI records declassified in August 2026 show former Congressman Eric Swalwell acknowledged having sexual encounters with a suspected Chinese operative, Christine Fang, per the Washington Post . According to the records , Swalwell said the interactions were casual and that they never formally dated. Flashback: In 2020, Axios uncovered that Fang had targeted politicians in California, including Swalwell. According to reports, Fang participated in fundraising for Swalwell's campaign and helped place an intern in his office. Intelligence officials told Axios at the time that Fang gained access to political power through fundraising, networking, personal charisma, and romantic or sexual relationships with at least two Midwestern mayors, too. The FBI never accused Swalwell of wrongdoing in connection with his relationship with Fang, per the Washington Post. Benjamin Bishop In 2014, defense contractor Benjamin Pierce Bishop pleaded guilty to disclosing classified information to a Chinese woman with whom he had a romantic relationship, according to the Department of Justice . Bishop was sentenced to more than seven years in prison for disclosing classified national defense information and unlawfully retaining classified documents. According to the DOJ , Bishop, a former Army lieutenant colonel, retrieved a classified photograph of a Chinese naval asset at his girlfriend's request.

3a3dafb62658.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/citing-government-pressure-russias-top-independent-newspaper-closes-its-office-after-three-decades Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Citing government pressure, Russia's top independent newspaper closes its office after three decades World Nov 9, 2026 6:46 PM EST MOSCOW (AP) — Novaya Gazeta, Russia's most celebrated independent newspaper, closed its Moscow offices Monday, citing relentless pressure from government officials. It was the last major independent media outlet critical of the Kremlin that remained active in Russia. Others closed or moved their operations abroad after President Vladimir Putin sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022. In a statement published Oct. 30, the newspaper said the Russian authorities and the security services had "forced our editorial team to cease operations." "Human rights and freedoms have been abolished in this country, and defending them is now treated as a crime," the newspaper said. "Elections and elected governing bodies have been effectively dismantled, civil society institutions have been wiped out, freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled underfoot." Nobel Peace Prize awarded journalist Dmitry Muratov, former editor-in-chief of Russia's top independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, left row top, and other members of the editorial board attend a ceremony of closing Novaya Gazeta's office in Moscow on Monday. Photo by AP Launched in 1993, Novaya Gazeta quickly became known for its fierce reporting and dedication to uncovering Russian human rights abuses and corruption. Six of its journalists have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya, who reported on atrocities during the second Chechen War at the start of Putin's first term as president. She was fatally shot in her apartment building in 2006. On the newspaper's final day in its office Monday, journalists slowly removed the portraits of their slain colleagues from the newsroom where reporters and editors planned their work. Tatiana Britskaya, the editor of Novaya Gazeta's investigations desk, said she had expected the outlet's closure almost every day for the past 4 1/2 years. "It is an incredibly difficult decision, because this is more than a workplace, more than an office — this is our home, and we're losing it," she said. Novaya Gazeta had faced growing government pressure as the Kremlin cracked down on critics, with repression sharply intensifying after the start of the conflict in Ukraine. Longtime editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov, who shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize with Philippine journalist Maria Ressa, was attacked on a train in 2022 by an assailant who poured red paint over him, causing severe irritation in his eyes. Muratov stepped down as editor in 2023 after being named a "foreign agent" by Russian authorities. The designation carries strong pejorative connotations in the country and can bring additional government scrutiny. The newspaper was fined after it was accused of discrediting Russia's armed forces, and it also was declared a foreign agent. Authorities blocked all of its online platforms, seized its printing house, revoked its media registration and shut down the donation system that allowed it to receive support from readers. In a final blow, the newspaper was ordered to clear out its Moscow offices. As reporters left the building and gathered in the street, a new sign was affixed atop the nameplate that once announced the newspaper's office. It read, "Here lived Novaya Gazeta." Sergei Sokolov, Novaya Gazeta's editor-in-chief, said he believed the newspaper would return one day "with renewed strength." "We will live, and I am sure that this country, caught in such a terrible era, will eventually stir. As soon as those first signs appear, Novaya Gazeta will return, to our readers and to our colleagues." Some of Novaya Gazeta's staff left Russia in 2022 and opened a separate project, Novaya Gazeta Europe. The new outlet has been sharply critical of the Kremlin and its military action in Ukraine. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Associated Press Associated Press

8774d54f0900.text: To discuss the national security risks of Nvidia's CEO having an affair with a possible foreign intelligence agent, Amna Nawaz spoke with Christopher Johnson. He spent 20 years in the U.S. intelligence community focusing on China. He now runs his own consulting firm, China Strategies Group. Geoff Bennett: Well, for its part, the broader market rallied today, but Nvidia shares took a hit, closing down more than 4 percent. And the economic stakes extend well beyond Nvidia itself. With a market value still exceeding $4 trillion, the company has become a major driver of the stock market and a central force in the AI boom. For more on that, we turn now to Mohamed El-Erian, professor at the Wharton School of Business and chief economic adviser at Allianz. Thanks for being back with us here on the "News Hour." We appreciate it. Mohamed El-Erian: Thank you, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: It is hard to imagine a CEO more synonymous with his own company than Jensen Huang. In many ways, Nvidia is Jensen Huang, and Jensen Huang is Nvidia. What does it mean for his company and the broader AI industry if his leadership is now suddenly in question? Mohamed El-Erian: So he's the founder, the CEO, the director, the president of Nvidia, and all that doesn't even capture how important he is to the company and to the sector. As we just heard, it is the most critical company in tech worldwide. It brings together software, hardware. It provides financing to many other tech firms. So it's also at the center of the financing relationship. And tech has been, and AI in particular has been an engine of growth and is the promise of future productivity. So this is really central, not just in terms of national security, domestic politics, and geopolitics, as we heard earlier, but in terms of economics and finance. Geoff Bennett: Jensen Huang, as I understand it, has some 60 direct reports. He has no obvious successor. He has built a company so closely identified with his own leadership that replacing him will be enormously difficult. Even the board, as I'm told, is loyal to him. There's been so much focus on what happens if he goes. My question is, what happens if he stays? Does Nvidia risk sending the message that he's simply too important to be held accountable? Mohamed El-Erian: Look, the board has two huge challenges. One is conducting an independent investigation into the founder of the company and into the person who probably asked you to join the board. So they have got to be independent, they have got to be comprehensive, and they have got to keep shareholder interest front and center. Then you have a second issue, which is what's called key man risk. One of the responsibilities of a board is to make sure that there is a succession. And, clearly, as you said, no one knows what would happen if Jensen Huang has to step down. So they also have to deal with this key person risk. So, this board, believe me, will be having lots and lots of calls trying to sort out these two issues, and doing so while the political arm is also interested in what is going on in the company right now. Geoff Bennett: Let's talk more about that, because the Trump administration has favored limited AI regulation. But do these revelations combined with the Democrats set to take over the House and Senate, does that does that change the political calculus in Washington? Mohamed El-Erian: So, even before we heard the news about Jensen, there was questioning about the let it rip approach of the Trump administration, just let AI go, because, if we don't, according to that view, China will take the lead, and this is really consequential. So there were concerns we were going to have some sand in the wheels, if you like, to slow this down, because we're starting to realize, Geoff, it's not just about the benefits of AI.There's also collateral damage and unintended consequences that need to be a risk-managed. And you can't just ignore them, because they may be problematic down the road. So what this will do is, it will get Congress even more interested into, how do you put more sand in the wheels and try to slow down a little bit the development, not a lot? But for example, it's not about not building data centers. It's about building data centers better. And it's going to be that sort of distinction that we're going to see come to the fore. Geoff Bennett: Mohamed El-Erian, always great to speak with you. Thanks for being with us. Mohamed El-Erian: Thank you.

A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution.
"By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorisation, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.
The effort will likely fail, as Republicans remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says the effort is aimed at pushing President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.
Hegseth has called the impeachment effort a "sham" and defended his record.
"You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said in a video statement last week. "It's not going to work. We will not back down."
He called Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" and said he was not concerned about the impeachment effort. In the video, Hegseth defended his leadership of the department and listed ways he has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda.
Massie formally introduced his articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon. The move starts a 48-hour clock for the chamber to take up the measure. Lawmakers could vote on the resolution directly, vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside.
"I'm doing this because it's the right thing to do," he told reporters after introducing the articles.
Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it started nearly nine months ago. He has previously garnered headlines over demanding the Trump administration release the files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and has now brought them back in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections.
He has said the effort was aimed at preventing a Democrat spectacle next year when they have control of Congress. He said he hoped to force Trump to name a replacement, who could be quickly confirmed while Republicans have power.
"My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials."
Democratic leadership has signalled openness to such an effort against Hegseth once they take control in January.
Asked about the effort on Monday, Hegseth said, "We're not worried about that".
He said he planned to hold a news conference on Tuesday to discuss the subject.
Impeaching a cabinet secretary is rare. It must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office.
Trump was impeached by the House twice in his first term in office but was cleared by the Senate after two trials and not removed.
As with the presidential process, the House would first hold a vote on charges against Hegseth and the Senate then would conduct a trial to decide whether to acquit or convict.
The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not convict either one.
While impeachment has been "an incredibly rare process", it has become far more normalised since the House impeached President Bill Clinton in 1998, said Paul Gowder, a law professor at Northwestern University in Chicago.
He said it has become "much more common as the country has become more politically polarised," adding a prediction that several more of Trump's cabinet members may face impeachment over the next two years.
Massie told reporters he was not sure if the measure had sufficient backing to pass. It would need a majority to pass the House and even with all Democratic support, it would still likely need some Republican support as the party holds a slim majority.
Peter Loge, a professor of public affairs at George Washington University, told the BBC that he believed it was likely to pass due to those slim margins.
"There are enough angry Republicans that more than enough Republicans are gonna simply not show up to vote," he said.
Currently, there are 218 Republicans and 214 Democrats in the House.
While the House requires a simple majority to pass articles of impeachment, the Senate mandates a two-thirds vote to convict, threshold that is difficult to meet in the current congressional term.
When Democrats take over in January, they are likely to have at least 54 Senate seats - though two races do not yet have winners due to slim voting margins. A total of 60 votes will be required to convict and remove an official from office.

The justices are allowing the Trump administration to continue building a section of border wall in a remote part of Texas that includes Big Bend National Park. This would involve barriers and surveillance equipment along a 500-mile stretch of the U.S. border with Mexico. Environmental groups and locals had challenged the construction, saying it would damage the natural area and historic sites. But the High Court decided to lift a halt on the work placed by a federal judge as a lower court battle plays out. Well, there's been another high-level resignation at the Department of Justice. Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate is stepping down as head of the department's civil division. Under his watch, the unit oversaw cases involving mail-in voting restrictions, in-state tuition for undocumented citizens, and laws that aim to ban federal agents from wearing masks. Russian officials say Ukrainian drones hit an apartment building in its Leningrad region, as well as an oil refinery. French officials are blaming Iran for a massive cyberattack last month on supermarket refrigerators. The attacks sent temperatures soaring for hundreds of fridges nationwide, forcing stores to throw out fresh and frozen goods. The French foreign minister blamed the attack on Iran's Revolutionary Guard and threatened further European Union sanctions against Iran. Similar attacks were reported last week in Sweden, Belgium, Ireland and other nations. Iran has consistently denied carrying out any malicious cyber operations. In Poland, the gunman who killed six people and injured 15 others this weekend died today in a hospital. (GUNSHOTS) Amna Nawaz: Eyewitness video showed people fleeing from gunfire near Krakow's historic Main Square on Saturday. Police say the 24-year-old assailant was a Polish national dressed in camouflage and a bulletproof vest. Police later shot him after he crashed his car. British comedian Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison today for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. Judge Joel Bennathan: The whole episode wreaks of casual disrespect and your belief that fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live. He maintains his innocence, saying that all the encounters were consensual. In New Delhi, a thick smog blanketed the city today after Diwali celebrations this weekend added to already high pollution levels. Residents of India's capital lit firecrackers and fireworks to mark the Hindu Festival of Lights last night. By this morning, the air quality index was severe and visibility was limited. They say anyone experiencing such problems should contact a health care professional immediately. 7bfbaac913ff.text: By — Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/what-we-know-and-what-we-dont-as-nvidia-investigates-an-alleged-spy-plot-involving-its-ceo Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What we know — and what we don't — as Nvidia investigates an alleged spy plot involving its CEO World Nov 9, 2026 6:35 PM EST Stunning allegations of a spy plot have prompted Nvidia to investigate whether its founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." Huang on Sunday admitted to having an extramarital affair, and acknowledged that news reports surrounding the relationship and potential national security concerns led Nvidia's board to investigate. He and his chipmaking company did not name the person he had been intimate with, but The New York Times identified her as business executive and Chinese citizen Alice Huang. The outlet said U.S. intelligence determined she was gathering information for Beijing.
