Huang himself has become a key face in the AI race, both across the industry and often on President Donald Trump's side in Washington. Here's what we know. What Nvidia has said about its investigation Watch the segment in the player above. On Sunday, Nvidia announced that its board was initiating an independent investigation. The company cited recent reporting about Huang being "the target of a foreign intelligence effort." Nvidia's board said it had "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. The company added that Huang would remain CEO — and that he had committed to cooperating fully during the investigation. "Today's news will not slow Nvidia," company spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement. "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." Jensen Huang apologizes for affair In a separate email to Nvidia employees, later also published by the company, Huang apologized for his affair. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children," Huang wrote, adding that he was "deeply sorry" and that his colleagues also "deserve better" from him. Huang also reiterated his support for the board's investigation. "I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security," he said Sunday. Huang, 63, founded Nvidia more than three decades ago. He and his wife, Lori, reportedly have two children who both work at Nvidia. China rejects spy allegation claims China has denied that it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Nvidia's CEO. "The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said during a routine briefing Monday. The New York Times reported that Alice Huang was a former executive of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed International, whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia. Last year, Megaspeed faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China — which the company in December maintained there was "no evidence" of. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times. Last month, the outlet reported that U.S. intelligence agencies discovered Nvidia's Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang — and determined she was feeding information directly to Beijing. Huang's relationship with Washington Beyond rising to fame in the AI space (often accompanied by his signature leather jacket), Huang has maintained a close relationship to Trump throughout the Republican president's second term in office. He's among tech CEOs who have dined at the White House, and even traveled on Air Force One. Trump has called Huang "smart" and "amazing," repeatedly insisting he accompany him on foreign trips. After news of Nvidia's investigation broke, the president said on Sunday the two hadn't spoken but that he hoped "everything's fine." He continued to praise Huang, including when asked whether he wished he had acted on intelligence when he was briefed about spying. President Donald Trump addressed the spy plot allegations involving Nvidia's CEO in a White House briefing Monday. "I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. He's done an amazing job for our country," Trump told reporters. He added that he was still open to taking Huang on his trip to Asia next week. Questions of wider ramifications for trading AI chips Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable companies. And it's become a leader for making chips that power AI. Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning Trump's approval for selling its H200 chips in January. Those are not the company's most cutting-edge chips, but are still powerful. Nvidia has said in regulatory filings that it has sold only a small amount to China, as such sales are also restricted by the Chinese government. Nvidia's investigation into whether Huang was a target of foreign intelligence is still ongoing, but some analysts suspect that the allegations will strengthen calls for stricter export controls with China. 1e96526d9697.text: One of the stunning upsets of last week’s election was in South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews defeated incumbent Republican Darline Graham in the Senate race. That wasn’t the only Democratic victory in the deep red state. Democrats also flipped a House seat and flipped 10 seats in the state house. Geoff Bennett discussed more with South Carolina’s Democratic Party chair, Christale Spain. Geoff Bennett: One of the more stunning upsets of last week's election was in South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews defeated incumbent Republican Darline Graham in the U.S. Senate race. And that wasn't the only Democratic victory in the deep red state. Democrats also flipped a U.S. House seat and flipped 10 seats in the Statehouse, breaking the Republican supermajority. Here to talk about why Democrats won and how they're aiming to build on that success is South Carolina's Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain. Welcome to the "News Hour." Christale Spain: Oh, thank you so much for having me. Geoff Bennett: So, South Carolina had been a Republican stronghold for decades. What changed in this election? What did Democrats figure out to do in this cycle that they hadn't been able to do before? Christale Spain: One of the main things that we did this cycle was make sure that we recruited a candidate for every seat for the Statehouse. Our Statehouse was up -- is up every two years, and we made a concerted effort to find, I think it was about 80-something candidates to make sure that no Republican went unchecked. So we have 124 House members. We had about 34 Democratic incumbents, and we filled every seat across the state with Democrats. So I really feel like that was one of the biggest changes that we made as a party. Geoff Bennett: What do those victories tell you about where the electorate is moving? Are you seeing a genuine political realignment in South Carolina, or was this just a particularly favorable election for Democrats? Christale Spain: You know, I want to say that we just -- the turnout showed that Democrats are all over the state. One thing that -- we're still waiting on the actual election data to see actually get is the get the names of folks who voted. But looking at raw numbers, one thing that we can tell is that Democrats collectively -- we look at the House district data, Democrats outvoted Republicans in all 124 House seats collectively. So what that does tell us, number one, is that our state is completely gerrymandered. If Democrats have more votes in those House districts than Republicans do, we do know that Democrats live everywhere and that Democrats will turn out and vote if you talk to them. So I don't know if we just saw that -- a shift like you're talking about, but we do know that we Democrats can win when we run really good candidates, because not only did we break the Republican supermajority. We had about 20-something candidates -- or 20-something races that were above 40 percent. So our voters are there, and when they show up, we're able to do pretty historical things. Geoff Bennett: And Black voter turnout in South Carolina was almost as high as it was in a presidential election. What drove that level of engagement? Christale Spain: You know, I just think that it was the attacks on Black folks. We have been seeing that all across the country, from the White House all the way here to our Republican-led Statehouse, that they wanted to attack DEI, thinking that that means they're attacking Black folks. And Black people decided to strike back. So, when Black voters turn out, it really helps the Democratic ticket. Like, Annie Andrews benefited greatly from the high Black voter turnout. Geoff Bennett: And South Carolina is slated to lead the Democratic presidential nominating calendar in 2028, a position it hasn't yet occupied in a genuinely competitive race. What difference do you think that will make in determining who emerges as the Democratic Party's next standard-bearer? Christale Spain: You know, I think it's going to be a big deal. I think it's going to -- it will probably be a difference maker. I think that anybody thinking about running for president of the United States, number one, has to come to South Carolina, number two, has to sit with our voters. They have to sit with voters all across the state. We don't have huge population centers here in South Carolina. Democrats live all the way from the Upstate all the way to the Lowcountry, where we flipped that U.S. House race. So they're going to have to be prepared to do the work of traveling the state, be prepared to do the work of talking to our voters and meeting them where they are. I know we say that all the time, but to me that means going into communities and being OK with sitting in small rooms of four and five people. You're not going to get big rallies and huge turnouts all the time, so you got to be comfortable talking to the people that show up to talk to you, and also be comfortable listening. And I think the biggest thing that is going to be a change in this cycle, this presidential primary cycle, is that we have a huge number of Black voters here. So anybody thinking about running for president is going to have to be unafraid to go into the Black community and to talk about issues that are unique to the Black community and figuring out what those solutions are going to be. Geoff Bennett: Is the national Democratic Party investing enough in South Carolina and more broadly in the South and building out an infrastructure that could support a big win in 2028? Christale Spain: You know, I think that our national party did a great job of trying to refocus the effort into the South and they. And this DNC has done more with investing in the South than previous DNCs, but we can always do better. And I'm committed. I believe that our party is going to make that effort to really invest in the Deep South. When I talk about the South, I want to make sure we're talking about the Deep South, the South Car

A Massachusetts judge has denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of killing her three children.
The judge's ruling follows her defence team's request to dismiss the case after the 12-person jury in her September trial failed to reach a verdict.
Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.
The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.
Clancy's defence team argued to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that prevents a person from being tried for the same crime twice.
Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the 26-day jury trial last summer, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative.
The five-week trial, its lead-up and aftermath gripped Americans, and put postpartum mental health issues such as psychosis in the spotlight.
In his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject Clancy to double jeopardy, according to court documents obtained by the BBC.
The possibility that "an unreasonably stubborn or eccentric juror" could be seated is "an unavoidable risk of the jury system", he said.
"Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury's deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy's right not to be placed in double jeopardy."
Sullivan also denied a defence motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath.
He said the defence failed to demonstrate that the records were needed for Clancy's defence at any retrial, and that questioning the juror "would have been impermissibly coercive".
The judge has marked 16 November to discuss scheduling a potential second trial. He previously suggested it could begin in March.
The BBC has contacted Clancy's lawyers for comment.
Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.
After weeks of emotional testimony, the jury took a week to deliberate, repeatedly telling the judge that they could not reach a verdict.
The deadlock stemmed from a lone juror who voted to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, while the 11 other jurors intended to acquit Clancy by reason of insanity.
In Massachusetts, as well as in all US criminal murder trials, juries must reach a unanimous decision to convict or acquit a defendant.
Because the jurors failed to unanimously agree on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law, the judge declared a mistrial on 4 September, which means that she was neither found guilty nor not guilty.
Clancy is currently being housed in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.
Ana Faguy contributed reporting.

bfe52dabb2b2.text: Seven Republican senators now are calling for their leadership elections to be delayed — with one even promising to walk out rather than vote Tuesday. Why it matters: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is still expected to be reelected to lead the Senate GOP tomorrow. But the growing push to delay is a sign of troubles ahead. Driving the news: Sens. Ron Johnson (R-Wisc.), Rick Scott (R-Fla.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Ted Budd (R-N.C.) and John Kennedy (R-La.) all signed a letter demanding that the leadership elections be delayed to allow for more discussion about what went wrong for the party last week. Sens. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.) and Jim Banks (R-Ind.) backed them up in statements posted on X. Johnson threatened to skip the vote if the delay doesn't happen. Between the lines: The decision technically falls to conference chair Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) — though it's usually made with leadership buy-in. The election is expected to be held as planned Tuesday morning unless a senator motions to delay and it passes with a majority — which seems unlikely with the number of public supporters, according to a source familiar with the planning discussions. Despite the arguments that Thune should not get to lock in his leadership so quickly, no one has thrown their hat in the ring to challenge him. The bottom line: At this point, none of the leadership elections are competitive. Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.), Conference Chair Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) Policy Committee Chair Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) and Conference Vice Chair James Lankford (R-Okla.) are expected to keep their spots as Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 5 atop the conference. Moreno is the sole candidate for NRSC chair.

2973797d7589.text: By — Michael Casey, Associated Press Michael Casey, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/judges-ruling-could-clear-the-way-for-lindsay-clancy-to-be-tried-again-in-the-deaths-of-her-three-kids Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge's ruling could clear the way for Lindsay Clancy to be tried again in the deaths of her three kids Nation Nov 9, 2026 6:25 PM EST BOSTON (AP) — A judge on Monday denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy, potentially clearing the way for her to be retried next year in the deaths of her three young children. Clancy's defense team had asked the court to end the case based on an unusual argument that the judge shouldn't have declared a mistrial in September when jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict. They argued that the judge should have removed the one juror who favored conviction, then allowed jury deliberations to continue. But Judge William Sullivan disagreed, saying he saw no other option than to declare a mistrial. "Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury's deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy's right not to be placed in double jeopardy," Sullivan wrote. A spokesperson for Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz declined to comment. Clancy has never denied that she killed her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued that Clancy had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behavior. Prosecutors have acknowledged that Clancy had mental health problems, but they said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong. Prosecutors said they intend to retry Clancy, but they haven't settled on whether they will pursue the same charges or opt for a reduced charge that might be more palatable for the jury. The next hearing is Nov. 16. In the motion to dismiss, one of Clancy's lawyers, Martin Weinberg, argued that the judge should have thoroughly interrogated jurors after the foreperson sent two notes saying the one juror who favored conviction wasn't following the court's instructions on reasonable doubt. Sullivan said that type of questioning is barred by law. "Because the secrecy of jury deliberations is a bedrock of our judicial system, any inquiry into the jury's deliberative process would improperly intrude into the jury's function," Sullivan wrote. The judge also said he didn't believe the jury foreperson's claim that the holdout juror — identified in court papers by the pseudonym Juror Doe — wasn't following the law. "In context, the notes appear to express the foreperson's belief that Juror Doe must be refusing to follow the law because Juror Doe would not agree with the majority's view of the case," Sullivan wrote. "Given that the jury unquestionably had reached an impasse, the Court did not and does not view the foreperson's notes as reliable evidence of Juror Doe's inability or refusal to deliberate or follow the law." On Monday, Sullivan also denied prosecutors' request for a gag order while the case remains pending, to avoid influencing a future jury. Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington gave interviews during the trial, while prosecutors generally didn't speak to reporters. Clancy's lawyers argued that it would amount to an unconstitutional restraint on speech. Sullivan also denied a defense motion to preserve certain records related to the first trial that potentially could have been used to further investigate the conduct of the juror who wanted to convict Clancy. "In the Court's view, Clancy is not entitled to any of the materials sought in this motion," Sullivan wrote. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Michael Casey, Associated Press Michael Casey, Associated Press

Amna Nawaz: Speaking of a different kind of combat too, you saw him back in the Press Briefing Room today with the UFC CEO, Dana White, as he joked about offering Dana White the job of press secretary. Amna Nawaz: Amy, we also saw the president less than a week after those elections casting doubt on them, posting today that there's questions about whether the election was honest or not. Tamara Keith: Yes, and on whether this election was stolen, it's like he's going through the stages of grief in reverse. He started with acceptance and he seems to be working backwards. Tamara Keith: And it comes at this time, the lame-duck period, when there are Republicans in Congress who do not have to answer to the president because they also do not have to answer to the voters ever again. Special correspondent Fred de Sam Lazaro now on an unusual partnership trying to fill part of the void. Fred de Sam Lazaro: Palestinian-American neurosurgeon David Hasan came to Gaza late in 2023 as a volunteer. Pediatric cases, in particular, moved him, he says, enough to venture way beyond his normal expertise. David Hasan: I encountered so many orphans, so I made determination to focus on the kids. c98430de23a5.text: By — Andrew Dalton, Associated Press Andrew Dalton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/judge-dismisses-case-from-dolly-partons-manager-alleging-her-nephew-threatened-her-estate Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge dismisses case from Dolly Parton's manager alleging her nephew threatened her estate Arts Nov 9, 2026 6:15 PM EST A Tennessee judge on Monday dismissed a case brought by Dolly Parton 's longtime manager who was seeking an injunction against her nephew and head of security, alleging he had threatened her estate and its employees. The manager, Danny Nozell, asked for the dismissal on Thursday after the two sides came to an agreement. The order from Chancellor I'Ashea L. Myles finalizes that request without prejudice, meaning it can be filed again. Nozell, who runs She's Alive, an entity founded to manage and protect Parton's estate, had secured a temporary restraining order against Bryan Seaver and his security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, in September. The complaint seeking the temporary restraining order said Seaver had threatened violence and the destruction of Parton's legacy and business empire. Nozell wanted to turn the order into a permanent injunction against Seaver. The two sides were to have publicly argued the claims on Tuesday. Seaver's lawyers said in a statement Monday that he "cares deeply about his Aunt Dolly, her music, her family, and the legacy she left behind." "He has made a career out of protecting his aunt while she was alive and remains committed to Dolly and his family" the statement said. "Mr. Seaver is grateful to put this misunderstanding behind him so that the entire family can continue to grieve peacefully and ensure that the bright light of Dolly's legacy remains completely untouched." The dismissal brings a sudden and quiet end to a serious rift in the beloved country superstar's inner circle that began while she was sick with cancer and spilled into public view in the weeks after her Aug. 25 death. Neither side nor court documents have revealed anything about why the complaint was withdrawn, though one court filing said the sides had reached an agreement. Emails requesting details and comment were sent to lawyers for Nozell and She's Alive. Seaver, who Parton had handpicked to announce her death, said in court filings that he considered Nozell a close friend and ally before the restraining order, and said the text messages Nozell cited as evidence of his threats were a "private conversation between two friends who were both frustrated, grieving and discussing strategy." Parton was a widely adored singer, songwriter, philanthropist and country music icon who rose from a log cabin in the Tennessee mountains to a stardom that spanned generations with songs including "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "9 to 5" and "I Will Always Love You." She also left behind a business empire, much of it based in her hometown, that employed many of her close friends and family. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The News
Nvidia and its embattled CEO can add Washington to their list of huge problems.
Members of Congress in both parties are pushing for strengthened export controls and investigations of company chief Jensen Huang after he admitted an affair with a woman accused by US intelligence of spying for the Chinese government. Beyond the corporate governance questions raised by the furor, lawmakers are incensed by reports that Nvidia may have pushed for access to its chips by dubious Chinese companies.
After Democratsâ resounding victories in the midterm elections â after campaigning on promises to investigate big corporations and CEOs â Huang is in line for especially sharp scrutiny. Huangâs future is up to his board, not Congress, but lawmakers can pass stricter export controls that would limit Nvidiaâs chip sales to Beijing and drag the CEO to Capitol Hill for an investigation of the companyâs dealings with China.
âNvidia says itâs going to investigate, but we need a Senate investigation, and Iâm going to be chairingâ the investigations arm of the Intelligence Committee next year, said Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.
âWhether itâs my subcommittee or another, there needs to be a really penetrating, comprehensive investigation of all the possible compromises of our intelligence that may have occurred, but also the reasons that Donald Trump is so high on the head of Nvidia,â Blumenthal added. âSo it is not just an intelligence issue; itâs also a potential corruption issue.â
Stronger export controls, which Nvidia has lobbied to kill, are a likely first consequence. The top House Democrat and future Speaker-in-waiting, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, said Monday that he âstrongly supportsâ the stricter chip export control provisions that the Senate has already advanced in its annual defense policy bill.
âWeâre going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version,â Jeffries told reporters, adding: âWeâre going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue, so we can all get to the bottom of what happened.â
The chief authors of the Senate-passed export controls plan, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., affirmed their proposal in a joint statement that said the Commerce Department also needs to immediately close any export control loopholes.
Huang is poised to face Hill investigations into his knowledge of the woman at the center of the scandal, Alice Huang, as well as his relationships with the White House and Commerce. Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., the incoming Foreign Relations Committee chair, said he wants a probe âto determine whether our national security was compromised.â
âWe need answers about the relationship between AI billionaires and the Trump administration, whoâs making these decisions, and whoâs really got their hand on the wheel,â added Coons.
Huang will have some backup from President Donald Trump, who defended him on Monday as âan amazing guy.â Trump said the Nvidia CEO told him during a conversation earlier in the day, when asked, that âhe had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.â
The Commerce Department and the White House did not respond to a request for comment.
The intelligence wrinkle
Republican leaders, fresh off bruising losses in the midterms, were quieter following the intelligence briefing they received in the Capitol on Monday.
âWe want to be responding in a serious way to anything that threatens Americaâs national security interests or our values,â Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters.
Asked how Congress should respond to the Nvidia crisis, House Speaker Mike Johnson told Semafor: âTheyâre still gathering information on all that.â
The more striking circumspection came from other lawmakers on intelligence committees, who were clearly hesitant to call for immediate action until more details were shared about Huangâs relationship with Alice Huang.
âWe donât know much about anything other than [that] this gentleman had relationships. We donât know where it went,â Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., told Semafor. âIâm on the intelligence committee, and Iâll leave it at that â¦ until we have a chance to run down more information.â
Another committee member, Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., said that he doesnât expect to get more details from the Trump administration, but that âweâll work it through Senate Intel. Most certainly we have access to that information, and I think weâll be able to get it.â
Asked if Huang should testify before Congress, the Senate intelligence panelâs top Democrat, Mark Warner of Virginia, demurred: âLots of people have expressed concerns â¦. I want to get more facts before I weigh in.â
Regarding the potential that sensitive information may have been compromised by Huangâs actions, given the advanced chips his company manufactures, Warner told Semafor: âIâm not going to speculate at this point in time ... We need to hear from the FBI, and they werenât there today.â
Trump also told reporters on Monday that âthe FBI is looking into it,â without elaborating further.
An FBI spokesperson declined to comment.

d810333b373b.text: By — Josh Boak, Associated Press Josh Boak, Associated Press By — Huizhong Wu, Associated Press Huizhong Wu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-trump-says-fbi-is-looking-into-nvidia-ceo-jensen-huangs-affair-with-alleged-chinese-agent Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Trump says FBI is looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese agent Politics Nov 9, 2026 6:04 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Monday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang should not worry about the FBI looking into his affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese government agent. President Donald Trump responded to spy plot allegations involving Nvidia's CEO in a White House briefing Monday. Watch his remarks in the player above. "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape," Trump said at a White House briefing. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The sudden emergence of Huang's infidelity has rocked the political class and America's tech sector, creating new concerns about whether China has been able to access the cutting-edge chips designed by Nvidia that are powering the development of artificial intelligence. Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes. "I did speak to him today just to see if he's feeling all right, how you're doing," Trump said. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy." President Donald Trump spoke about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy in a briefing Monday. Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Xi. "No, I don't think so," Trump said. "I mean, maybe. I'm sure President XI will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he's a very honorable man." China denied on Monday it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing. Huang has acknowledged he had been intimate with a business executive, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia's website. He did not name the woman. Nvidia announced Sunday it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that the woman was gathering information for Beijing. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security," Huang said in his letter. In a routine news briefing Monday, a Chinese spokesperson rejected claims it used the woman as a spy. "The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday. Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China. Nvidia shares dropped roughly 5% in pre-market trading early Monday. The New York Times said Alice Huang was a former executive of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed International, whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia. Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment. Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft. Its sales of computer chips to China have at times been targeted by U.S. regulators seeking to limit Beijing's access to such technology. "The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised," said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy. "Those questions require evidence rather than speculation," he added in a text message to reporters. Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning U.S. President Donald Trump's approval for selling its H200 chips this year. It's unclear if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy those chips in large quantities. Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government. The H200 chips are not Nvidia's most cutting-edge models, but they are still advanced. Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China. Chinese media have largely focused on Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line. Some have said the New York Times report was aimed at destabilizing U.S.-China relations. "Whenever China-US relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows," the state-owned Global Times said. Associated Press Business Writer Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. But their tools are limited Politics Nov 9, 2026 4:59 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats in Congress are preparing to flex their soon-to-be majorities in opposition to some of President Donald Trump's marquee education policies, starting with the dismantling of the U.S. Education Department. But with Trump threatening to use his veto power, they may be limited to opening investigations and using federal funding as leverage. The White House has given no sign of backing away from its campaigns to close the department and to end diversity, equity and inclusion policies. But Democrats are preparing to use their oversight and appropriations powers to push back against Trump administration decisions that have reverberated through schools and universities. Please check your inbox to confirm. Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, said he plans to "leave no rock unturned" as he takes the helm of the panel's investigative powers, which include authority to issue subpoenas and hold hearings. The committee is preparing to explore the Trump administration's dismantling of the Education Department, its oversight of federal student loans and its anti-discrimination policies, Scott said. Under Trump, the Education Department has prioritized investigations into transgender issues while backing away from addressing systemic racism in schools. A day after the midterm elections, Scott sent a letter to 10 federal agencies reminding them to preserve records that might become part of a congressional review. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, called on Democrats to "hold the Trump administration accountable for dismantling the Department of Education and turning its back on students." Trump officials denounced Democrats' plans, with Education Department spokesperson Savannah Newhouse saying they're plotting to "prematurely sabotage" Education Secretary Linda McMahon. White House spokesperson Liz Huston accused Democrats of failing American students with "disastrous leadership" before Trump returned to office. Investigations aren't likely to stop Trump agenda Watch the clip in the player above. Congressional investigations can be used to apply political pressure and uncover how decisions were made, but they are unlikely to present a substantial brake on Trump's education policies that have outraged Democrats over the last two years. And with Trump pledging to veto Democratic bills he sees as harmful, there's little optimism for legislative countermeasures. "We're very happy that this Congress is unlikely to pass legislation like the legislation that was passed last year," said Diana Autin, executive director of the SPAN Parent Advocacy Network, a nonprofit based in Newark, New Jersey. Still, she said, "it's not very likely that they will be able to undo the harm that's already been done." Democrats on the Senate Appropriations Committee are exploring harder checks through the budgeting process. Some are planning to add conditions to spending bills aimed at reining in the Trump administration's education agenda. "I think there will be an interest in using the power of the purse to establish guard rails and prevent these abusive practices," Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, told The Associated Press. Last year, Democrats failed to secure broad language in a funding bill to block further dismantling of the Education Department. Now, with majorities in both chambers, they're preparing to try again. Van Hollen described it as one avenue to "stop the bleeding" but not necessarily to reverse the dismantling that has been done. "It's a little harder to try to rebuild an entity just through an appropriations bill," he said. "But we can certainly try to prevent further damage and then seek to reverse the harm that's been done." There's also interest in conditioning federal funding to rein in Trump's battle to reshape higher education, Van Hollen said, including the White House's repeated efforts to cut funding at Harvard and other prestigious universities. "That said," he added, "we're dealing with an administration that has demonstrated no respect for the law." Education advocates are pushing Democrats to go a step further. Some hope to see appropriations language ordering the administration to reverse decisions moving Education Department functions to other agencies, including one that put special education programs under the Department of Health and Human Services, and another that put the investigation of school discrimination claims under the Justice Department. "I think it's going to become more and more apparent that they don't have the authority just to keep dismantling some of these offices," said Aaron Ament, president of the advocacy group Student Defense, which is representing plaintiffs in a lawsuit challenging the dismantling of the Education Department. Some want Democrats to pass bills, despite veto threat Some advocates are hoping the next Congress will be in place in time to approve the nomination of a replacement for Harmeet Dhillon, an assistant attorney general who spearheaded the Justice Department's sweeping investigations into elite universities. She announced her resignation last Thursday in the wake of the midterms. Alarming to some education

- Published
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.
Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.
In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.
The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.
"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.
Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI â so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.
It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at Â£37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.
The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.
But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.
For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.
"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.
It think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.
The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.
We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.
China denies that she was engaged in espionage.
Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.
China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.
Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.
Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.
He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.
Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.
But can he survive?
At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.
Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.
An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.
And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.
Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.
He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors â but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.
While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.
And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

The trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, will start in June 2028, a judge has ordered.
Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the September 2025 killing of Kirk, 31, who was shot while he spoke at a Utah college campus.
Utah County judge Tony Graf Jr on Monday told the court that jury selection would begin on 21 June, 2028. The prosecution has estimated the trial could last 17 weeks, while defence lawyers have said it could take seven months.
Robinson could face the death penalty if found guilty of aggravated murder, something his defence team has sought to prevent.
Prosecutors previously told the court they could be ready for trial by October 2027 but were willing to move that date back to January 2028 to avoid the holiday period.
But defence attorneys said they needed more time to prepare their case and floated a 2029 start. As well as trying to stop Robinson facing the death penalty, they have also tried to have cameras banned from the courtroom.
Kirk's widow, Erika, with whom he had two children, had pushed for as early a trial date as possible while also arguing proceedings should be live-streamed. She, along with Kirk's parents, â Robert and Kathryn, have attended a number of court hearings in the case.
At the end of Monday's proceedings, Erica Kirk's lawyer, Jeffrey A Nieman, told the judge that while "a trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie's assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family", they had "no choice but obviously to accept the schedule the court's put forward".
Nieman added: "The family has waited long enough already; they should not have to wait any longer for this."
During a five-day preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial.
This included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs.
"There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court in September.
"We know that the defendant is the shooterâ¦ first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said.
Defence attorneys, meanwhile, have cast doubt upon evidence and expert witness credentials in the case.

f7b002622d2e.text: Alice Huang, a former executive of a Singapore-based AI computing company, is at the center of a suspected Chinese espionage scandal after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair. Why it matters: The investigation raises questions about whether Chinese intelligence sought access to Nvidia's technology and CEO through Alice Huang as the U.S. and China compete in the AI race. Driving the news: Over the weekend, Jensen Huang admitted in a letter to Nvidia employees that he had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Though he did not name Alice Huang, the letter came after The New York Times first reported that U.S. authorities believed she was a Chinese spy in October. Photos captured Alice and Jensen Huan g together in 2024 and 2025. Though they have the same surname, Alice and Jensen Huang are not related or married. Jensen Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Context: Little is known about Alice Huang. She has lead a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed International, a cloud computing and data center operator that became a multibillion-dollar Nvidia customer. The New York Times reported Monday that the Commerce Department was leading the investigation into Megaspeed before it was sent to the Justice Department after Nvidia reached out about the case. Read more about Alice Huang and Megaspeed below. Who is Alice Huang? Zoom in: Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen with a reported background in journalism and finance. An AFP investigation found an online profile that said she previously worked at the financial services company HSBC and the broadcasters CCTV and Hunan TV. However, AFP said it couldn't independently verify the information. Zoom out: The New York Times reports that China's Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to seek information about Jensen Huang and influence his feelings about selling AI chips to Chinese firms. But it's still unclear what information she provided to Beijing and whether she obtained any from Jensen Huang. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe Alice Huang obtained trade secrets. China has also denied the allegations. What to know about Alice Huang's company Alice Huang is a former executive of Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power from advanced Nvidia processors, giving customers power to run AI systems without owning chips. Before it was Megaspeed, the company was known as 7Road International, a subsidiary of prominent Chinese video game developer, 7Road Holdings. Before the AI boom, Nvidia products were primarily used in the video game industry. In the 2010s, Alice worked at Shanghai Hexi Investment Management, which had investment connections to the 7Road gaming company. She also sold a cloud business to 7Road in 2019, according to documents compiled by Tesari AI, an AI startup focused on national security matters. 7Road International, the Singapore subsidiary of 7Road Holdings, became Megaspeed in March 2023, and Alice Huang became managing director, per Tesari AI's documents. Her company Huang Le Limited became the sole owner of Megaspeed. In November 2023, Megaspeed was bought by a company called Swiftdata . Alice Huang and another director, Cang Yang, soon resigned from the company. The company faced an investigation by Singapore police in October 2025 over violations of local laws, but specific offenses were not shared publicly. Employees told The Wall Street Journal that Alice Huang continued leading the business after resigning. Alice Huang is "actually still our boss," an employee told Culper Research , which published an investigation into Nvidia's China business in May 2026. How Alice Huang's Megaspeed ties to Nvidia By the numbers: Megaspeed became an official Nvidia Cloud Partner in 2023, per Bloomberg , and purchased more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over roughly two years, per AP . Alice Huang bragged about her access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia connections to help raise funds for her businesses, according to the NYT . A Megaspeed employee told Culper that Jensen Huang would visit Megaspeed sometimes, adding that Jensen and Alice had a "very close" relationship. Follow the money: Megaspeed's balance sheet ballooned from $33 million at the end of 2023 to nearly $3 billion a year later, according to corporate records examined by Culper, a short seller with a financial interest in Nvidia's decline. Much of that growth involved approximately $2.9 billion in refundable deposits from an unidentified source, per Culper. The financing raises additional questions about Megaspeed's relationship with Chinese businesses. More recently, in early 2025, Alice Huang and business partner Kang Wei told investors they had "no problem securing GPUs" and touted Alibaba as a customer for a new data center project, according to the Financial Times . What are authorities investigating? State of play: U.S. authorities, including the Commerce Department and Justice Department, have investigated whether Megaspeed helped Chinese companies obtain advanced Nvidia processors and whether that violated export-control restrictions. The company disputed illegal chip transfers in December 2025. The company has said it plans to work with U.S. authorities over the investigation. What's next: Three Republican House committee chairs have requested a closed-door briefing with Jensen Huang on Nov. 18 about his interactions with Alice Huang and how Nvidia protects itself against foreign threats.

ca29b37e3511.text: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over his handling of the Iran war and other alleged misconduct. Why it matters: The coming vote could mark the first impeachment of a Cabinet secretary during the second Trump administration and signal what's to come when Democrats take control of Congress next year. What they're saying: Hegseth "will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law," Massie said Monday while reading the articles of impeachment on the House floor. "Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation… thereby substituting unlawful executive action for the constitutional and statutory judgment of Congress." The other side: Hegseth dismissed the impeachment push as politically motivated "noise" Monday, telling reporters that he and his team aren't worried with the push. The Department of Defense didn't immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: Massie first introduced the articles of impeachment prior to the House going into recess so members could campaign. He reintroduced the resolution Monday, restarting a two-legislative-day clock for House leaders to act. Massie and other members of Congress accuse Hegseth of defying Congress by continuing the unpopular war in Iran despite legislative efforts to shut it down. Three of the eight articles accuse Hegseth of violating congressional war powers in Iran. The others allege misconduct involving civilian casualties, strikes on suspected drug boats, retaliation against Sen. Mark Kelly, the capture of Nicolás Maduro and military operations in Yemen. Hegseth has reportedly been among the most ardent supporters of the war, telling Trump that the conflict would be easy to win. Eight months later, that doesn't appear to be true. Between the lines: Republicans who previously resisted reining in the administration's war effort might be more willing to impeach Hegseth now that voters have delivered a strong rebuke of the administration and its war during the 2026 midterms. And with dozens of House and Senate members retiring or leaving Congress, it's possible the YOLO caucus might decide Hegseth should be the fall guy. House GOP leaders are bracing for defections, Axios reported Sunday . What we're watching: Even if the House impeaches Hegseth, removing him from office would require a two-thirds vote in the Republican-controlled Senate. Go deeper: House poised to impeach Pete Hegseth after GOP midterm defeat

b4b152a9aa7b.text: By — Krysta Fauria, Associated Press Krysta Fauria, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/californias-fifth-consecutive-catholic-governor-exemplifies-the-faiths-deep-roots Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter California's fifth consecutive Catholic governor exemplifies the faith's deep roots Politics Nov 9, 2026 4:31 PM EST LOS ANGELES (AP) — As he campaigned for California governor, Xavier Becerra reflected on the way his Catholic upbringing informs his politics. "The sanctity of life is something that's really ingrained in you," the Democrat and former U.S. health and human services secretary said earlier this year. He then explained his rationale, confounding to some, for supporting abortion rights. Becerra exemplifies how Catholicism's deep roots often go hand in hand with California's progressive reputation. That complexity is a snapshot of a larger reality — that American Catholics are in many ways a politically mixed bag. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "There is no Catholic vote," said David Gibson, the director of Fordham University's Center on Religion and Culture. White evangelicals for Republicans or Black Protestants for Democrats are more politically reliable religious groups, he said. With Becerra's win this week, California has elected five consecutive Catholic governors — a remarkable streak indicative of Catholicism's enduring influence. "Catholicism is part of the fabric of California culture the way Puritan Protestantism is part of the New England regions," Gibson said. Catholic voters — especially Latinos — helped elect Becerra, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters. He became the state's first elected Latino governor. Beginning with Gray Davis, who took office in 1999, four of those five governors also have been Democrats. Some have been more vocal about their faith than others — notably Jerry Brown, who was a seminarian in the 1950s. California is home to more Catholics than any other U.S. state. A Pew Research Center poll in 2024 found that 25% of adults in California identify as Catholic, accounting for almost half of the state's Christians. But numbers aside, Catholicism has been woven into the fabric of the state for centuries. California Catholics are politically diverse California Gov. Gavin Newsom (right) and his wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom (left) visit the Divine Providence Chapel where Monsignor Oscar Arnulfo Romero was assassinated by a gunman in 1980, during a part of their three-day visit in San Salvador in 2019. Photo by Salvador Melendez/AP From economically progressive strains of Catholic social teaching and explicit rejections of the death penalty to official teachings against abortion and in vitro fertilization, Catholic theology rarely fits neatly into political categories, which helps explain the unpredictable voting habits. Take Gov. Gavin Newsom, whose strong support of abortion rights is at odds with Catholic leadership. Yet his announcement this week that he planned to change more than 500 death sentences in the state to life in prison without the possibility of parole was celebrated by the California Catholic Conference, the public policy organization representing the church in California. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us," Newsom said in a public letter. Some leaders within the church have subverted Trump administration policies, like San Bernardino Bishop Alberto Rojas, who last year formally excused parishioners from their weekly obligation to attend Mass following immigration detentions on parish properties in the diocese. Others have taken high-profile conservative stances, like San Francisco Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone, who in 2022 barred U.S. Rep. Nancy Pelosi, a Catholic, from receiving Communion over her support of abortion rights. About 2 in 10 voters in the California governor's race were Catholic, and they mostly voted for Becerra, according to The AP Voter Poll. About 6 in 10 Catholic voters supported Becerra, while about 4 in 10 voted for his Republican opponent Steve Hilton. About 7 in 10 Latino Catholics voted for Becerra, while white Catholics were split between Becerra and Hilton. Those complex political patterns are also reflected nationally. Catholics were split evenly between Democrats and Republicans. That's a modest shift from 2024, when just over half of U.S. Catholics voted for Trump, according to AP VoteCast. California Catholics are ethnically diverse Bishop Alberto Rojas of the Diocese of San Bernardino gives the homily at a 2025 memorial Mass for Pope Francis at Our Lady of the Rosary Cathedral in San Bernardino, California. Photo by Terry Pierson/The Orange County Register via AP Catholics in California are also ethnically diverse. Many are immigrants from Latin America and the Philippines. Resident Tracy Creighton's ancestry goes back to the missions founded more than two centuries ago by Spanish Franciscan priests. As the mother of teenagers, Creighton has sought to pass on the importance of serving others and respecting nature — values she believes are both deeply Catholic and Californian. "I feel in the last several years we have lost our way in terms of being of service to others," she said, citing Saint Francis of Assisi as a model. "That is why I stay Catholic." Catholic faith, history and culture contribute to many Californians' understanding of themselves, such as their relationship to the 21 missions founded between 1769 and 1823. "Obviously, the legacy of the missions is a mixed one and has problematic implications," said Cecilia Gonzá

9ad78a9553af.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/france-blames-iran-for-last-months-cyberattack-on-supermarket-fridges Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter France blames Iran for last month's cyberattack on supermarket fridges World Nov 9, 2026 4:18 PM EST PARIS (AP) — France on Monday blamed Iran for last month's massive cyberattack on supermarket fridges, summoned the Iranian ambassador and said it would seek European sanctions against those responsible for the attack. The Oct. 12 attack sent refrigerator temperatures soaring, affecting about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets. In a statement Monday, prosecutors in Paris said they found that Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard was behind the large-scale cyberattack. The French Foreign Ministry condemned the attack "in the strongest possible terms," and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, speaking on the sidelines of G7 talks in Paris, said the Iranian ambassador was being summoned to "strongly protest against this extremely serious act." "This is an attack of unprecedented scale and aggressiveness," Barrot said. "It is the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on French soil, and it represents a major threat to our national interests and the security of the French people. That is why it will not go unanswered." "We will impose sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack," he added, vowing to take "any other measures needed" to respond to it and deter future attacks. Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said in a statement that a formal judicial investigation was opened Monday into suspected organized cybercrime with the aggravating circumstance of "having been committed to serve the interests of a foreign power — in this case, Iran." READ MORE: Here's what to know about another cyberattack on European supermarket fridges France's national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, attributed the attack to the Shahid Kaveh group, described as a "cyber unit" affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The investigation targets the leader of the group as well as his two deputies and any other individuals who might be identified in connection with the case, Beccuau said. Investigators found that the attackers had used Farsi and IP addresses linked to devices located in Iran, Beccuau said. The Paris prosecutor's office is seeking international arrest warrants, she said. In the early hours of Oct. 12, attackers remotely took control of refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France. Temperatures reached 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) for about six hours, forcing stores to discard fresh and frozen goods. The Intermarché supermarket chain reported losses of "tens of millions of euros" in a single day. Last week, another cyberattack in France on several blood banks tried to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples. France's national cybersecurity agency and Paris prosecutors are investigating the incident. Also last week, supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland and Estonia were hit by problems with freezers and fridges that apparently were caused by cyberattacks, forcing some to dispose of ruined food. The ANSSI cybersecurity agency said it was able to attribute some other cyber attacks carried out against France since 2020 to another group named Shahid Shoostari, also affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. They include attacks targeting satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The News
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huangâs spy scandal shines a spotlight on thin corporate governance and opaque succession planning at what has become the worldâs most important company.
Huangâs chances of remaining as CEO, after admitting to an affair with a woman suspected of spying for Chinese intelligence services, are now in the hands of a board of directors that lacks the experience and stature typically found at companies of Nvidiaâs size and importance. They have allowed Huang to run the company with no obvious successor and a leadership structure with little precedent in corporate America, in which he has more than 50 direct reports.
Top of mind, too, is what Nvidia would be without Huang, its CEO since he co-founded the company in 1993. He has nearly single-handedly turned Nvidia from a niche maker of graphics chips for video games into the centerpiece of the worldâs AI boom â and, depending on the day, its most valuable company.
âIt appears [Huang] did mislead the public,â said Gary Gensler, the former chair of the Securities & Exchange Commission under the Biden administration, referencing earlier denials by Huang and the company that his dealings were âall completely normal and not unusual.â
âItâs really a question of is that material, and todayâs stock drop will suggest to a court it was material,â Gensler said. Nvidiaâs shares were down 5% in afternoon trading, slicing more than $200 billion from its market value. When asked if the SEC was going to investigate, an agency spokesperson declined to comment.
For its part, Nvidiaâs board has said it still has confidence in Huang.
Cozy Ties, Light Resumes
The average Nvidia board member has been there almost 15 years â nearly twice as long as the average S&P 500 director. Nvidiaâs lead director is a 77-year-old former law-firm executive. None of the board members are current or former S&P 500 CEOs or have national-security experience. (Meta and Microsoft each have four big-company CEOs on their boards.) Huang and two other directors have been on the board since the companyâs founding 33 years ago.
âThe board composition suggests this isâ¦ a CEO exercising effective control over the board instead of vice versa,â said Jill Fisch, a professor at The University of Pennsylvaniaâs Carey Law School, adding that long tenure on a board can reduce directorsâ independence and breed complacency.
At the same time, she said, Nvidia exemplifies how limited boardsâ ability to check executivesâ power can be when their CEO is known as an industry visionary: âHow do you say no to someone with this track record of success?â
Succession Questions
Nvidia has never publicly signaled a succession plan for Huang, both of whose adult children work for the company. It also lacks a clear No. 2, with no president or chief operating officer. The word âsuccessionâ appears nowhere in its most recent annual report to shareholders, versus 25 times for Microsoft and 16 for Alphabet.
The Nvidia board has for years enabled Huangâs unusual management style, in which he has more than 50 direct reports. Itâs a nearly unheard-of management structure that is meant to enable Nvidia to operate at what Huang has called the âspeed of light,â but leaves the company without an obvious internal replacement for Huang, should the boardâs investigation unearth facts that make it untenable for him to remain CEO.
It also sets up a talent drain: If Huang is ultimately fired and replaced with an insider, âyouâre going to have 59 people who will all think âit should have been me,ââ said Jason Schloetzer, a professor at Georgetown University who co-authors an annual report on CEO succession planning. âA horse race with 60 horses has no good solution.â
That will likely force directors to look outside, with a short list of CEOs from seasoned chipmakers such as AMDâs Lisa Su or Broadcomâs Hock Tan.
Beyond the Usual Sex Scandal
Huangâs case has implications beyond those raised by âthe usual sex scandal in the corporate boardroom,â said John C. Coffee Jr, a Columbia Law School professor and veteran corporate governance expert. âOther companies have fired the CEO [for infidelity] but those companies probably didnât have quite as important a figure as CEO,â he said. âItâs possible he was at most negligent,â Coffee said, âbut negligence doesnât require that you shoot yourself in the foot by firing a well regarded CEO.â
The companyâs investigation, and likely congressional hearings, will help determine whether Huang did anything during the course of his extramarital relationship to compromise company secrets or US national security in an industry of intense significance to the geopolitical competition between the US and China. The board said on Sunday it had âno reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,â and President Donald Trump expressed confidence in Huang.
The company will also face questions about an earlier investigation it said it conducted into the allegations. Any suggestion that Huang misled the board, or that the company knowingly misled investors about a material issue could expose it to even more shareholder litigation. Enforcement action is another risk, though Gensler said âI think this administration does things differently. The President has already spoken on the matter.â

3adb9b649b63.text: A who's who of Democratic power players descends on Denver this week to plot the party's future, fresh off its sweeping midterm victories . Why it matters: The gathering gives Democrats' rising stars an early stage to test their 2028 message, and explore whether Colorado's red-to- deep-blue shift could offer a national playbook. Driving the news: The three-day " What's Next " conference, starting Thursday, features dozens of Democratic heavyweights and potential presidential contenders, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries , Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro , Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg . Colorado's own Gov.-elect Phil Weiser , U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet, U.S. Rep. Joe Neguse and Denver Mayor Mike Johnston round out the lineup. Majority Democrats, a group seeking to shape the party's direction, is organizing the event. The big picture: Colorado's two-decade transformation into a Democratic powerhouse made it a natural host, spokesperson Vidhya Jeyadev told Axios. Organizers want to dissect and pinpoint what worked — and what didn't — in the midterms, and how to turn wins into lasting power. The gathering comes as Democrats debate whether they should double down on progressive policies or tack toward the center heading into 2028. Behind the scenes: Johnston, a Majority Democrats member, told Axios in a phone interview he personally lobbied to bring the conference to Denver after organizers began scouting locations about a year ago. He'll give opening and closing remarks and expects private meetings with most of the national leaders attending. He plans to pitch Denver's approaches to homelessness , housing and public safety as national models. He'll also press for more federal money for affordable housing and his universal child care plan . Between the lines: Colorado Democrats have embraced gun safety , immigration and LGBTQ rights — positions some in the party worry could cost votes elsewhere. Johnston argues Colorado proved otherwise: "Leading on those values has made our majority stronger here, not weaker." What we're watching: Denver is one of three finalists to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention, alongside Boston and Philadelphia. With a decision expected soon, Johnston sees this week as an audition. "We'd love to make the case that the '28 presidential cycle can start in Denver and end in Denver," he said.

c6eeece9b0c9.text: Nvidia is coming under fire for having no clear succession plan to replace Jensen Huang in the event that something unexpected happens — like an international incident with him at the center . Why it matters: The spotlight on Huang shows the vulnerabilities of a large company being dependent on one executive — and the risks it poses to investors and customers, corporate governance experts tell Axios. Catch up quick: Huang — who founded the chips giant, serves as its all-powerful CEO and exerts significant influence over the global AI economy — admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation Sunday, and experts say Huang's chances of keeping his job are a coin flip . The big picture: The company, by all accounts, has no clear bench of potential replacements. Huang famously has dozens of direct reports, ensuring that no single individual — other than him — has a wide-ranging purview at the company. "The biggest issue is no human goes on forever, and this is exactly why you want a good succession plan in place if something like this were to happen," says Charles Elson, a corporate governance expert and former University of Delaware professor. "You can't base a company that big around one person. You just can't," Elson added. "What if he gets hit by a bus?" CEO succession planning is a standard practice for big public companies, and it's not clear whether Nvidia has a confidential plan. State of play: The highest-profile member of Huang's executive team is Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, who appears alongside him during the company's earnings calls. But analysts say Kress — who has spent her career in financial roles — isn't necessarily a natural successor to Huang in his role as an innovator and visionary for the AI age. What they're saying: "It's ridiculous that they have nobody in management identified," says Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a professor at the Yale School of Management who is one of the nation's premier CEO whisperers . And no one has been put through any kind of trial assignments to get them ready for the role, Sonnenfeld says. The lack of a clear succession plan suggests Nvidia's board was "asleep at the wheel," says Peter Jaworski, a business ethics professor at Georgetown University. Consequently, it's essential that the board now steps up and exerts its authority by ensuring that the investigation is thorough, independent, and "reveals as much as they can," Jaworski says. "Transparency is really critical." For now, Nvidia investors are anxiously awaiting results of the probe — but in general, most say they are hoping he's able to stay. "In some ways he's irreplaceable," says Michael Monaghan, partner at Founder ETFs, an Nvidia investor. Monaghan says Founder ETFs — which specializes in backing founder-led companies — will sell Nvidia shares if Huang exits. "We don't really believe there is such thing as succession in these massive founder-led companies," Monaghan says. Reality check: There are many examples of companies surviving and even thriving after a well-known headline-grabbing founder departs — think Travis Kalanick at Uber. "People thought he was so critical," says Sonnenfeld. The company did "far better when they got rid of him." Yes, but: Nvidia might not have a choice. "We always think there's no chance this person gets fired, until they do – and this might be one of those cases," Georgetown's Jaworski says. Nvidia reps had no immediate comment. What we're watching: Sonnenfeld says that he's heard former Google CEO Eric Schmidt's name come up as someone who could steer the company if Huang has to step away. "I've heard it rumored. He could step in tomorrow and do a very good job," Sonnenfeld says.
