9b733aeb0098.text: The White House is "cautiously optimistic" as peace talks between Russia and Ukraine resume in Abu Dhabi this week, U.S. officials said on Monday. Why it matters: The talks on Tuesday and Wednesday will be the first time the parties have met with U.S. mediators present since February, when they were suspended due to the war in Iran. White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have worked for weeks to convince Russian President Vladimir Putin to restart negotiations. President Trump and his team hope Putin will be more willing to compromise after the U.S. lifted sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. "The relations we have built with Putin will be instrumental in these negotiations," a U.S. official said. After the meetings in Abu Dhabi, Witkoff and Kushner may travel to Moscow and Kyiv to speak directly with Putin and Zelensky, a U.S. official said. Yes, but: The parties remain far apart, particularly over potential territorial concessions by Ukraine. Russia's escalating attacks on Ukrainian cities and Putin's refusal to agree to a ceasefire have cast doubt on prospects for meaningful progress. Behind the scenes: Over the last two weeks, Witkoff and Kushner had daily phone calls — sometimes multiple times a day — with Russian and Ukrainian officials to prepare for the upcoming talks, U.S. officials said. What they're saying: U.S. officials who briefed reporters on Monday struck a positive tone despite skepticism in Europe and Ukraine about Putin's willingness to end the war. "There is a shot to make significant progress towards a deal and to try and bridge the gaps," a U.S. official said. "Getting the parties back to the table wasn't easy to do and we see promising signs as mediators." The official added that Witkoff and Kushner want to use the talks to "crystallize" the decisions Putin and Zelensky will have to make. Driving the news: The talks in Abu Dhabi will focus on two tracks: A military working group led by the commander of U.S. European command, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, will discuss post-war ceasefire monitoring and security arrangements. The working group made significant progress on this front during the last round of talks in February. A political working group that focuses on the most sensitive topic: territorial demands. There was no progress on this issue in February. State of play: The two sides haven't budged publicly. Russia is demanding control over the entire region of Donbas, while Ukraine insists that territory be divided based on current front lines. In private, though, U.S. officials say that both sides "have shown a little bit of flexibility" on the territorial issue in recent weeks. They say an agreement on territory won't be possible until security guarantees are reached. The big picture: Witkoff and Kushner invited senior officials from NATO, the EU and four major European powers — the UK, France, Germany and Italy — to Abu Dhabi to hold separate discussions on the sidelines of the Russia-Ukraine negotiations. Ukraine's European allies will play a key role in any post-war security arrangements. The U.S. also wants to start a third track of negotiations between European countries and Russia to create new ways of easing tensions and avoiding conflict. But many European countries are highly suspicious of the idea. They believe it endorses a Russian narrative that Europe is a security threat to Moscow and worry it will result in weakening NATO. U.S. officials stress that the proposed Europe-Russia security initiative would not replace or diminish NATO and the central role it plays in protecting Europe. But a new security agreement between Europe and Russia would help end the war in Ukraine, they say. A U.S. official said Witkoff and Kushner hope Russians will agree to include European representatives in the next round of peace talks after Abu Dhabi. What to watch: Ukrainian officials say they have three priorities for the talks: Clinching a deal to de-escalate tensions on the Black Sea and allow grain exports. Reaching an agreement to stop attacks on Ukrainian power plants and Russian oil refineries before the winter. Organizing a trilateral summit between Trump, Putin and Zelensky, possibly during the G20 summit in Miami next month.

At least 17 people have died and 12 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.
All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.
The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.
Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.
President Recep Tayyip ErdoÄan originally said the death toll was 16, but the Health Minister, Kemal MemiÅoÄlu, later announced that one of those who had been critically injured had later died, taking the toll to 17.
Eyewitnesses at the scene said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.
In a statement, the company that runs the factory said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.
Izmir Governor SÃ¼leyman Elban told media that some people were believed to still be under the rubble.
Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, ErdoÄan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued.
At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports.
The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs.

8d90595b5e43.text: By — Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-rep-massie-speaks-after-filing-hegseth-impeachment-resolution Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Rep. Massie speaks after filing Hegseth impeachment resolution Politics Updated on Nov 9, 2026 6:57 PM EST — Published on Nov 9, 2026 3:26 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, pressing his fellow Republicans to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping election losses blamed in part on fallout from the war in Iran. Watch Massie's remarks from the House floor Monday in the video player above. Massie, a Kentucky Republican, read the impeachment resolution from the House floor just hours after it opened for the first day of sessions after the midterms. It largely focuses on the war in Iran but also includes references to Hegseth's role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela. The congressman, who was defeated by a Trump-backed challenger in a primary earlier this year, said Hegseth's actions amounted to "high crimes and misdemeanors." Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News. Hegseth, he said, "knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders" and "remains a threat to the Constitution." President Donald Trump lashed out at Massie personally just hours after the congressman read the resolution, calling him a "loser" who "has a lot of hatred in his heart." In a briefing Monday, President Donald Trump addressed the impeachment threat that looms for his defense secretary. Watch his remarks in the player above. A vote in the House could come by mid-week, but next steps are highly uncertain. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries supports the measure. If most Democrats follow him, Massie would only need support from a few Republicans to impeach Hegseth. WATCH LIVE: House returns to Washington after blowout election for Democrats If the House votes to impeach, it would fall to to the Senate to either dismiss the charges or hold a trial. Republicans remain in the majority in both chambers, until the new Congress convenes in January with Democrats in control. Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Democratic leader, endorsed the impeachment push. "Hegseth must stand trial before the Senate," he said. Republican leaders, who are eager to use their final weeks in power executing their own agenda, expressed frustration at the move. House Speaker Mike Johnson, who has tried to prevent the vote, said impeachment "in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look, a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see that." Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he wasn't sure why the vote was being held now. "We'll see what their ultimate decision is over there," he said of the House. "We'll have to deal with it accordingly here." Hegseth issues his own defense and prepares for a fight Hegseth is stepping up his public statements ahead of the vote, telling reporters that he's eager to defend the military actions that he and Trump have taken against Iran, Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela's previous leaders. After giving a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island, he brushed aside the impeachment push. "There's a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success," he told reporters. He added that "if we want to litigate" the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, "I'm happy to do it all day long." WATCH: Hegseth speaks at the Naval War College as possible impeachment vote looms Asked about Vice President JD Vance blaming the Iran war for the massive GOP losses in the election, Hegseth noted that Trump said he would do it again, and "I agree." Hegseth also announced that he would hold a rare news conference on Tuesday — his first in over 180 days — on the impeachment threat. Hegseth argued that the war was necessary because "someone had to confront the Iranian regime's pursuit of a nuclear weapon" and said "the choice was don't act and wish it away or take a bold move." Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%. Trump defended Hegseth to reporters on Monday, commending him for having "won the war" in Venezuela and "winning the war" in Iran, which continues to drag on. Pentagon chief insists 'Iran is devastated' Hegseth reiterated that "Iran is devastated," even though the Islamic Republic has been able to keep striking military bases in the Middle East that are used by the United States, causing billions of dollars in damage, as well as commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Disruptions to shipping in the waterway, where one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the war, have led to higher energy prices that hit voters' pocketbooks. Hegseth's defense of the war comes after about 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the "wrong decision" in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States. Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended his fellow Cabinet secretary, saying that he believes Hegesth has been doing "a great job" and that its unfair that a Republican is pushing the impeachment effort. "I work with him. And so I see perhaps a side of him that the media doesn't see and members of Congress may not see," Rubio told reporters at the Group of Seven industrialized democracies gathering in Paris. "But I think Pete works really hard. He's incredibly smart." Associated Press writers Kevin Freking, Lisa Mascaro, Joey Cappelletti and Farnoush Ami

Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report, external.
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.
The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.
Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."
After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.
US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".
However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (Â£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.
While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.
But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry.
"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.
Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.
Huang's position vulnerable unlike other tech bosses
A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.
Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.
He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.
By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.
Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."
The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.
Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.
Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.
Additional reporter by Samira Hussain, North America business correspondent.

Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.
"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."
Trump's comments came after he met the Qatari prime minister. Qatar is a US ally in the Gulf region, and one of Iran's neighbours, which has been a key mediator in efforts to end the war.
Addressing reporters in the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.
Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about Trump's prior comments about resolving the conflict.
This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.
The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war.
Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict.
Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the war, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.
"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," he said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.
Global oil prices, which have fallen sharply since the midterms, dipped further after Trump's comments.
On Tuesday afternoon in Asia, Brent crude was more than 1% lower at $91.50 (Â£52) while US-traded was down by 1.2% at $85.82.
Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war.
In a post on X, the Qatari leader said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region".
Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February.
Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to the threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region.
Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration.
Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him.
Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham".
While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate.

Kim Kardashian's Skims is offering customers refunds for its $148 (Â£110) advent calendar which has been widely criticised on social media.
The accessories advent calendar promised "twelve days of fun surprises" but has been mocked online for the quality of its contents, such as hair clips and keychains, with some comparing them to something you would find down the back of a sofa.
A spokesperson for Skims has told a number of media outlets "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations" and the company has "personally contacted every customer" to offer a full refund or credit to put towards other products".
The BBC has contacted Skims for comment.
The shapewear and clothing business was co-founder by Kardashian in 2019 and has made the reality TV star a billionaire, according to Forbes magazine.
Skims was valued at $5bn in 2025 when it raised millions of dollars in new funding.
One account on TikTok called spicychathouse compared the contents of the calendar to things "my cat collects from around my house". Another account said it looked like "a bunch of stuff that Kim Kardashian was emptying out of her bedside table".
A number of accounts showed people cleaning out their own sofas and claiming they had accidentally created the Skims advent calendar.

At least 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in the Democratic Republic of Congo for cowardice, mutiny and refusing to obey orders, local media report.
The sentences followed a trial of 71 soldiers before a military court in Walikale, in North Kivu province, in eastern DR Congo. Four soldiers were acquitted, while another was sentenced to 10 years in prison.
The army said the trial was intended to improve discipline among troops as they battle armed groups in eastern DR Congo.
The region has endured decades of conflict, with fighting continuing between government forces and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), a rebel coalition that includes the M23 group.
The soldiers were reportedly arrested on 20 October in Walikale, where they were accused of abandoning their positions and fleeing during clashes with FRN fighters.
The Congolese army's campaign against armed groups, including the M23, has long been undermined by poor discipline and disorganisation within its ranks.
The government has repeatedly accused neighbouring Rwanda of supporting the M23, an allegation denied by both Kigali and the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
The army has faced persistent criticism over its lack of professionalism and disciplined, while soldiers have complained of poor pay and inadequate equipment.
Last month, another 27 soldiers were sentenced to death on similar charges of cowardice after reportedly withdrawing from the frontline during clashes with rebels.
In March 2024, DR Congo lifted a 20-year moratorium on the death penalty, citing the need to remove "traitors" within the army.
The government said capital punishment would also apply to people involved in armed groups, insurrection, as well as committing treason and war crimes.
The decision to reinstate the death penalty was widely criticised by rights groups. However, no formal executions have been carried out since the moratorium was lifted.
Since the beginning of 2025, at least 507 soldiers have been convicted, including 381 death sentences, according to figures compiled by French broadcaster RFI.
In October 2025, former Congolese President Joseph Kabila was sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself. He has since been named as the FRN's leader.

Local villagers are hoping to buy an ancient woodland so it can be saved from private sale and continue to be a sanctuary for generations to come.
Landowners Margaret and David Lloyd have allowed the public to enjoy their 17-acre Ruscombe Wood near Stroud for the last 20 years but have now decided to sell up.
Keen for it to go into the hands of local residents, the couple have given Ruscombe Woodlands Committee one year to raise Â£164,000 to cover purchase, legal and survey costs.
Martin Humphreys from the committee said: "I like the idea that if we own the woods, nature will become part of the community and we can have that instead of a community hall."
More from Gloucestershire
Made up of local residents, the committee have now launched a fundraising campaign to raise the funds for the purchase and said it hopes to protect wildlife and habitat, along with guaranteeing permissive footpaths at the site continue to stay open for everyone.
It also hopes to offer free workshops, including on woodland care, natural skills and creative crafts.
Margaret, 79, said they had decided it was time to sell their "pretty special piece of ancient woodland" after realising it had become "too much work" for them.
"We want the community to buy it because they all love it and we want it loved like we've loved it all this time," she said.
"Really, we'd like it sold now and we could put it back on the market, but it wouldn't be the same, so the only snag for us is that it wont get done until November 2027," she added.
Margaret said the group also have plans to use the space as a forest school.
Martin said it was "very nice" that the couple had given them time to raise the money needed for the purchase.
He said while the group has to get through a lot of legalities, he likes the idea that the woodland could eventually be owned by everybody.
"It has no public rights of way, it's not been spoilt or overworked, it's wild and has lots of creatures that have made their homes there.
"It has a wonderful silent quality," Humphreys added.

Up to 900 artificial nest "cups" for threatened house martins are set to be installed in Hampshire as part of a conservation project.
The birds migrate from Africa each spring and are on the UK's Red List of endangered bird species. They are thought to have suffered from a lack of wet mud to build nests during the extreme heat in the summer.
Following a pilot project, The Hampshire House Martins Project is offering free cups which save the birds time and energy compared to building their own mud nests.
Project co-ordinator Nigel Matthews encouraged residents, schools and businesses to apply for the free artificial nests "to give these remarkable birds a safe place to raise their young".
Between 1995 and 2024, the UK House Martin population fell by 40%, partly due to poor breeding success.
The birds build distinctive cup-shaped nests beneath the roofs of houses and other buildings, carrying around 1,000 pellets of soft mud to complete each one.
Each April and May, house martins return from Africa to spend the summer in the UK.
The birds often form colonies with several nests in close proximity.
The decline in numbers has been blamed on a fall in quantities of insects, as well as hotter, drier weather - as seen during the summer of 2026 - resulting in less wet mud available for nest building.
Modern homes tending to have uPVC soffits also makes it difficult for mud nests to adhere.
Last year the Hampshire Ornithological Society initiative launched a survey, allowing members of the public to record house martin nest locations.
The group is now looking for additional properties where artificial nests will be provided and fitted free of charge - thought to be the biggest such project in the country.
During the project's pilot, 249 artificial nest cups were installed on buildings close to known nesting sites across northern and eastern Hampshire.
Twenty seven were used by house martins this summer, more than the project team had expected.
Keith Betton, chair of Hampshire Ornithological Society, said: "The response to the first pilot stage of this project showed how strongly people across Hampshire want to help house martins.
"This next phase turns what we have learnt into action by offering hundreds more safe, ready-made nests.
"It gives homeowners, schools and businesses a simple, practical way to support the recovery of this threatened bird."
To quality for a cup, which are provided and installed for free, properties must be within 1km (0.6 miles) of a previously recorded house martin nest.
Host buildings must have suitable overhanging eaves at second story level, between four and seven metres from the ground.
Applications for the nest cups can be made on the Hampshire House Martins Project, external website.

Most people know rainforests are vital in the fight against climate change, but now scientists say wetlands could be even more important.
Saltmarshes, mangrove swamps and wetlands can absorb carbon "four times faster than trees", according to the charity the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT).
Celebrating 80 years since WWT's first wetland bird reserve was founded at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, the charity's leaders have called for one million hectares of wetlands to be restored across the world.
Sarah Fowler, CEO of WWT, said: "They are mood-boosting, flood-buffering, water-purifying, incredible habitats. But we have lost 85% of the world's wetlands."
WWT now runs 10 wetland bird reserves across the UK.
Many people come to enjoy the swans, geese, flamingoes and migrating wildfowl, but do not realise how powerful these habitats can be in soaking up carbon and slowing down climate change.
So how vital are wetlands for birds, and how powerful can they be in the fight against climate change?
'Patron Saint of Conservation'
In November 1946, a naturalist called Peter Scott came to a wild marshy area on the banks of the River Severn, near Slimbridge. He was drawn by the thousands of migrating geese and swans that flew thousands of miles from the Russian Arctic to spend the winter here on the mudflats and marshes.
Captivated, Scott settled in a small cottage and later built a house right on a lake, with a huge window to watch the wildfowl.
He dug lakes and connecting channels, built hides and even towers to watch the birds without disturbing them.
Over the years, the reserve grew and became home to thousands of ducks, swans , geese as well as the migrating wildfowl.
"He really was a pioneer in conservation," said Chris Moore, a historian of Slimbridge and author of Peter Scott and the Birth of Modern Conservation.
As well as creating a safe haven for endangered species, Scott was a vigorous campaigner for nature.
He led the fight to stop commercial whaling, presented some of the BBC's first natural history programmes called live from Slimbridge, and helped set up WWF, the World Wildlife Fund.
In 1973 Sir Peter Scott became the first person to be knighted for conservation work.
Moore explained: "Scott was talking about the impact that man was having on the natural world, long before we started talking about climate change and global warming.
"David Attenborough called him the Patron Saint of Conservation, and I think that is more than deserved," Moore added.
More from Gloucestershire
One of Scott's typically ambitious projects was to save the Hawaiian Goose, or NÄnÄ.
Unique to the Pacific islands, the NÄnÄ was hit hard by road building and development. By 1949 barely 24 birds remained.
Scott heard of its plight, and asked Hawaiian authorities to send a few geese to Slimbridge where he hand-reared them.
"Unfortunately they sent us two females," chuckled Enid Cole, a WWT volunteer at Slimbridge.
"Peter asked them for a gander - 'It would help', he said."
Nine chicks were later born, and hand-raised successfully to adulthood at Slimbridge.
Today there are more than 3,000 NÄnÄ geese, most of them living peacefully on Hawaiian golf courses. But a handful still live at Slimbridge, where Enid Cole and her friends hand feed them lettuce every day.
"It's a marvelous project, and typical of Sir Peter," Enid smiled.
Over the last 80 years, the teams at Slimbridge have hand-reared several other species, including the Common Crane and the world's rarest diving duck, the Madagascan Pochard.
It was while they were working to save the Madagascan Pochard that they realised how vital the wetland habitats were.
"We realised that to save that species, we had to bring the wetland back," explained Sarah Fowler, WWT's chief executive.
"And to bring the wetland back, we had to work with the whole community in Madagascar."
Ian Hollister, a volunteer warden at Slimbridge, said: "The wetlands are great at absorbing carbon, they're like a soggy secret weapon."
Saltmarshes 'bury carbon'
Scientists calculate that 85% of the world's wetland habitats have been lost as marshes drained for agriculture, and swamps cleared for construction as cities expand.
And yet, as Fowler explained, "40% of the world's species rely on wetland habitats for survival".
What started at Slimbridge has spread to 10 wetland reserves across the UK with the charity now working with local councils to restore wetlands, even in small city areas.
A scheme in Bristol has seen small floating islands of wetland plants moored in the city's harbour.
Across the world, they are campaigning to restore one million hectares of lost wetland, partly to provide safe habitats for endangered species but also because wetlands help absorb carbon far quicker than even forests.
"Salt marshes bury carbon," said Fowler.
"Every time the big tides go over them, the plants that have grown up in the salt marsh get buried. Those plants are full of carbon, so they are a massive carbon sink.
"And the brilliant thing about salt marshes is they do this four times faster than trees. Wetlands are vital in our fight against climate change, and we must restore them."
What started 80 years ago as a bird reserve on the banks of a river in Gloucestershire has grown into a global campaign to restore wetlands, which they call the "soggy secret weapon" against climate change.

The University of Oxford has returned the remains of 39 people taken from the Naga community during British colonial rule in India.
A delegation of around 30 people from Nagaland, a mountainous state in north-eastern India, attended a ceremony at Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum on Monday to mark the handover.
The remains, most of which are skulls, will be taken back to India and given what Naga tribal leaders have described as a "respectful rest". There are plans to bury them under a joint memorial in a park in Nagaland.
Museum director Laura Van Broekhoven described it as "a historic moment that will be part of stories told to next generations".
She said the remains were finally on their way home after overcoming "so much red tape everywhere".
The human remains were displayed at the Oxford museum for decades before being removed from public view in 2020 as part of what it described as a "decolonisation process".
The Pitt Rivers Museum holds more than 6,000 objects associated with Naga culture, believed to be the largest such collection in the world. Most were acquired during British colonial rule in India and Myanmar (the former Burma).
The museum's website lists 219 items as human remains.
These were added to the museum's collection between 1910 and 1940 and mostly collected by two colonial administrators who were anthropologists.
The museum's website, external mentions that the objects collected during this period were "frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given".
During their visit to Oxford, the Naga delegation also met descendants of one of the anthropologists involved in collecting the remains.
"The manner in which these human remains were taken away from our land leaves much for us to speculate," one of the tribal leaders, Thejao Vihienuo, told AFP.
"I suspect that nobody would have given the skull of his father or his grandfather as a gift to another person."
Anthropologists say that the Naga people once practised head hunting, severing the heads of enemies as trophies. But they also kept the heads of their own chiefs at the centre of villages.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, founded in the 19th Century, has previously returned human remains to indigenous communities in Australia, New Zealand and the US.
The latest handover to India concerns only the 39 ancestral remains and comes after a visit by a Naga delegation to Oxford in 2025, when it formally requested their return.
The museum had announced in September that the remains would be returned to India.

8f981035a6a6.text:
- Published
Thousands of people joined a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night, in memory of those killed and injured when a gunman went on a violent rampage at the weekend.
The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times.
As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower.
Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, each one marking a spot where someone died.
Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened.
The alleged gunman has been named as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski by local media.
Critically injured in a shoot-out with police, he did not regain consciousness and died in hospital early on Monday.
Initially, the interior minister claimed that Oksinski was driven by far-right, extremist views. The national prosecutor's office now says that it is too soon to say he was "inspired" by any ideology.
"The minister wanted to win domestic political points. That's not responsible behaviour," Pawel Musialek of the Jagiellonian University suggests, in a country where politics is highly - and often viciously - polarised.
"So far we've seen no clear message that this guy was strongly ideological, and that it's not more like something from the darknet."
There has been no mention of any letter or manifesto that Oksinski left. One neighbour told Polish news site Onet that the 24-year-old was a "bit of a loner" but few who knew him well have spoken publicly.
In addition to his electronic devices like his phone, investigators are examining a number of badges that Oksinski had attached to his military-style outfit.
The prosecutor's office says a yellow Gadsden flag with a coiled snake symbol was displayed in his bedroom. "It has various meanings of freedom and rebellion," a spokesman emphasised. "Not necessarily negative."
It was at Oksinski's home that the bodies of his parents and sister were discovered.
It is alleged that he shot them, before driving some 200km (125 miles) south to continue the killing in Krakow.
Two days on, shops and cafes around the market square are beginning to fill up again, but the mood is subdued.
A Zara clothes shop is still boarded up, after bullets smashed the glass. A local man in his 50s died just outside.
Jo, a Scottish tourist, saw paramedics "who got there ridiculously fast", fighting to save him. "It was all pretty grim."
Like many, she initially mistook the rifle shots for fireworks.
On the opposite corner of the square, beside another cluster of flowers, people keep pausing to take pictures of the holes that were blasted into the wall by gunfire.
One of the six victims has been identified as a Polish painter in her 50s, who was a mother of four, and in town with friends for an exhibition opening.
A British citizen and an Austrian who died are yet to be named publicly.
Several drivers of the horse-drawn carriages that are usually poised to trot tourists around the square were seriously injured.
Olha, who works in a nearby chocolate shop says everyone is now nervous.
On Saturday, people rushed into her store to escape the gunman who was tearing around in his car, firing through the window.
Olha is Ukrainian, and moved to Krakow when Russia invaded. "We left our own country for safety. This is supposed to be a safe place!" she said.
"It's so sad, and so scary. Especially that he drove all the way here for two hours, planning this and thinking about it."
She regrets that the gunman did not survive: "So many are dead, so many lives have been ruined, and now there will be no justice."
When Oksinski's car was searched, four firearms and "hundreds of rounds of ammunition" were found, all owned legally by the alleged killer and his father.
Both were members of the Swit Starachowice sports club, where there is a shooting range. A spokesman recalls Michal Oksinski as unremarkable: average competition results and normal behaviour.
He had been just three times this year, most recently in August with his father. The club spokesman is adamant that it does not train combat firing, only shooting from a fixed point.
Gun ownership in Poland has grown considerably since war broke out in Ukraine just across the border, but this is the first mass shooting anyone here can remember.
Inevitably, it has brought scrutiny of the checks over who qualifies to handle such weapons, including psychological tests, as Michal Oksinski passed all of them.
On Monday, the government announced an urgent review.
At the spot where Oksinski's car was intercepted and he was shot by police there is another memorial, this one in honour of the officers still in hospital.
Some have brought flowers, but a girl called Bianka has left a card that reads: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon."
A couple of steps away, there's a series of bullet holes in the glass.
"This man was a real hero, he didn't hesitate," Ania says, referring to officer Jakub Kulik who was shot in the chest. His condition remains serious. "We're here to help him fight for his life."
"Nothing like this has never happened before, it's terrible," a young man called Wojtek tells me.
He's only glad that the gunman responsible for such horror turned out to be Polish.
"People here are already against immigration, so that would have been even worse."
Ania thinks Poles will pull through, though the country's image as a low-crime oasis has been shattered.
Most of all, she's angry that Michal Oksinski died without being held to account for the devastation.
"I think we deserve to know why."

Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.
In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

- Published
California voters have voted to reject a wealth tax on its billionaires.
The ballot proposal would have levied a one-time tax on the state's mega wealthy to help fund healthcare. It took nearly a week of counting votes after the midterm election to determine a projection on the measure.
There are about 200 billionaires in the state, including Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, reality television star Kim Kardashian and media mogul Oprah Winfrey.
Proposition 40 targeted Californians with a wealth of more than $1.1bn (Â£800m) with a 5% tax on their total wealth, including assets such as shares as well as income. It failed amid divisions among Democrats and labour unions.
Had it passed, experts believe it would have been the world's first wealth tax targeting billionaires.
The tax would have raised about $100bn to make up for federal funding cuts to healthcare in California as a result of President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.
Those who backed the measure had argued it would help ensure that the ultra-wealthy were contributing their fair share and helping backfill gaps in the state's budget.
The wealth tax faced fierce opposition, including from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, as well as California Governor Gavin Newsom and labour unions.
Newsom, whose tenure as governor is coming to an end, had expressed concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.
Some billionaire critics of the measure spent millions trying to crush it, with a handful even moving out of the state to evade the possible tax. Brin gave more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the tax, according to the Los Angeles Times.
Dave Regan, head of the union that led the charge for the measure, said on election night that the billionaires' efforts to block the tax created "a lot of confusion and a lot of second-guessing among people who really in their hearts know what the right the thing to do is".
Regan, who is president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, pledged to seek a billionaire tax once more in 2028.
The measure had odds stacked against it, with two other propositions on the ballot that would have effectively reversed it, even if it passed.
California, home to some 23 million registered voters, has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy. It is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world, but also has one of the highest wealth gaps.

2e464a213b94.text:
Trump nominates Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA
If confirmed, the cybersecurity executive would take over an agency rebuilding after workforce cuts and nearly 22 months without a permanent director.
President Donald Trump nominated Palantir’s chief information security officer, Michael LoSapio, to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on Monday, seeking to fill a leadership vacancy that has stretched through nearly two years of staffing cuts and other changes to the agency.
LoSapio would oversee the federal government’s main civilian cyberdefense unit, which helps protect agency networks and works with operators of water systems, power grids, telecommunications networks and other critical infrastructure to prevent and respond to attacks.
He has served as Palantir’s CISO since September 2024, according to his LinkedIn profile. Before that, he led the company’s infrastructure and network security group, starting in December 2017.
CISA has been without a permanent Senate-confirmed director since then-Jen Easterly’s departure in January 2025. Nick Andersen has led the agency in an acting capacity since February after a series of incidents tied to its previous acting director, Madhu Gottumukkala.
LoSapio’s nomination faces a crowded Senate calendar, with lawmakers working to fund the government and approve defense legislation before the year ends. It’s possible his consideration would fall to the incoming Democratic majority if Republicans do not complete his confirmation during the remaining session.
If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic majority. That could bring additional scrutiny of his work at Palantir, whose government contracts and handling of sensitive information have drawn questions from Democrats.
Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., previously said he plans to renew inquiries into the company’s work with the administration when he begins chairing the Senate Finance Committee, and said lawmakers could compel answers if the company does not cooperate.
Democratic lawmakers have questioned whether Palantir’s work with the Department of Homeland Security enables government surveillance of Americans. The company has denied conducting or enabling mass surveillance.
LoSapio did not immediately respond to a request for comment. He previously worked at Palantir as a systems engineer from 2013 to 2016, then spent more than a year at database company SingleStore before returning. Earlier roles included systems engineering at New York University and Seton Hall University.
Trump’s previous choice for CISA director, Sean Plankey, withdrew from consideration in April after spending more than a year awaiting confirmation. His nomination became entangled in a dispute with Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., over Coast Guard contracting.
If confirmed, LoSapio would inherit an agency attempting to recover from cuts that reduced its workforce by roughly a third since Trump returned to office. CISA has since moved to refill a few hundred positions.
In line with possible opposition to his employer, House Democrats have also pledged to investigate CISA’s workforce cuts and changes to its election security work.
Last month, the agency released a strategy calling for a review of its services and greater attention to infrastructure whose disruption would cause the most harm to public safety, the economy and national security.

Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.
In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".
The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.
Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.
The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.
On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".
Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; Â£514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.
"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.
The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business".
The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI".
Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia.
Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work.
The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

154a39172dfa.text:
- Published
A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.
The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.
Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".
The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.
"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".
Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.
The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.
Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (Â£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.
"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.
However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.
While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.
CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.
It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.
Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".
The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.
As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.
It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

cde614515744.text: Current and former House Democrats, flush with victory following their landslide midterm wins , are already looking at potential opportunities to run for Senate in 2028, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Democrats' 2026 romp — with wins in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and possibly even Mississippi — has some party members reevaluating what were once considered impossible targets. A source close to Rep. Sharice Davids (D-Kan.) — who was reelected by 21 percentage points in a district former Vice President Harris carried by four points in 2024 — did not rule out her running against Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.). "All options are on the table," the source said, adding that Davids' "focus right now is on delivering actual results and overcoming the chaos from these extreme policies we're seeing." Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) was defeated by Democrat Adam Hamilton last week, marking the first time in nearly a century a Democrat has been elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas. North Carolina: Rep. Don Davis is "taking a look at" a run against Republican Sen. Ted Budd, a source familiar with his thinking told Axios. Davis won a third term on Tuesday after defeating his GOP opponent in a district President Trump carried by 12 points in 2024. Republicans redrew the district with the express goal of ensuring Davis' loss. Former Rep. Wiley Nickel, who was elected Wake County district attorney on Tuesday, would consider a Senate run if state Attorney General Jeff Jackson doesn't, a source close to him told Axios. The two served together in the House. Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper won North Carolina's other U.S. Senate seat last week in a nearly 20-percentage-point landslide over Republican Michael Whatley. Pennsylvania: A huge field of Democrats is gearing up to potentially run for the seat held by Democratic Sen. John Fetterman. Fetterman, who has morphed from a populist firebrand to an arch-centrist, has angered much of the party by siding with Republicans on key votes. Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) told Axios in a statement: "I am thinking hard about my next steps and will be having that conversation with my family and supporters." Said former Rep. Susan Wild: "I am not ruling anything out at this time. ... I think PA is long overdue for a woman senator, and that will factor into my eventual decision." Florida: State Rep. Angie Nixon is already hinting at a 2028 run against Republican Sen. Ashley Moody after losing to her on Tuesday by three percentage points. But some in the party's centrist wing believe Nixon's left-wing politics and her affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America may have cost her in a Democratic wave year and are looking to recruit elsewhere. Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.), who won reelection in a district Trump carried by nine points in 2024 and is often mentioned as a potential candidate for statewide office, is in the mix, sources said. Sources also pointed to Rep. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), who won in a district that went for Trump by 11 points, as another possible candidate. A Castor spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

aa8d4bb52e38.text: The French government has blamed an Iranian military hacking unit for cyberattacks that disrupted refrigeration systems at roughly 700 grocery stores and other retail locations last month, causing food losses and at least 15 fires. Why it matters: The attacks underscore how Iranian government hackers are moving beyond stealing data and disrupting websites to manipulating the physical equipment that keeps essential services running. Driving the news: France's Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs attributed the Oct. 11–12 attacks to Iran on Monday, calling them the country's first cyberattack campaign conducted purely for sabotage on French territory. The government's Cyber Crisis Coordination Center specifically attributed the attacks to Shahid Kaveh, a hacking unit within Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Hackers manipulated refrigeration equipment to raise temperatures, causing tens of millions of euros in food losses and at least 15 fires, according to French officials. The same operation also targeted equipment at small hydroelectric facilities in France, with limited effects, according to an intelligence report. Yes, but: The French government has not publicly attributed a separate wave of refrigeration attacks that occurred last week to the same hackers. Zoom in: French intelligence linked Shahid Kaveh to several online hacktivist personas, including CyberAveng3rs and Soldiers of Solomon, that publicly claim responsibility for the unit's operations. Investigators found that infrastructure used in the refrigeration attacks was also used to scan industrial equipment using techniques previously associated with Shahid Kaveh. They also found traces of Farsi in the attack infrastructure and identified a propaganda outlet linked to the unit that publicized the attack. The big picture: Iran has a history of targeting industrial equipment in cyber operations, including American water systems and Israeli refrigeration equipment. French intelligence linked Shahid Kaveh to attacks on Israeli refrigeration equipment earlier this year and a 2023 campaign targeting industrial controllers manufactured by Unitronics. What to watch: France plans to summon Iran's ambassador and propose new European Union sanctions against Iranian individuals and entities involved in the attacks.

- Published
Former US President Joe Biden has unleashed a barrage of criticism on President Donald Trump in a soon-to-be released memoir, saying he believes the Capitol riot on 6 January 2021 "should follow him to his grave".
In an excerpt published in The Atlantic on Monday, Biden also said Trump should not have pardoned supporters who stormed Congress in a bid to thwart the certification of Biden's election victory.
"The criminals who attacked law-enforcement officers that day didn't deserve pardons," the former president wrote. "They deserved prison terms."
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis called Biden "the worst president in American history" in response to the BBC's request for comment.
In the excerpt of the book, which is due to be released later this month, Biden assailed Trump and his administration for pushing to "tear down institutions and inflame hatreds".
Biden accused him of turning a "blind eye" to their violent acts, writing: "You don't get to turn a blind eye to cops being punched, speared, sprayed, and brutalised and call yourself a friend of law enforcement."
"What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave," he said.
Trump has previously denied any wrongdoing in connection with the riot, which happened after he held a rally.
Upon returning to the White House last year, he pardoned more than 1,000 people convicted for their role in them and commuted the sentences of a dozen members of far-right groups the Proud Boys and the Oath Keepers. Trump defended these pardons, saying "these people have been destroyed".
Bis, the White House spokesperson, said on Monday that what Biden and his administration "did to this country should never be forgotten".
She asserted they "created the worst border crisis in history, were soft-on-crime, produced the worst inflation crisis in 40 years, and championed America-Last policies".
The excerpt of Biden's memoir also detailed a long meeting between himself and Trump following the latter's 2024 election victory.
Biden wrote that he was shocked when Trump purportedly said: "if it weren't for politics, I believe we'd be good friends".
The former president said the statement left him "too stunned to respond".
"He said my performance on job creation had been 'extraordinary,'" Biden wrote. "He added that he'd been relieved he didn't have to run against me. I didn't really understand why he was buttering me up, so I cut off his compliments to move on to the business at hand."
Biden's memoir comes on the back of Democrats' success in midterm elections last week.
He was not seen much on the campaign trail as he has continued treatment for prostate cancer and has said he is limiting a promotional tour for his book because of this treatment.
"Some days are better than others," Biden said in a social media post on Sunday about his cancer experience. "It hasn't stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down."

d4e4465d957b.text: Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday said that the vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "isn't about Iran," but rather his willingness to take on challenges at the Pentagon. Why it matters: It's the latest instance of the Trump administration backing the embattled Cabinet member, who is facing the possibility of enough GOP members defecting for the impeachment effort to succeed. The Iran war is at the center of the allegations against Hegseth, with three of the eight articles of impeachment specifically concerning the conflict. Other allegations include that Hegseth illegally initiated military conflict in Venezuela and Yemen. What they're saying: "Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes? The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not," Vance said Tuesday on X . "Like so much of Congress, impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking. Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements." Vance added that Congress was choosing to impeach Hegseth as they did President Trump. "Legislation is hard. Impeachments are easy (and ultimately, inconsequential)." "The irony is that legislators are most angry at Pete on the issues where he's most correct: repositioning forces away from Europe/Ukraine and reorganizing the general officer corps," he continued. "This isn't about Iran, this is about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon." Go deeper: Hegseth faces impeachment resolution from GOP member with little to lose Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

- Published
Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together.
Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.
Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.
Shortly after they were sworn in, Netanyahu and Eisenkot warned parliament about the perils of supporting a government led by the other.
"[And] to those who are thinking of establishing a government that includes supporters of terror and haters of Israel, or that will be dependent on them, I ask you, are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" said Netanyahu, alluding to the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government reliant on support from Arab parties.
He also appealed for the formation of a government of national unity as the only way to confront what he said was the threat of "a nuclear Iran".
Eisenkot sharply criticised Netanyahu's comments.
"I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," he said. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."
The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months.
One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition.
On Sunday, President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with trying to form a government.
Speaking at the president's residence, the centrist Yashar party leader called for the formation of a "national emergency government" - an implicit appeal to parties to put ideological differences aside to remove Netanyahu from office.
This, he said, would "require creative and unconventional political steps".
Eisenkot said any party or MK prepared to accept four principles could join his proposed government. Those are recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence; backing mandatory military, national or civilian service for all, including communities currently exempt; and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation and committing to dismantling its military and governing capabilities.
The four requirements, however, could present significant obstacles to Eisenkot's potential partners.
The conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, who are exempt from military service if they are in full-time religious study, was a major election issue.
The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas parties, which won 13 seats in total, have fiercely objected to attempts to change the status quo - something that all parties in Eisenkot's bloc campaigned to do.
Eisenkot's four principles are also contentious for the Arab parties. Both emphasise equal national and civic rights for Israel's Arab citizens, who form about 20% of the population; the vast majority of Israeli Arabs are not required to serve in the military; and neither has publicly recognised Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
The Arab parties could, though, help Eisenkot form a minority government. The United Arab List, which won eight seats, has said it is willing to be part of an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, which won 11 seats, has offered parliamentary support from the outside.
If Eisenkot accepted such an arrangement, he would still have to persuade other parties in his bloc to agree. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a minority government dependent on Arab MKs.
In return for their support, the ultra-Orthodox parties would be likely to demand major concessions on military conscription, which might be unacceptable to most of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc.
