- Published
The dangers in Slovyansk are clear from the start.
"If I say run, you run," Tetiana tells us. She and her colleague Yasha are escorting us into a city now under constant bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.
It is raining and cloudy as we enter the city, and our military escorts call this "good" weather, meaning it is bad for drones.
But the threat is still there, and Yasha keeps his eyes peeled on the skies, while 21-year-old Tetiana scours her phone for the latest military intelligence on likely threats from the air.
They are members of a drone unit who call themselves Peaky Blinders and their distinctive emblem is a flat cap of the type made popular by the cult BBC TV series, although theirs are camouflaged.
Slovyansk is one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.
Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.
Ukrainians worry that doing so would make it much easier for Russia to advance further west, including to the capital Kyiv.
Once inside the city, we leave our vehicles hidden under the cover of trees and venture out on foot. Yasha carries a shotgun â a last resort to shoot down Russian drones. In halting English, Tetiana tells us walking is safer than travelling by car.
Abandoned vehicles litter the streets â recently destroyed by remotely operated Russian first-person view drones. The anti-drone netting that covers the roads is no guarantee of safety.
Tetiana shows us a video on her phone taken a few days earlier.
You can hear several drones buzzing above her, and then the cacophony of small arms fire as Ukrainian forces try to shoot them down. Tetiana admits it can be scary but explains how she felt compelled to help her country, abandoning her dreams of becoming an opera singer.
Slovyansk is now a husk of its former self. Very few buildings have been left unscathed, with many reduced to rubble.
Tetiana shows us a school recently destroyed by Russian glide bombs. Across the road there is a gaping hole in an abandoned residential block. Broken glass litters the pavement. The few shops still functioning are boarded up â making it hard to distinguish what is still open. Most have closed.
Tetiana says the Russians are doing everything they can to intimidate people and drive them out of the city. That, she says, "is their strategy â to make people leave in chaos, gathering up their last belongings and fleeing amid enormous fear and suffering. They want people to have nowhere left to live".
It is a familiar pattern already seen in other Ukrainian towns and cities in the Donbas â like Pokrovsk and Bakhmut. These are now ghost towns reduced to rubble, but eventually falling into Russian hands.
Russia has already taken nearly 90% of the Donbas â made up of the regions of Luhansk and Donetsk - but its advances this year have all but stalled in the face of strong Ukrainian resistance.
The White House is sounding positive about the revived talks in Abu Dhabi, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's refusal to cede the territory.
October was the deadliest month for Russian troops since the start of its full-scale invasion â with more than 54,000 killed or injured, according to Ukraine's general staff. Despite this, Russian forces are still making life in the Fortress Belt cities almost impossible.
Before the war, Slovyansk was a city of more than 200,000 people. Less than 10% of those remain and the population diminishes by the day.
But amid the wail of near constant air raid warnings, there are still signs of people clinging on to life here. Iryna works in one of the city's last remaining coffee shops. Slovyansk is where she was born.
"I'm forced to walk around crying," she tells me. "How can they do this?"
Life, she says, has become incredibly difficult. She has already lost her house. But despite her tears, there is still defiance: "I won't leave Slovyansk. This is my home."
Inga, 53, was also born and raised here and continues to work in the city despite the danger.
"It's stressful. Honestly, I don't even know what to say," she says, but she is staying because of what she calls the "fear of the unknown".
"I simply have nowhere to go, and I don't have the money to leave or support myself afterwards." Nor, she says, is there anywhere else in Ukraine she would consider truly safe.
We first met the drone unit two years ago fighting in the Kharkiv region, in north-eastern Ukraine.
Just four of the original team remain - the rest have moved to other units, or they have been wounded or killed.
Among the dead was the brother of the man in charge of the unit, Oleksandr, who now describes his unit as his family.
He jokes it is just like the Peaky Blinders TV show â "but without the crime and the drugs". Back at their base they share a meal every evening.
Oleksandr reads out a prayer of thanks for surviving another day â he says it strengthens their spirits. The meal is accompanied by classical music played on a speaker. It helps drown out the noise of the explosions nearby.
"I feel this is the most difficult situation we've ever faced," says Oleksandr, who underlines the importance of holding the line.
"We must be here to inflict maximum damage on the enemy. We're fighting here because this is where the most intense phase of the war is taking place. Russia's claim that they will reach the borders of the Donbas, seize it, and then the war will end is absolutely false," he insists.
The remaining fortress belt cities provide Ukraine with a strong defensive line and are a major obstacle to any Russian advance. The saturation of drones in the area is also now making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance here.
Peace talks may have resumed, but Oleksandr notes they have not led to anyt

5b8576c497c9.text:
The Senate voted Monday to advance long-sought bipartisan legislation to speed permitting of big energy projects, amid acrimony over whether the bill’s support for clean energy will be overwhelmed by the fossil fuel industry’s expansion plans.
Less than a week after Democrats’ overwhelming victory in the midterm elections, the party’s incumbents were divided over the measure. Republicans propelled the 73-25 vote to get the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, or BAAJA, over the first in a series of parliamentary hurdles. It means the current Congress, one of the least productive in the past 40 years, will have a chance to reshape energy project decision-making in the United States before the GOP surrenders the reins of leadership.
The legislation is an attempt to streamline the rules and regulations that have increased over the past 70 years, hindering the nation’s ability to build infrastructure rapidly. High-voltage transmission lines, crucial for delivery of clean energy, take 10 years on average to build. The issue has become more urgent as electricity demand surges, in part due to the proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers.
After years of effort, proponents of clean energy and fossil fuel energy struck a compromise that they say will get projects moving while protecting communities.
But the bill still faces challenges.
Some Democratic senators who voted for cloture, thereby limiting debate on the bill, made clear they will work to amend the measure to ensure that it does not erode the rights of Native American tribal nations to make decisions on projects that affect their lands. But any changes to the legislation risk losing Republican support. And the bill still must pass the House, where Republicans have a slimmer majority and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has already voiced opposition.
Perhaps the wildest card is President Donald Trump, who even while the Senate vote was underway, denounced wind energy. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser,” he said during an impromptu news conference.
Despite his opposition to wind energy, Trump praised the legislation as “a great bill that’s supposed to be bipartisan.”
“We are behind it 100 percent,” Trump said.
Afterward, the legislation’s co-author, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), released a statement making clear that Democrats could withdraw their support if the president’s war against renewable energy continues. “As I have said all along, the ultimate success of this bill depends on the Trump administration getting wind turbines up and spinning to get affordable energy on the grid, and we still need to make progress on that front before final passage,” he said.
Weighing the Trade-Offs
The deep divisions over the measure reflect how much permitting reform has become a referendum on the chief weapon the environmental movement has used thus far in the drive to curb climate change: the power to block fossil fuel projects, mainly through lawsuits.
Not only has that approach failed to reduce U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, it has also been turned against clean energy projects and the transmission lines they need to deliver renewables from remote wind farms and solar arrays to population centers. Proponents of the bill argue that it is time to discard defensive environmentalism and turn instead to a strong offense—leveraging the power of low-cost wind, solar and storage to propel a transition.
Since unveiling the permitting deal before the election, Whitehouse, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, has sought to reassure fellow advocates of climate action that the legislation would remove roadblocks that have limited clean energy expansion.
“This bill is the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations,” Whitehouse said in a news conference just prior to the vote. “We look forward to accomplishing big things with our big Democratic majorities.”
But many environmentalists hoped that the Senate would fail to reach the 60-vote threshold, allowing the huge Democratic majority in the next Congress to rewrite the legislation wholesale. Opponents’ biggest concern are provisions that make it more difficult for state and tribal governments to stop oil and gas pipelines and other infrastructure projects through lawsuits and environmental review.
“This bill was shaped by the very industries that have spent decades damaging our health, exploiting our resources, and putting our futures at risk,” said Mar Zepeda Salazar, legislative director at Climate Justice Alliance, after the vote.
One major fossil fuel industry proponent, Williams Companies, even had advocates in the Senate this year: Sen. Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), former chief executive of the pipeline company, and the staff he brought on. He said the legislation was his top priority when Oklahoma’s governor appointed him to fill a Senate vacancy in March.
And yet, the measure had overwhelming support from the clean energy industry, which has been stymied by backlogs in permitting and connections to the electric transmission grid.
The Senate vote “is a critical step toward modernizing our outdated permitting process and getting ready-to-build clean energy projects moving,” said Frank Macchiarola, chief advocacy officer for the American Clean Power Association, in a statement.
While most climate and environmental groups oppose the bill, several prominent ones urged the Senate to support the initial vote, including the Environmental Defense Fund and Evergreen Action.
“In our judgment, the trade-offs right now, as they exist in the bill, are a risk-to-reward proposition that we are willing to take,” said Pete Wyckoff, Evergreen Action’s vice president of policy, in an interview.
Wyckoff said Evergreen’s support is based on an optimistic view that governors, future Congresses and presidents will do more work to promote renewable energy and reduce carbon dioxide emission

John Thune as their leader, just a week after steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority. The Senate meets at 12 p.m. EST. Watch live in our video player above. Thune is expected to be reelected, given that he remains popular with his GOP colleagues and is running unopposed. But some Republicans who returned to Washington on Monday for the first time since the election wipeout that cost them at least seven seats said it's too soon to endorse the status quo. Ron Johnson, who circulated a letter to the conference asking for a delay in the closed-door, secret-ballot leadership elections. Join Press Pass from PBS News Still, Johnson conceded that there's no one else on the ballot. "That's part of our problem, who would want the job?" he said, turning to a reporter and joking, "Do you want it?" READ MORE: Trump says his deportation policy 'might have been too tough' for midterm voters The angst comes as the party is just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for GOP lawmakers and how soon they can try to rebuild their ranks. Two additional races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers. The Republican leadership declined to move the elections, which include contests for other party leaders as well and are held in the small Old Senate Chamber just down the hall from the large one used Tuesday. But senators could still seek a vote to delay them. Thune said on Monday they will have a "very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here and then we'll see what the consensus of the conference is." "Ultimately that's a decision made by Republican senators," Thune said. Despite some critics, Thune has respect from colleagues Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, has spent much of the last two years navigating President Donald Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate. While backing up Trump on most policy, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president's political base. But Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is "a very fine man." The election is "up to the Senate," Trump said. Thune has made it a point to hear out different viewpoints before he makes major decisions and has maintained close relationships with the rank and file — a different approach from his predecessor, McConnell. Thune "has widespread support" among Republican senators, said Oklahoma Sen. Jim Lankford, who said he supports having the elections on Tuesday when many of the new GOP senators are already in town for freshman orientation. "It's a pretty complicated role to be able to manage," Lankford said. "No one wants that job." Walking into the meeting, South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds said most senators are ready to move forward. It is time to have "leadership in place," he said. Republicans push to delay leadership elections Still, Johnson and others in his conference say Tuesday's leadership election is too soon. The midterm election was "an incredible repudiation of the focus of this Congress for the last two years," said Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley, citing reductions to Medicaid and rural hospital funding in the sweeping tax cuts bill that Republicans pushed through last year. Hawley voted for the legislation after criticizing it. Hawley said he hasn't "heard any acknowledgement of that yet from leadership, which I think is extremely alarming," and he also hasn't heard from Thune personally. "I want to hear that we are going to have a different direction," including ways to lower costs for Americans, Hawley said. Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick in a statement over the weekend said Republicans shouldn't choose a leader until the lessons of the election have been "digested and debated." Indiana Sen. Jim Banks said Republicans need to "sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short." Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, one of a few senators who signed Johnson's letter asking for a delay, said any leadership contest should come after the two outstanding Senate elections in Alaska and Mississippi are decided. Neither of those races has yet been called, so it's unclear if Republican Sens. Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi will be returning to the Senate next year. Thune looks to the next Congress The soul-searching comes as lawmakers are trying to wrap up the year's work — funding the government and seeing if there are some issues where they can work together, including an energy permitting bill that moved forward on a bipartisan vote Monday evening. French police have made arrests after three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, were searched in relation to an investigation into Mohamed Al Fayed's abuse.
The Paris prosecutor's office told the BBC that several individuals were taken into custody for questioning last month and later released.
In a confidential letter sent to survivors, the Metropolitan Police said its officers were present during the searches on 13 and 14 October, in what is understood to be a joint operation between British and French authorities.
It is the first time any arrests have been made in relation to alleged abuse and trafficking by the former Harrods and Ritz owner.
Several victims of Al Fayed were also interviewed by French investigators, the prosecutor's office said.
It added that the searches were part of a preliminary investigation into "allegations of human trafficking committed by an organized group, aggravated pimping committed by an organized group, and rape".
The investigation is ongoing and digital material seized during the searches is being analysed.
The late Egyptian billionaire bought the Ritz Paris hotel in 1979, and it is still owned by the Al Fayed family.
The Villa Windsor in western Paris, another property involved in the search, was a holiday home for the Al Fayed family. It was previously the home of King Edward VIII, following his abdication, and his wife Wallis Simpson.
The Met shared this statement from French authorities with victims:
"At this stage of the proceedings, several victims have been interviewed by French investigators, and the investigations are being conducted in liaison with the British authorities.
"In this context, searches and evidence-gathering operations were carried out in mid-October 2026, notably within the Hotel Ritz in the 1st arrondissement of Paris, as well as at the Villa Sainte-ThÃ©rÃ¨se in Saint-Tropez, a former property of Mohamed Al Fayed, and at the Villa Windsor in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, in the presence of British investigators.
"Several suspects were taken into police custody, measures which were lifted following their interviews, specifically for the purpose of analyzing digital material seized during the search operations.
"The investigations are continuing under the direction of the Paris Public Prosecutor's Office."
A Met Police spokesperson confirmed its officers travelled to France in October and were present during the operation.
Al Fayed, who died in 2023 aged 94, was accused by more than 20 women of sexual assault in a BBC documentary and podcast in September 2024.
One of the women featured in the documentary said she was sexually assaulted by Al Fayed at the Ritz hotel in Paris, while another woman said she had been raped by him at the Villa Windsor residence.
Since those allegations, more than 400 alleged victims or witnesses have come forward to lawyers.
A woman has also told BBC Scotland she was trafficked, drugged, sexually assaulted and held prisoner on the Balnagown Estate by Al Fayed's brother, Salah Fayed, who died in 2010.
Both brothers died without facing legal charges in relation to these allegations.
Earlier this year, Police Scotland said it was carrying out further investigations into allegations connected to Balnagown Estate.
In a statement, a force spokesperson said: "Three people have been identified in connection with offending against a number of victims.
"Our inquiries are ongoing and it would be inappropriate to comment further."
The Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors group said it welcomed the "significant developments" and cooperation between the Met and French authorities.
"We believe that all properties owned by Fayed should be investigated with the same thoroughness as those already searched, wherever they are located, to ensure that no potentially relevant evidence is overlooked," the group said.
"We hope these developments represent meaningful progress towards identifying and holding to account all those who facilitated, concealed or assisted his offending, wherever they operated."
The survivor advocacy group No One Above said: "France is treating this as organised human trafficking, led by specialists, with properties searched and evidence seized. That is what a serious investigation into a network looks like.
"Two years on, survivors are still waiting for the same from the Met. It is time the National Crime Agency took this investigation over."
The management of the Ritz Paris told AFP news agency that it "does not tolerate any form of harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour" and that it was ready "to cooperate fully with the competent judicial authorities".
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support is available at BBC Action Line.

Twelve people have been killed after dozens of cars and lorries were involved in two pile-ups on the Trakia motorway in south-eastern Bulgaria, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said.
Health Minister Katya Ivkova said 11 people died at the scene on Tuesday, near the town of Zimnitsa, while another person later died in hospital. About 50 others were taken to hospital with injuries.
Sliven regional governor Mihail Kasherov told journalists that more than 70 vehicles were involved in the incident, Bulgarian state news agency BTA reported.
Officials have said dense fog reduced visibility and was the likely cause of the first crash, which occurred on the eastbound carriageway.
Radev declared Wednesday a day of national mourning following the incident.
The second crash, on the Sofia-bound carriageway, was likely also caused by the fog, with drivers also distracted by the first crash, BTA reported an official as saying.
The Trakia motorway runs from west-to-east of Bulgaria, and connects the capital Sofia to the Black Sea coast.
Road administration director Galin Kostov added that speeds were unsuitable for the conditions, which included wet road surfaces, and the motorway would remain closed until it had been cleared, BTA reported.
Yambol regional governor Georgi Chalakov said reports first came in at 07:10 local time (05:10 GMT), with the injured taken by ambulance to hospitals in the Yambol, Sliven and Burgas regions.
Chalakov told BTA rescue teams had to remove sections of the crash barrier to reach people. He added that the fog meant that helicopters could not be used in the evacuation efforts.
One witness who helped rescue a man from a burning vehicle blamed "very thick fog" for the pile-up.
"I got out of the car, I ran forward and pulled that man out," the witness told Reuters news agency.
Another told Reuters that "many, many people died".
"As for me, there were four cars behind me - trucks - and I don't know how I got out or what happened, but in the end, thank God I'm still alive," that witness said.
Radev - who had been hosting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen - cut short a news conference after learning of the incident and visited the scene.

3e57848c6976.text: By — Kevin Freking, Associated Press Kevin Freking, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-house-expected-to-hold-preliminary-vote-on-hegseth-impeachment-as-gop-chooses-next-leader Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: House expected to hold preliminary vote on Hegseth impeachment as GOP chooses next leader Politics Nov 10, 2026 10:44 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — House Republicans will move Tuesday to select their leader in the minority after a brutal drubbing at the polls, with the two candidates being House Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio. Watch the House floor live in the video player above. The lawmakers and those set to join the next Congress are gathering in the morning for a vote expected in the afternoon. WATCH: Hegseth says House impeachment push is about 'policy disagreements' not high crimes Scalise and Jordan have faced off before, both running to serve as House speaker after Kevin McCarthy was ousted from the job a little more than three years ago. Neither was able to rally the support necessary to secure the position, which eventually went to Mike Johnson, who is stepping aside from the leadership in the new Congress. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Now Republicans are headed into the minority, changing the nature of the job. The winner of the leadership race will inherit a historically small House Republican conference that is only beginning to grapple with its loss of power as President Donald Trump serves out his final two years in office. Leading the party back to the House majority in 2028 is sure to be a stiff climb, given the scope of Democratic victories in the midterms. Scalise, 61, has held key GOP leadership positions going back to 2014, serving as party whip and then as majority leader. In 2017, he was critically wounded when a gunman opened fire at a baseball practice where several Republican lawmakers and staffers were preparing for an annual charity baseball game against Democrats. In 2023, he was stricken with multiple myeloma, a blood cancer that was successfully treated. READ MORE: Johnson won't seek reelection as House leader after Republican wipeout "Overcoming adversity is nothing new to me," Scalise said in his pitch to colleagues. Jordan, 62, is a co-founder of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus and served as its first chairman. He has been the chairman of the House Judiciary Committee for the last four years. "Our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democratic Party is — offense, not defense, wins elections," Jordan said, a nod to his pugnacious reputation in committee hearings. Trump hasn't publicly weighed in on the race. Scalise and Jordan are a familiar match-up Both men have been here before. Scalise edged Jordan in head-to-head voting to become the Republican speaker nominee three years ago, but he ended up withdrawing from the race when he could not secure the near unanimity it required from Republicans to win a majority vote on the House floor. At the time, some of the more conservative members declined to back Scalise following Trump's endorsement of Jordan. Trump was not president at the time, but his voice still carried the most weight for many. Jordan then became the nominee, but others within the conference were adamant they would not reward the hardball tactics used to topple McCarthy and then Scalise, so he fell short in multiple rounds of votes. Eventually, Republicans turned to a new face who was not part of their internal skirmish — Johnson. In a letter to colleagues, Scalise emphasized that he was ready to lead on Day One of the next Congress. He cited his work in helping deliver legislative wins, such as Trump's big tax and spending cut bill. He also emphasized his fundraising prowess, noting he raised $67.9 million for this year's midterms, with about a third of that going directly to individual House campaigns and the National Republican Congressional Committee. He said his grassroots fundraising operation is the most prolific among House Republicans. "In competitive districts, every dollar counts and those resources are critical to winning back the majority," Scalise said. Jordan warned of the coming Democratic efforts on oversight, with numerous investigations of the Trump administration expected. "I am battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats' playbook," Jordan said. Republicans are weighing their choice Rep. Andy Harris of Maryland said he would be supporting Jordan. "I think you need to change the team and I think you need an excellent communicator, and he fits both those bills," Harris said. Rep. Mike Kelly of Pennsylvania said he believes Scalise is better suited for the job. "I like people who do legislation and appropriations. I think that's important," Kelly said. "I know other people have maybe had more time on Fox, but I like guys that work more on facts." Rep. Steve Womack of Arkansas called it a "really, really close race." "There's a school of thought a lot of members have that a new broom sweeps clean after going through what we just went through last Tuesday," Womack said. "There's also a school of thought of people that believe Mr. Scalise, who has led us back before, can do it again." Johnson said he was close to both men and would not try to dictate the outcome. "I want the body, I want the members to make those decisions themselves," Johnson said. "I'm not weighing in here on the leadership elections." Other positions are also up for grabs In addition to the race for minority leader, Reps. Tom Emmer of Minnesota and August Pfluger of Texas are vying to serve as Republican whip, the No. 2 position in the leadership hierarchy. Three candidates are seeking to serve as conference chair: Reps. Lisa McClain of Michigan, Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida

Hegseth denounces impeachment charges in rare press briefing
The defense secretary called his potential removal an attack on his “success.”
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth publicly defended his record Tuesday in the face of an impending impeachment vote, throwing off any remaining pretense that he views the defense secretary job as a nonpartisan role subject to congressional oversight.
Hegseth spoke from the Pentagon briefing room for the first time since May, as the House of Representatives prepares for a vote on articles of impeachment against him that were reintroduced on Monday by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.
“It's what happens when you put people with ideological agendas in charge of institutions,” he said of a possible trial by the Senate next year, without a hint of irony, nearly two years into a tenure that has seen him subvert the senior officer promotion process, attempt to remove honorably serving transgender troops, and promote a particular type of Christianity in the ranks—all based on his ideology.
Hegseth called Massie’s impeachment campaign an attempt to “do damage to this president, this country, and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it.”
“For the first time in American history, a cabinet secretary overseeing America's military is being attacked not for losing conflicts with our enemies, but for winning them,” he said. “Condemned not for defeat, but for military victory. The disgruntled congressman even admitted this himself yesterday. No failure here, just impeachment for success.”
Among the eight articles of impeachment are allegations that Hegseth illegally carried on the war in Iran, extrajudicially executed suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean, and kidnapped Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro—three operations he defends as lawful despite widespread criticism from legal experts.
Hegseth referred to President Trump’s two impeachments during his first term, repeating the president’s line about a “perfect call"—the 2019 phone conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in which Trump threatened to withhold aid to Ukraine unless the government investigated Joe Biden and his son.
"I'll stand by him," Trump told reporters Monday. "He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won."
It is unclear to which wars the president was referring. Hegseth’s boat-strike campaign has reportedly been ineffective in slowing drug flows. The U.S. and Iran continue to fight for control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Hegseth said that at least some congressional Republicans would decline to vote to send the articles of impeachment to the Senate.
“There's also an understanding that this is one disgruntled guy who drew up some really flimsy articles that aren't grounded and actually in the Constitution, or things that are high crimes and misdemeanors, and so whether they love everything that's been done, they they don't want to vote for something that isn't real,” he said.
The secretary also addressed the possibility that commanders who ordered strikes on suspected drug boats, in particular, could be investigated for carrying out unlawful orders.
“Put the secretary on trial today, and the men and women who carried out those orders tomorrow,” he said. “If they want to come for the warriors, they're going to have to come through me.”
They may not have to. Articles of impeachment don’t expire, and an impeachment proceeding does not have to be completed during one term of Congress. That means the incoming Democratic majority could pick up the ball and run with it when the next Congress is seated in the new year.
Help us report on the future of national security. Contact Meghann Myers: mmyers@defenseone.com, meghannmyers.55 on Signal.

How do you fire a CEO who has delivered 700,000% returns? One easy way is for the government to make you, but President Donald Trump thinks Nvidiaâs Jensen Huang should keep his job. US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has called on Israel to immediately allow all necessary humanitarian supplies into Gaza after rain flooded tens of thousands of tents.
The US-backed body, established to oversee the implementation of Trump's Gaza peace plan, acknowledged the steps now being considered by Israel, but said "the response remains insufficient".
Israel's military agency in charge of co-ordinating aid into Gaza said it had allowed in tens of thousands of tents and trucks with winter supplies, but added reconstruction "can only begin after Hamas fully disarms".
On Sunday, three children and a woman were killed when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents in the central Strip.
Most people in Gaza have been displaced because of Israel's military actions. Around 65% of the population, about 1.4 million people, now live in tents or makeshift shelters, the UN says.
Standing soaked in Gaza City, Mohammed Jneid told the AFP news agency that heavy rains hit from one side and sewage overflowed on them from the other, with the ground and tents no longer able to hold.
"We have nothing left, no bedding, no food, nothing," he said.
Sitting inside her tent, Islam Al Mobayed told AFP there were seven children there, five of them young.
"This is not life," she said. "We are exhausted, we are tired of this entire life."
In rare criticism of Israel, the Board of Peace said it had been urging the Israeli government to authorise the entry of essential goods for temporary shelter and water and sanitation infrastructure.
The Board added that delays in approving the entry of supplies "exacerbated the consequences of a foreseeable humanitarian challenge" and delayed the start of decommissioning weapons and transferring Hamas authority to a transitional government.
It also said Hamas's failure to disarm and transfer power had compounded the difficulties facing Gaza's civilians.
The UN's humanitarian agency OCHA said more than 150,000 tents were outside Gaza ready to go in, but aid efforts were constrained "by Israeli restrictions on the entry of supplies and equipment and funding shortfalls".
UN humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov said on Monday that stocks of essential shelter and winter items inside Gaza had been exhausted.
"Israeli authorities must immediately lift all restrictions on entry of the supplies," he said, adding "we have run out of time".
Israel's foreign ministry spokeswoman Michal Maayan on Monday said Israel had in recent months put in place a winter plan in coordination with the Board of Peace and international charities.
That plan has brought in more than 91,000 tents and 8,200-plus trucks with tarpaulins, blankets, winter clothing, and other equipment, according to Cogat, the Israeli military body responsible for aid.
Cogat said it would not allow in equipment that could be used for military purposes.
Maayon accused Hamas of hoarding aid, saying: "Hamas is responsible for the delays in making more progress in the Strip, and winter-related hardships are a consequence of Hamas's action and policy."
In response to the Board of Peace, Hamas said in a statement published on Palestinian media that its comment "presents a distorted account of the causes of the disaster". The group denied it was responsible for ceasefire delays, pointing to a statement in August , externalfrom Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish mediators that accused Israel of violations.
Hamas said Israeli restrictions prevent the entry of materials necessary for shelter and recovery - and added the Board as the ceasefire implementor should look at its own "serious shortcoming".
Under the deal to end the two-year-long war in October 2025, Hamas agreed to give up governance and its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the 60% of Gaza it still occupied. Israel, however, has insisted Hamas must fully disarm before withdrawal.
The dispute has left the next stages of the peace plan stalled, with both sides blaming each other.
The war in Gaza began after the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 when around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage.
The Israeli military campaign in response has killed 74,645 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable. More than 1,600 people have been killed since the ceasefire in October last year.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza since then.

Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, research indicates.
Hand sanitiser sales were up 83%, sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%, according to data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator.
The government's public awareness campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.
However, Worldpanel said that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.
The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.
Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.
After the campaign launch, the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, Worldpanel said, although the typical amount remained at 500g, which suggests a gradual stocking-up.
"Shoppers clearly took notice of the 'Be Ready' campaign, but this wasn't panic buying, with less than a third of households buying bottled water in October," said Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator.
"Growth came from more people adding the recommended items on the government's checklist to their weekly shop, not from shoppers piling their trolleys high, which is very much in line with what the government wanted households to do," he said.
Sales of tinned and jarred goods rose from Â£58.2m in the 10 days to 2 November 2025 to Â£79.5m over the same period in 2026.
Bottled water sales jumped from Â£13.6m to Â£22.8m compared with a year earlier and hand sanitiser sales climbed from Â£497,000 to Â£908,000.
Further evidence of stockpiling came from food firm Princes on Tuesday, which said demand for tinned tuna, meat and vegetables had risen following the government's campaign.
Princes interim chief executive Giuseppe Mastrolia said the jump in demand "further reinforces the relevance of our core categories in providing affordable, nutritious and convenient food solutions".
The "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need - for example, bottled water, and long-life food that doesn't need to be kept in the fridge such as dried fruit and nuts.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".
Disaster recovery expert Lucy Easthope previously told the BBC that the UK was playing "massive catch up" to other European nations in terms of preparedness.
These include France, Germany Denmark, Sweden, and Norway.
A number of experts have been calling for the UK to put more emphasis on food security, with some arguing that the government itself should take responsibility for food stockpiling, rather than individual households.
In October, a group of more than 180 experts signed an open letter, external to Burnham and first secretary of state Louise Haigh calling for local authorities to have a duty to prevent and respond to food supply emergencies.
They pointed out that a government survey found that 29% of people in the UK could not afford to keep a few days worth of food in the house.

Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (Â£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and will raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.
It would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some backers of the firm predicted in summer, according to the Financial Times.
It is floating at a volatile time for AI firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.
There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.
In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year.
However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.
Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".
She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."
At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn.
Anthropic is just five years old. It was co-founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei along with five others - all of whom worked at OpenAI, the rival AI giant behind ChatGPT.

US inflation rose at a faster-than-expected pace in October, according to official figures.
Prices rose by 0.4% in the month, which was lower than the 0.6% increase in September.
However, analysts had expected prices to rise by 0.3%, and the higher-than-expected pace could add to arguments for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting in December.
The new figures come a week after the midterm elections which were fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US.
What is inflation?
Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.
Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).
It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.
The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.
What causes inflation?
There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.
If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.
Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.
Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.
Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.
What is the current rate of inflation?
Over the month of October, prices rose by 0.4%, driven by increases in housing, food and energy costs.
However, the pace of energy price rises, at 0.7% in October, was much lower than the 5.2% increase seen in September.
While the Bureau of Labor Statistics would normally provide figures for the 12-month change in prices, it did not collect data in October 2025 so it could not provide that estimate.
For the 12 months to September, inflation was 3.7%.
What does inflation mean for interest rates?
The US Federal Reserve has a target for keeping annual inflation at 2%.
When inflation is too high the Fed tends to raise interest rates in order to encourage people and businesses to save more and spend less money in the hope this will slow price rises.
While there was no annual figure published for inflation this month, analysts say the fact inflation was higher in October than expected increases the chance of an interest rate rise at the Fed's December meeting.
Federal Reserve governor Chirstopher Waller, who spoke before the latest inflation figures were published, also suggested he was leaning towards a rate increase in December even if October's figures were slower than expected.
How have tariffs affected inflation?
Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.
While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.
Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.
In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.
Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.
Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.
Has inflation been worse lately?
While inflation is currently above where the Federal Reserve would like it has been much higher in previous years.
During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.
Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.
Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.
Can inflation ever go down?
It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.
A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.
Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.
Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.
How has inflation changed Social Security payments?
The value of social security benefits is changed to largely keep up with inflation, protecting people's ability to purchase their usual goods and services through the cost-of-living adjustment.
Shortly after September's inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027.

Washington wants to make it harder for US solar firms to rely on China. A panel factory in Texas shows how thatâs already happening â but why weaning them off entirely could be harder than it looks.
The industry is bracing for one of its biggest shocks in years: In December, new Commerce Department rules will require panel manufacturers to pay a fixed minimum price and a tariff of up to 15% for cells and certain other specialized components they import from abroad. The rules, under a provision called Section 232, are designed to finally quash a cat-and-mouse game US trade officials have been playing with China for years, in which Chinese solar makers shift between factories in various Asian or African locales to stay one step ahead of American tariffs.
One of the companies navigating this change is the Texas-based panel manufacturer T1 Energy, which has roots linked to China but is now racing toward greater independence. Because the new rules will drive up panel prices, some solar installers are panicking; at least 1 gigawatt worth of large-scale solar projects has been cancelled in recent months because of 232-related price adjustments, according to solar research firm Anza.
But T1 CEO Daniel Barcelo canât wait. The rules âwill really level the playing fieldâ against Chinese rivals, he told me. âBuilding something in America still takes longer and costs more than building it in most countries.â
Timâs view
US President Donald Trump may not be a big fan of solar, but itâs the countryâs fastest-growing source of power generation. Standing up an independent domestic solar supply chain is critical to the countryâs energy security and AI ambitions, and to lowering power prices, especially as Beijing moves to restrict the export of some key solar technologies.
But, although it may be wise to raise trade barriers that push more China-affiliated solar components out of the US market, Chinaâs role in global solar supply chains is so pervasive that instantly severing all ties could kill many US solar manufacturing efforts in the crib. Future growth for this industry depends on a more nuanced trade policy that gives US companies the space to benefit from Chinaâs world-leading solar expertise while the next phase of home-grown plants gets built.
At this point, the US imports almost no solar cells or other core components from China, and imports of panels from anywhere recently hit a seven-year low now that more US module assembly factories are cropping up. But even T1, like many of its peers, still needs China for some vital aspects of its operations. And when I visited the companyâs factory, it was clear that achieving a full divorce between the American and Chinese solar industries could be more complex than many in Washington appreciate.
T1 operates a sprawling, cutting-edge solar module factory on the outskirts of Dallas, and is a few months away from finishing a second factory to manufacture its own cells based on technology that was first developed for the Chinese firms itâs looking to supplant. Last month, the company was granted special permission from Commerce to continue importing cells from Asian suppliers without being penalized for stockpiling ahead of the 232 deadline. It is also awaiting a verdict on a second Commerce waiver that would allow it to dodge the 232 tariffs altogether while it completes its onshoring investments.
The company was born from the clean tech trade wars that have engulfed the US, Europe, and China in recent years. In the early 2020s Barcelo, whose background is in global oil and gas finance, was working to set up an EV battery factory in Norway. But that company, Freyr, got pushed by intense competition from Chinese rivals â and simultaneously pulled westward by inducements in Bidenâs Inflation Reduction Act. The companyâs first plan was to build a $2.5 billion battery factory in Georgia. But that was scrapped after Barcelo spotted a better deal in solar, where there were only a few domestic manufacturers at a moment when demand was exploding and Chinese firms, who could see a US crackdown coming, were looking to pull up stakes. He pivoted, and agreed in December 2024 to a $621 million deal to buy the Dallas factory, along with supply contracts and other assets, from Changzhou-based Trina Solar, one of the worldâs biggest producers, which had just completed building it.
A wave of similar US takeovers swept the industry around that time, including some in which Chinese firms retained a minority stake. Indeed, more than 40% of the 66 GW of operational US module manufacturing capacity today originated as facilities owned by Chinese manufacturers or joint ventures involving Chinese firms, according to Wood Mackenzie analyst Elissa Pierce. In T1âs case, Trina dropped its stake entirely. But T1âs relationships with Trina and other Chinese firms remained essential: A Trina executive briefly came over to serve as the new ventureâs chief strategy officer. The factoryâs anchor customer became Trina itself, which committed to buy 1 GW of panels per year, one-fifth of the factoryâs capacity; on the day I visited, robotic arms were gingerly packaging panels into Trina-branded boxes. The first thing I saw on the factory floor was a stack of specialized glass from a company in Zhejiang.
Other Asian countries are essential, too: T1 imports cells and other components from a range of suppliers in Southeast Asia and elsewhere. T1 inherited Trinaâs polysilicon supply contract from a Michigan company called Hemlock, which is minority owned by a Japanese chemical firm. In July, it paid $135 million to a Singaporean solar firm for intellectual property behind the cell and module technology that Trina and others use.
Russell Gold, a veteran Wall Street Journal energy journalist who is now T1âs spokesperson, said that although the company now feels âpretty comfortable running this factory by ourselves,â it still works closely with outside contractors, including some from China,

f2e300a8bd50.text: Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Inflation remained hot in October, according to data from the Labor Department released on Tuesday. Why it matters: The Consumer Price Index shows that even as gasoline prices steadied, inflation pressures elsewhere remained stubborn. By the numbers: CPI rose 0.4% last month, slowing from the 0.6% increase in September. Gasoline prices gained 1% in October, a sharp slowdown from the 9.1% surge in September, the Labor Department said. Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, advanced 0.3% for the third straight month, with higher prices for recreation, medical care, car insurance and airline fares contributing to the increase. Of note: The Labor Department did not publish year-over-year inflation rates for October. Last year's government shutdown left a gap in the data that prevents direct comparisons with October 2025. But if one assumes the October 2025 readings were halfway between September and November, year-over-year inflation comes to 4% — or 2.8% excluding food and energy. That compares with September's annual inflation rate of 3.7%, or 2.6% excluding food and energy. The big picture: The inflation report was already shaping up to be a crucial piece of the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision next month. But the stakes grew just hours before its release when Fed governor Christopher Waller raised the prospect of a larger-than-usual rate hike if inflation remains stubbornly elevated. In a speech , Fed governor Christopher Waller said a half-point rate hike should be considered next month if core inflation rose by at least 0.3% in October — exactly what Tuesday's report showed. The yield on the two-year Treasury note, which is particularly sensitive to expectations for Fed interest rate policy, jumped 0.13% on Tuesday following Waller's comments and the CPI report. What to watch: The report also offers a fresh measure of the inflation problem that helped shape last week's midterm elections. Nearly nine in 10 voters said the cost of living was a "crucial" or "major" factor in their vote in last week's midterms, according to national exit polling data . Democrats won on promises to lower prices for groceries and other essentials. Now they face the more difficult task of delivering on their promises, with limited power to reverse years of price increases. The bottom line: Inflation remains stubbornly hot, strengthening the case for another Fed rate hike and prolonging the cost-of-living pressures that have frustrated American households. Scientists are racing to restore people’s ability to communicate. Powerful AI-based methods to decode speech signals and predict words, along with advances in technology, promise success.
This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me takes listeners through the breadth of scientific efforts to restore words, emotions and even gestures to people who can’t move or talk.
We’ll hear from Casey Harrell, a man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis who can no longer talk. A user of today’s technology, Harrell has a unique perspective on what he’d like to see improved for the technology of tomorrow.
And as season two wraps up, listeners will be left with a reminder of the power of a voice: a piece of comedy from Jules Rodriguez, performed with his voice clone in front of a live crowd.
“Being backstage and then seeing him come out, like, roll out his wheelchair, and everybody goes nuts because they’re like, ‘What is going on here? This doesn’t make sense,’” says Jules’ wife, Maria Aleandra Fernandez. “And every time I was like, ‘This is life. This is love. This is passion. What else is there?’ I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here.”
Episode 6 transcript

[Audio] You have my love, my respect and we’re thinking about you guys all the time.
Sanders: As you were talking earlier, it made me think about what it means to make somebody laugh and to entertain them, and like how actually very, very special that must be. Just kind of, at its heart, it’s, it is joy and humans connecting. And so, extra special.
MA: That’s the other thing I’ve learned mainly through Jules, about humor and comedy. And who were we watching yesterday? The NPR interview with Dave Chappelle.

[Audio] We’re like the nation’s kidney. We help everyone metabolize not just facts, but feelings around facts, or ideas. And jokes are just a shorthand for all of that.
MA: And I’m also a nerd and I’ve been reading some Greek tragedies and studying about how, you know, that’s also like the artists that help people metabolize feelings and emotions. And when he said that, I was like, that’s exactly it. And that’s what Jules has done.
It’s something that heals. And it’s not even like it’s self-deprecating. It’s not like, oh, let’s make fun. And the way he does it is so smart and genuine, but also not taking himself seriously. And that idea of metabolizing the really hard feelings that come around grief, mortality, losing a person, seeing how he’s trapped in his body, but he chooses not to be trapped in that really big way is so profound.
Sanders: Science is iterative. It builds. It may take a wrong turn or two, but overall, it’s moving toward a deeper understanding of our world and of ourselves.

Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall by 0.4% in 2026, driven by the rapid expansion of solar and wind power and the energy supply shock caused by the Iran war, according to research by the Global Carbon Project. But the decline is not yet fast enough to be durable, an accompanying study published in the journal Nature found. Emissions from oil are expected to decrease by 1.9%, which is likely a short-term response to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. âA reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,â said Pierre Friedlingstein, an Exeter University professor who led the GCP study and was a co-author of the Nature paper.
Total carbon emissions are set to rise around 1% this year, as emissions from deforestation and land-use change are projected to increase for the first time in a decade. df56ca36ada0.text: The Senate's bipartisan permitting bill advanced in a lopsided vote on Monday, but key hurdles lie ahead. Why it matters: The legislation could have far-reaching consequences for how energy projects get built across the U.S. A few takeaways from Monday's vote: The big margin was politically lopsided. The 73-25 split to advance the bill "was as good or a little bit better" than what co-author Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) was expecting, she told reporters in the Capitol. The GOP split was 51-1 in favor, with only Sen. Mike Rounds (S.D.) voting no. 21 Democrats and Maine independent Sen. Angus King voted yes, while 23 Dems and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders were against advancing the bill toward full debate. It was tentative. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement afterward that he has "outstanding concerns" with the bill that he'll "fight to address" through amendments. He's not alone in only a tentative yes vote. For instance, Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) is against final passage unless changes to the National Historic Preservation Act are jettisoned, citing tribal concerns. Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) is in a similar place. Climate hawk vs. climate hawk. The most outspoken Senate Democrats on climate change split on the vote. Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) joined coauthors Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) in backing the measure. But Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Ed Markey (D-Mass.), along with Sanders, all voted no. Watch the clock. Whitehouse pledged a "very healthy" amendment process. But the Senate is now up against the lame duck calendar, and the House would still need to act on whatever emerges. Plus, any changes would need to thread a political needle of maintaining Democratic support without losing too many Republicans. Climate's cachet has fallen. Heinrich and Whitehouse, at a pre-vote press conference, emphasized affordability, data center accountability and jobs before touting power sector emissions curbs from the bill. But Whitehouse also sought to reassure climate and environmental organizations. "This bill is the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations, and we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities," he said in the Capitol. President Trump is a wild card. His comments shortly before Monday's vote that he would not approve wind turbines, while reiterating his full support for the bill, rocketed around the Capitol. And the White House reaffirmed that the president "stands 100%" behind the bill. The bill's success depends on Trump officials "getting wind turbines up and spinning to get affordable energy on the grid," and progress is needed before final passage, Whitehouse said in a statement. What we're watching: Proposed amendments as they roll in, but also the politics in the closely divided House. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) criticized the bill last week and called for more engagement with his caucus. Asked Monday whether the Senate co-authors' revisions addressed his concerns, Jeffries told reporters that it's still under review. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.
