Geoff Bennett: In the day's other headlines: U.S. authorities charged three men today of being Iran-backed operatives who planned to carry out nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and in the U.S. They're also accused of plotting an attack at a British air base the U.S. has used to carry out strikes against Iran. The U.S. withdrew some of its bombers from RAF Fairford last month following a suspected security incident involving Iran. Then, today, officials said the U.S. air force has moved military aircraft from another base, RAF Mildenhall, because of a security threat. The Wall Street Journal first reported the moves, saying the threat was linked to Iran. Tehran has not commented. Separately, Britain's counterterrorism police say they have arrested a member of the U.S. Army on suspicion of spying for Russia. The unnamed 41-year-old is in custody pending charges. Russian and Ukrainian representatives met for peace talks today for the first time in nine months. President Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, led the nearly four-hour talks in Abu Dhabi flanked by delegations from both sides. While he was not a part of today's dialogue, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the meeting quite substantive during a visit to Denmark. And while at a G7 gathering in Paris, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the talks potentially open the door to more multilateral discussions. Marco Rubio, U.S. Secretary of State: It looks like the talks in Abu Dhabi were very productive. I think the most important thing, obviously, there's a lot of work to be done in that regard. It's not like something that's on the verge of being solved in the next 24 hours or anything like that. But what's really important is that the Europeans are at the table. Geoff Bennett: Russian officials have pushed back on European involvement in the talks, as Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov made clear again today while speaking with reporters in Moscow. Sergey Lavrov, Russian Foreign Minister (through interpreter): Let the Europeans stay at the hotel. The Americans have said that prior to talks with our delegation they intend to meet with the Ukrainians and the Europeans, presumably to be inspired by their spirited commitment to a lasting peace. I do not believe this is a particularly promising approach. Geoff Bennett: Lavrov added that Moscow would not accept any form of temporary cease-fire while talks are ongoing. Negotiations in Abu Dhabi are set to resume for a second day tomorrow. Israel's Parliament was sworn in today without a new government in place after no major party secured a parliamentary majority in last month's general election. Former military Chief Gadi Eisenkot has been tasked with forming a new government. He and his allies introduced a series of bills today aimed at unwinding some of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies. In a speech following Tuesday's inauguration ceremony, Netanyahu called for unity while also attacking his opponents. (SHOUTING) Geoff Bennett: His address turned contentious when he demanded an inquiry into alleged foreign election funding. Meantime, in Gaza, local authorities say several Israeli attacks killed at least seven people across the territory yesterday and into today. Health officials say one of the Israeli airstrikes in Gaza City hit a metal factory, sparking a fire that killed at least three people. The Israeli military says it targeted militants in one of the recent attacks, but did not provide further details on the others. In California, voters have rejected a proposed tax on the state's wealthiest residents, raising questions about the political future of similar measures across the country. Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time 5 percent tax on residents with a net worth exceeding $1 billion. The revenue would have helped fund health care, education, and food assistance programs. The measure's defeat is a victory for Democratic leaders, including Governor Gavin Newsom, who warned that the tax could drive billionaires out of California. But supporters say they are not giving up. They plan to bring the proposal back to voters in 2028. The Trump administration has proposed new restrictions on the nation's largest food assistance program that could leave millions more Americans without benefits. The proposal would eliminate automatic eligibility for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, for households already receiving another form of government assistance. An estimated 6.3 million people could be affected, and that comes on top of more than five million people who've already lost benefits following a tax law enacted last year. Supporters argue the changes would reduce government spending on assistance programs. Critics warn they would make it harder for struggling families to put food on the table. In the business world, Anthropic says it plans to price shares of its upcoming IPO between $70 and $78 each. That would value the maker of the Claude AI tool as high as $1.4 trillion. Anthropic's IPO is seen as a test case for the health of the AI sector. It's due to list on the Nasdaq as soon as next week. Meantime, on Wall Street today, the Dow Jones industrial average fell around 150 points. The Nasdaq shed about three-quarters of 1 percent. The S&P 500 pulled back after yesterday's rally.

f8a5c73bea33.text: With Congress back this week, Republicans and Democrats alike are wasting no time preparing for the new session that begins in January. House Republicans elected Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan to be their next leader. Although Democrats haven’t voted yet on their leadership team, Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the speaker. He joined Amna Nawaz to outline his priorities. Amna Nawaz: With Congress back this week, Republicans and Democrats alike are wasting no time preparing for the new session that begins in January. As we reported, House Republicans today elected Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan to be their next leader. Although Democrats haven't voted yet on their leadership team, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York is poised to become the next speaker. And he's here now to outline his priorities. Leader Jeffries, welcome back to the show. Thanks for joining us. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY): Great to be with you. Amna Nawaz: So we're speaking a week after sweeping midterm Democratic wins. You're on track to win the largest House majority since 2008. The news, of course, is that you're also slated to vote later on whether or not to move forward with impeachment of Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. You have said you're a hard yes on that move to impeach him. Will this new Democratic majority mean more impeachment efforts of more Trump administration officials? Rep. Hakeem Jeffries: Well, we will cross that bridge when we get to it. We will focus right now on making sure we're doing everything possible to hold people accountable for what has happened up until this point, which is why I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. He's abused his power. He's undermined our national security, and Pete Hegseth is the architect of this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has made our country less safe and made life more expensive for the American people. Amna Nawaz: Could that accountability mean more impeachment efforts along the way, though? You haven't ruled that out? Rep. Hakeem Jeffries: We haven't ruled anything in and we haven't ruled anything out. Amna Nawaz: I want to ask you about just yesterday. You received a classified briefing about the Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, and his affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. What did you learn in that briefing that told you if U.S. national security had or had not been compromised? Rep. Hakeem Jeffries: Well, because it was a classified briefing, I'm limited in what I can reveal, but it certainly is the case that the Nvidia issue came up. There was a discussion about it. And, clearly, there's a need for members of Congress to be briefed moving forward so we can fully understand exactly the implications for America's national security. I think the president himself yesterday indicated that the FBI has launched an investigation into the Nvidia situation. That's another indication of the serious nature of what may have gone on in terms of involvement by the Chinese Communist Party. And so members of Congress, both the Gang of Eight, as well as the broader House and Senate, are going to need additional briefings and additional information, certainly in a classified setting, so we can unpack the nature of the damage that may have been done to our country. Amna Nawaz: It was also reported that the president had been briefed on this affair a year ago. Did you see anything that says to you the administration should have acted on this earlier, before these revelations became public? Rep. Hakeem Jeffries: We haven't gotten any information that's been disclosed to us yet to be able to draw any conclusions with respect to the timeline, but that certainly will be exactly the type of questions that we're going to need to ask. Secretary Rubio wasn't present at that briefing. He's overseas, as I understand it. We were briefed by the director of national intelligence, as well as the CIA director. The FBI director was not present. Certainly, if in fact it is the case that there has been an FBI investigation, which would certainly be appropriate, that has been launched, we're going to need to hear from the FBI as well. Amna Nawaz: I'm sure you have heard President Trump also say after those sweeping Democratic wins that he would love to work with you and the incoming majority, particularly on something for immigration. He then promoted Stephen Miller, the man behind his hard-line immigration approach, to chief of staff. Yesterday, you called Mr. Miller a stone-cold racist. You said you have zero interest in working with that kind of individual. So what is one thing that you think you can prioritize getting done with this White House? Rep. Hakeem Jeffries: Well, in this Congress, we were able to pass a meaningful housing affordability bill that was bipartisan in nature. That effort was led, of course, by Maxine Waters in the House, working alongside French Hill, a conservative Republican from Arkansas. And in the Senate, that effort was led by Senator Elizabeth Warren, working in partnership with Tim Scott. We were able to get that bill to the president's desk. He didn't sign it, but it has become law, and it was a meaningful step forward in terms of trying to create a supply of housing that the American people can afford. And that's the type of foundational work that hopefully can be done in the next Congress. We're committed to driving down the high cost of living in every area, that's housing, that's health care, that's groceries, that's gas, that's caregiving, and to making this country affordable again for everyone. Amna Nawaz: Leader Jeffries, what about on the immigration front? Is there something you can do with this White House? Rep. Hakeem Jeffries: Well, certainly, on the immigration front, we have a broken immigration system. It needs to be fixed. It should be fixed in a comprehensive way. Immigration enforcement should be fair, just and humane. We're not going to provide a dime to the administration's violent mass deportation mac

1ea8f1a97f6f.text: When Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with his G7 counterparts in Paris on Tuesday, he told them that President Trump had considered resuming the war with Iran or cutting a deal — but chose a third option: strangling the Iranian regime, three people who attended the meeting told Axios. Why it matters: The Iran war has become a political albatross in Trump's second term, costing Republicans dearly in the midterms. For months, the president has alternated between threatening to obliterate Iran and predicting it will capitulate and give him the deal he wants. "He's been searching for the solution, but he wasn't sure what's the best way to go," a U.S. official close to Trump said. This debate over which course to follow has led to strife between several factions within the top echelon of the administration. Each faction had the support of U.S. allies in the Middle East — namely Israel favoring renewed strikes and most Gulf countries opposing them. Driving the news: After meeting with the Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani on Monday, Trump said that a new round of strikes against Iran is "quite unlikely" and "doesn't seem to be necessary." Trump said he instead favors continuing the economic crackdown and naval blockade against Iran, in addition to a new operation dubbed "Iron Gate" to cut off land routes that Iran uses to move advanced weaponry and other technology. Behind the scenes: Rubio explained the U.S. Iran policy in a closed meeting on Tuesday with the foreign ministers of the G7 countries in Paris. "The President doesn't just have two options. It's not just return to war or sign a ridiculous peace deal. We won't do a stupid deal. The third option we have is to continue to do what we do now," Rubio said, according to three people in the room. Rubio went on to say that the U.S. is imposing devastating costs on Iran's economy, making it harder for it to fund terrorist organizations or rebuild its military. And there's no end date. "The President is not under false time pressure, the Iranians are inflicting major damage on their own economy," Rubio said. The intrigue: U.S. officials say that Rubio was among the members of Trump's national security team who pushed for the strangulation strategy, along with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Jared Kushner, Trump's adviser and son-in-law. That group opposed the resumption of war, didn't believe Iran's current positions could lead to a deal that serves U.S. interests and lobbied for the third option. State of play: Rubio is deeply skeptical of a diplomatic breakthrough. " Iran would love a deal. The problem is the conditions they continue to place are absurd. Like, they're not even serious right now," he told reporters after the G7 meeting. That could change if the Iranians feel more economic pain, he said. "Eventually you have to eat," he said. "Eventually the economic realities penetrate the skull of even the most radical lunatic. So I think as time goes on that will have an impact." Yes, but: Several U.S. allies — such as Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan — are concerned about Trump's intention to prolong the economic squeeze, a U.S. official said. The person said those allies worry that U.S. pressure on them to stop doing business with Iran — including by stopping flights and closing their borders — will create instability in their own countries. The other side: The course Trump has chosen is completely at odds with the directive Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei gave his government and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Khamenei ordered an end to the "no war, no deal" status quo, demanding a clear conclusion to the war. Iran's civilian leadership interpreted this as a green light to negotiate a deal. But if the current stalemate continues and pressure on Iran intensifies, the IRGC could see it as a green light for more aggressive attacks in the region in an attempt to break the status quo. "Iran has no intention of simply accepting this situation indefinitely," said Danny Citrinowicz, an expert on Iran at the Atlantic Council. "Tehran may conclude that increasing the economic and security costs for Washington and its regional partners is the only way to force a change in American policy." He added: "The danger is obvious: Iran escalates, Washington responds, and both sides find themselves in another military confrontation that neither necessarily wanted." What to watch: Qatar's prime minister briefed the G7 meeting on mediation efforts and his conversation with Trump the previous day. Al Thani said he came away from his meeting with Trump believing there's more breathing room for diplomatic efforts. The sticking points remain which side will take the first step toward de-escalating and which confidence-building measures the parties will agree to take. The Qatari prime minister said he wants to bring in China and European countries as guarantors, to help ease deep Iranian suspicions that Trump will break the agreement and resume the war in a few months.

966525820ed0.text: Mississippi, a state not known for close elections, now sits in the center of the national spotlight as an unusually high number of absentee and provisional ballots will determine the size of the Democratic majority in the Senate. In partnership with the Pulitzer Center, Liz Landers reports on how election officials are handling the ongoing vote count and the historic nature of this Senate race. Amna Nawaz: Mississippi, a state not known for close elections, now sits in the center of the national spotlight, as an unusually high number of absentee and provisional ballots will determine the size of the Democratic Party's majority in the U.S. Senate next year. Liz Landers reports on how election officials are handling the ongoing vote count and the historic nature of this Senate race. And the story is in partnership with the Pulitzer Center. Liz Landers: In a chapel at Tougaloo College in North Jackson, Mississippi, civil rights groups and community members celebrated a historic election. Man: I'm so glad that Mississippi has not been silent. (CHEERING) Liz Landers: Mississippi is one of the last races yet to be called in this election, where Democrat and district attorney Scott Colom could unseat Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. He would be Mississippi's first Black senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. Cindy Ayers Elliot, Mississippi Voter: If it can be done in Mississippi, it can be done anywhere. Liz Landers: Many, like seventh-generation Mississippian Cindy Ayers Elliot, see this moment as the culmination of decades of organizing. Cindy Ayers Elliot: We are definitely the fruit of the labor of the seed that was planted years and years ago. Liz Landers: More than 100,000 people in Mississippi voted absentee by mail. Today is the deadline for those ballots to be returned to election offices. Thousands of others who could not confirm their registration at polling places cast provisional ballots, also known as affidavit ballots, and their eligibility must be confirmed before their votes are counted. Now the race hinges on local officials in each of the state's 82 counties, who must examine each of those ballots and submit results to the secretary of state by Friday. This is the Hinds County election office. This is one of the largest counties in the state and a Democratic stronghold. And they are still counting days after the election a record number of these affidavit or provisional ballots. Jessica Carter, VoteRiders: A lot of people are confused right now. They don't know why they were asked to do an affidavit ballot or told they needed to do one, and they don't know why or what the process is. Liz Landers: Jessica Carter works for VoteRiders, a nonprofit focused on voter education efforts. She is worried that not every ballot will be counted. Jessica, how do Mississippi's voting laws compare to other states? Jessica Carter: Well, I feel archaic, because there's not a lot of flexibility. There's not a lot of really thinking about the voter and how -- and making it easier. Liz Landers: Monday, voters throughout the state continue to cure those affidavit ballots, showing up to county clerks' offices to verify their identification or addresses. David Wilson, Mississippi Voter: I have been voting in the same place since I have been voting. Liz Landers: Some at Hinds County Courthouse had found themselves mistakenly removed from their voter rolls. Why did they take you off the rolls? David Wilson: I have no idea. That's the reason why I'm down here today. It's resolved, but they couldn't explain to me why I was not able to vote. Lynntina Liddell, Mississippi Voter: Well, they mixed my address up. They had my old address, and I want to make sure that my ballot count today. Darrell Arnold, Host: Welcome to the "Unleashed Media and Talk" show with Darrell Arnold. Liz Landers: Conservative talk show host Darrell Arnold heard from plenty of his listeners about the affidavit ballots too. Darrell Arnold: It's never happened that I know of in my lifetime where all these affidavit votes, everybody showed up to vote. They said you have to vote affidavit today, and they're like, what do you mean? Liz Landers: More than 230,000 voters were designated inactive by Election Day, some mistakenly, after inaccurate address lists were provided to local officials, civil rights groups said. Professor D'Andra Orey of Jackson State University sees a link between Mississippi's history of voter suppression efforts and the historic nature of this midterm turnout. D'Andra Orey, Jackson State University: Some people actually really literally thought that they were going to lose their right to vote, which then mobilized them to get out the vote. Liz Landers: Across the South, Black turnout surged this year after several states redrew congressional maps to favor Republicans, often by eliminating majority-Black districts. Mississippi could follow suit next year. But the cost of living was overwhelmingly the top issue for Mississippi voters. Man: Pick another protein? Shhh, I'd rather pick another senator instead. Liz Landers: A frustration captured by a viral ad from Colom's campaign. Orey says that concern caused some white voters to shift their vote from red to blue this year. D'Andra Orey: I think it was really the perfect storm for the Democrats. And I believe they crossed over because of the economy. That, in itself, I think was enough to serve as an incentive for people to get out and vote. Liz Landers: The Colom coalition included split-ticket voters like Ginger Vaughn from Decatur. Ginger Vaughn, Mississippi Voter: I voted for the other guy. Liz Landers: Scott Colom. Ginger Vaughn: Because I feel like she's been there for a while now, and nothing has really gotten done, and his message was very positive, and hopefully, he can bring some change. I don't think she put very much into her campaign to begin with. And he went all out. Liz Landers: Arnold voted for Hyde-Smith for her conservative values, but c

a3f9a8ef5cba.text: High inflation persisted last month, providing little relief for Americans struggling with affordability. It is driven largely by food and energy price increases, but housing costs also rose. The country appears to be headed for an annual inflation rate of about 4% this year. To discuss what it means for the economy, Geoff Bennett spoke with Austan Goolsbee of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago. Geoff Bennett: Inflation remained stubbornly high last month, adding to the financial strain on Americans already struggling with the high cost of living. The latest Consumer Price Index shows prices rose four-tenths of a percent, driven largely by higher food and energy costs. Housing costs also climbed three-tenths of a percent, accounting for roughly a third of the larger-than-expected monthly increase. Economists now expect inflation to run at about 4 percent for the year, outpacing wage growth and further squeezing household budgets. Let's turn now to Austan Goolsbee, president and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago. Welcome back to the "News Hour." Austan Goolsbee: Yes, thank you for having me again. Geoff Bennett: So, today's inflation report came in hotter than many economists expected. When you look at the numbers, what stands out to you? Austan Goolsbee: Well, it's another distressing report, borderline disturbing. We have been hoping to get progress, not -- everyone understands that the war in the Middle East leads to higher energy prices, and we have been dealing with that. But several of these things that have been driving up costs were supposed to have gone away by now. So the impact of tariffs on goods prices was supposed to have faded by now. It still continues. And the -- perhaps the most troubling part is that services inflation, including health care and a bunch of things that people don't need reminders to know that inflation remains too high, services inflation is not coming down, is probably not mostly driven by oil prices or tariffs or things that might be transitory. And so we have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing, and we're going to have to deal with that. Geoff Bennett: And you have got food and housing costs that continue to climb, and unlike other expenses, these aren't things that families can simply cut out of their budgets. What does persistent inflation in these essentials mean for the Fed's ability to bring prices under control? Austan Goolsbee: Well, the Fed has a limited tool set, only has the interest rate, and it can try to cool off the economy to cool inflation. Everywhere I go out here -- and the Chicago Fed's district is kind of heart of the Midwest -- it's on everyone's mind. It's on business mind. It's on nonprofits' minds. It's on ordinary consumers' mind. I got a farmer Downstate Illinois sent me a diesel pump, says prices are killing them, and it's cost-side-driven. And now we're getting demand-side-driven component that's coming from the AI build-out, unfortunately, that everywhere you're going in the country, they're saying the costs of construction are high, the cost of computers, electrical equipment, computer chips, very high. And it's because they attribute this excess demand, almost conventional stimulus, if you want to think of it that way, that's coming from the data center build-out of multitrillion dollars. Geoff Bennett: I was going to ask you about the inflationary effects of the AI data center boom. What can policymakers do realistically to ease those kinds of pressures? Austan Goolsbee: It depends which policymakers. At the Fed, again, like I say, we just have a interest rate tool, but business investment does get affected by interest rates. And you have seen, as interest rates have gone up, you have seen various players in that space respond. That's all you can do. This is -- if it transpires the way it has been going, that's just old-fashioned demand overheating from excess stimulus that's coming from massive hype about AI overloading the economy in the short run. Now, up until now, this has mostly stayed in its lane in the directly affected and adjacent sectors to AI.My fear and my concern is that we're starting to see this drift out into just overall overheating prices of a whole bunch of things, including services, rising way too fast, far higher than our target rate of 2 percent inflation. At the same time, the job market has been pretty steady and stable. And the law gives the Fed two jobs, the so-called dual mandate, stabilize prices, maximize employment. The employment side is doing pretty well. The inflation side is not doing well, and we're going to have to come to terms with that if this inflation is going to prove persistent. Geoff Bennett: And inflation has remained above the Fed's 2 percent target for nearly six years now. Is there a concern that you have got businesses and consumers accepting high inflation as the new normal? Austan Goolsbee: Yes, that's a major concern. If that's what happened, it'll be that much more painful to try to get rid of inflation if it kind of gets built into the expectations that everyone has about prices. It doesn't have to be that way. And the only thing I will say is, it is true we have been above the 2 percent target for almost six years, but that hasn't been flat and high over that time. There were periods where we were making progress, and I thought we were headed back to 2 percent. Now what we have been dealing with is a series of shocks, some from oil prices, some from tariffs, now some from the demand side, and those -- a lot of those things were supposed to go away. And they might still go away and prove transitory, but whenever you start hearing the word transitory, your -- the hair on your neck should be standing up a little bit, because we went through that, where it was supposed to go away. And we found out that, when you have major disruptions to the supply chain, those oftentimes end up being far more persistent than let's call it the th

616fd83ed3a5.text: By — Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press By — Scott Bauer, Associated Press Scott Bauer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/farewell-to-the-electoral-college-democrats-now-control-enough-states-to-elevate-the-popular-vote Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Farewell to the electoral college? Democrats now control enough states to elevate the popular vote Politics Nov 10, 2026 6:28 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The midterm elections already upended national politics. Due to the number of state governments that have flipped to Democratic control, they also could change the way the U.S. elects a president. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The sudden blue tint to so many more statehouses opens the door to enough states joining 18 other Democratic-run states in a deal that would effectively neuter the Electoral College. It would remake the battle for the presidency into one for the most votes nationwide, rather than candidates concentrating on a half dozen or so swing states. READ MORE: Critics of Electoral College push for popular vote compact The states that have joined what is known as the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact account for 222 Electoral College votes. Once the number of states involved hits the 270 needed to win the presidency, the arrangement would effectively require a candidate to win the national popular vote to get an Electoral College majority. It's not clear that the strategy has support from all the newly elected lawmakers and governors in the key states, and it's almost certain to draw legal challenges from conservative groups. If it does go forward, it could land before the conservative-majority Supreme Court. Yet the sweep of the Democratic wins for governor and in state legislatures has the plan's supporters optimistic. In Tuesday's elections, Democrats won full control in six states representing 71 Electoral College votes: Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Minnesota, with its 10 electoral votes, had joined the compact when it was previously under full Democratic control in 2023. Some governors express support while others are noncommittal "We can do away with it," Wisconsin's new Democratic Gov. David Crowley said of the Electoral College, now that he has a legislature in his party's hands for the first time in 16 years. "I am interested in having those conversations with the state Legislature." Over the weekend, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a likely 2028 contender for the Democratic presidential nomination, said he would like his newly Democratic legislature to take steps toward making the Electoral College obsolete. "I think that the national popular vote makes sense. My views on that have not changed," Shapiro said on a liberal podcast. "I'll work with lawmakers to figure out what the right mechanism is for moving forward on that." If Pennsylvania and Wisconsin supported the compact, reaching the 270 threshold would require Michigan and either Arizona or Nevada to join. On Tuesday, the office of Michigan's new Democratic governor, Jocelyn Benson, said it would not comment on the matter. Not every Democratic governor is embracing the push yet. In a television interview on Monday, Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs declined to say whether she favored her state joining the compact. She said she's focused on other issues, like the cost of living. Nevada's previous experience with the issue also is a cautionary tale for supporters. WATCH: Can the Electoral College system be changed? In 2019, then-Democratic Gov. Steve Sisolak vetoed a measure that would have committed Nevada to joining the compact after it was passed by Democratic majorities in both houses of the Legislature. Sisolak said at the time that the popular vote idea would diminish the influence of smaller-population states like Nevada in national elections. Democrats passed another measure to join the compact in 2023, but couldn't figure out a way around the state's then-Republican governor. Tai Sims, a spokesman for Nevada's incoming Democratic governor, Aaron Ford, said in a Tuesday statement, "There will be a time to talk about presidential elections, but right now Ford's focus is lowering costs for working families." Republicans will use their diminished power to push back. "Our Constitution gives states a voice in choosing the president for a reason," Tyler August, the Republican leader in the Wisconsin Assembly, said in a statement Tuesday. "This would undermine that balance and disenfranchise Wisconsin voters by letting results in other states override their choice." Two presidents 16 years apart lost the popular vote The idea of shifting to a national popular vote gained traction among Democrats after Republican George W. Bush won the 2000 presidential election by inching ahead of Democrat Al Gore in the Electoral College even while losing the popular vote. It became turbocharged after Republicans again won the White House that way in 2016 with Donald Trump's victory over Democrat Hillary Clinton. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Under the National Popular Vote plan, the candidate who wins the popular vote nationwide would receive the Electoral College votes from the states that have joined the compact. There's nothing inherently partisan about the idea, said Patrick Rosenstiel, a Republican strategist in Minnesota who is a senior consultant to the popular vote movement. Occasionally GOP-majority legislative chambers, including the Oklahoma Senate, have passed proposals to join the compact, but the bills haven't gone further. He said his own presidential vote is essentially meaningless because Minnesota has reliably voted D

9a9f584660cc.text: Jim Bildner is the CEO of the Draper Richards Kaplan Foundation, one of the world's largest venture philanthropy organizations. It finds and funds entrepreneurs tackling big issues from health care access to clean water initiatives. In his new book, "A Matter of Hope," Bildner shares stories of impact and how hope fuels that work. He sat down with Amna Nawaz to discuss more. Amna Nawaz: Well, hope is tough to hang on to when faced with some of the world's most pressing problems, but it's also a tool to help solve them. Jim Bildner is the CEO of the Draper Richards Kaplan Foundation, one of the world's largest venture philanthropy organizations. It finds and funds entrepreneurs tackling big issues, from health care access to clean water initiatives and more. One of those entrepreneurs is Kiah Williams, co-founder of SIRUM, which redirects unused medications to people in need. Kiah Williams, Co-Founder, SIRUM: My life's work is trying to impact the communities like the one I grew up in, which are Black, brown, and low-income communities in this country. SIRUM started as a student project. And it was like a ragtag group of students, alumni volunteers. The original idea was this idea that it's just as easy to donate as to destroy medicine. We have grown to a platform and a program that broadly distributes medications, and we have done over a quarter-of-a-billion dollars of medicine to over 300,000 people. Amna Nawaz: In his new book, "A Matter of Hope," Jim Bildner more stories of impact and how hope fuels that work. For the record, Jim Bildner and his wife, Nancy, are supporters of the "News Hour." I sat down with Jim recently to talk about the book and his work. Great to see you. Thank you for being here. Jim Bildner, CEO, Draper Richards Kaplan Foundation: No, so, so glad to be here. Thanks for inviting me. Amna Nawaz: So Kiah is just one of the leaders, changemakers, visionaries, as you call them, that you profile in this book. How did you decide who to choose, who to include in this book? Jim Bildner: So, at Draper Richards Kaplan, we have funded nearly 280 leaders like Kiah. And you're asking me which one of these children, these adults who are making amazing things do I love the most. I love them all. (LAUGHTER) Jim Bildner: And the nine folks that are profiled in that book share this common characteristic, which is all of them have been profoundly impacted by the problems they're addressing. And unlike too many, they have refused to walk away from it. And the characteristic that has led them to be able to do these things -- and, by the way, they're not super-resourced, they don't have a ton of money, they don't have incredible networks. It's this ability to see the world as it exists, but also to imagine a future that's different, and here's the key, to be able to turn that imagination into reality. Amna Nawaz: You capture all of that resilience, this idea to imagine a better world, as you say, under the word hope, which can feel very wishy-washy sometimes. What did you learn about each of these leaders in terms of where that hope is derived from? How did they hang on to it in the face of what can be enormous challenges? Jim Bildner: Right. A soldier in the US Army has been arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia, British counter-terror police have said.
The 41-year-old senior serviceman was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday.
Counter Terrorism Policing London said the man had been arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023.
Section one of the Act relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while section three relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.
As part of the investigation, officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire.
The BBC understands the soldier was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire. The barracks serve as the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC), a strategic operational base for the alliance.
Counter Terrorism Policing said it was not linked to any other ongoing investigations.
FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement: "This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies."
He added: "While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message â this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."
Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, from Counter Terrorism Policing London, described the arrest as "significant".
"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," she said.
The unnamed soldier is currently in custody at a London police station.
He has been detained under the National Security Act 2023, allowing police to hold him without charge for up to 14 days.
Brig Gen Sean Stinchon, commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, said: "The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.
"I encourage anyone who thinks they've witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office."
Additional reporting by Daniel Sandford, UK correspondent.

aa7a6317df2b.text: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over a failure to place Nvidia customer Megaspeed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, sources familiar told Axios. Why it matters: The Commerce Department oversees the export of sensitive U.S. technologies and Lutnick's actions — or lack thereof — are increasingly under scrutiny following revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with Megaspeed employee and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. Driving the news: At a White House Situation Room meeting on Thursday after the midterm elections, Bessent pressed Lutnick on why Megaspeed was had not been added to the Commerce Department's entity list, to which Lutnick responded he would "look into it." Commerce Undersecretary Jeff Kessler also was repeatedly warned about Megaspeed in deputy meetings. But sources told Axios that Lutnick has spent the last year "undoing" efforts by other administration officials to hold Megaspeed — a company accused of illegally diverting U.S. chips to China — accountable because of concerns it would escalate the trade war with China. Catch up quick: The Commerce Department is increasingly at the center of scrutiny over the broader Trump administration's handling of an intelligence memo overseen by State Department head Marco Rubio. Lutnick was among the officials who received the report in May, ahead of a trip to China, Axios first reported. On Tuesday, the New York Times reported Commerce Undersecretary Kessler abruptly stopped an investigation into Megaspeed after Nvidia intervened. The Financial Times reported the department was delaying efforts to blacklist Megaspeed despite several U.S. government agencies pushing it to do so. Inside the room: White House and intelligence officials have pressed Lutnick and his top advisers to take action against Megaspeed since the fall of 2025, sources tell Axios. But they refused, so Bessent spoke up Thursday. "How come Megaspeed isn't on the entities list?" Bessent asked Lutnick, according to a source briefed on the meeting. Lutnick initially stammered, sources said, and then replied: ""I don't know. I'll look into it." One source, who has extensive experience concerning the chip controversy, said the reply was "bullshit" because Lutnick had resisted action ever since he was personally handed a memo, drafted by National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, that outlined the problems with Megaspeed.

A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run.
Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires.
His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded.
Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa.
He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements.
Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary.
When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained.
Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper ClarÃn.
However, the experts found that while Bertulazzi had tampered with the device, he had done so to prevent the alarm from sounding once he removed it.
A nationwide manhunt is now under way.
Italian media say that his extradition to Italy had been imminent after his last appeal was rejected.
Bertulazzi was first arrested after using a false passport to cross into Argentina from neighbouring Chile in 2002.
However, he was granted refugee status in 2004 and lived freely in the South American country until his re-arrest in 2024, when the current right-wing president, Javier Milei, took office.
Milei's government said at the time that "Bertulazzi is responsible for crimes that undermined democratic values and the lives of many victims".
He was a member of the Red Brigades, which kidnapped and killed a number of state officials in the 1970s and '80s.
Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades' Genoa section that kidnapped Pietro Costa on the street and then held him for 81 days before receiving a big ransom.
The money it made from the kidnapping was then used to buy a flat in Rome, which was used in 1978 for the Red Brigades' most notorious crime, the kidnap and murder of Italian former Prime Minister, Aldo Moro.
Moro was abducted when his car was ambushed on the way to the opening of parliament. He was held in the flat for 54 days before he was shot and his body abandoned in the boot of a Renault car in the centre of Rome.

Bafta-winning actors Toby Jones and Emily Watson have finished work on a film about the scientist behind Britain's first spacecraft to land on Mars, which got "lost".
Mars Express, directed by Mackenzie Crook, will see Jones play Colin Pillinger while Watson is his wife Judith.
The couple began developing the unmanned Beagle 2 probe to search for life on Mars while Pillinger was a professor of planetary sciences at the Open University in Milton Keynes. The probe went out of contact upon landing in December 2003, until it was finally spotted in 2015, after Pillinger died.
Crook said: "It's a complete honour to be telling the extraordinary story... for my first feature film as director."
Pillinger, originally from Kingswood near Bristol, became a familiar face in the 1990s as he sought public support and funding for the ambitious mission, enlisting celebrities and pop stars to help promote it.
Beagle 2 was launched into space on board the European Space Agency's Mars Express orbiter.
His Beagle 2 lander was due to touch down on 25 December 2003, but failed to send a signal confirming it had landed safely.
The mission was considered a failure for years, however, in January 2015 images taken by US space agency Nasa showed the lander had reached the surface safely.
Pillinger died eight months earlier following a brain haemorrhage.
The director added: "Joe Bone's beautiful script has made it easy to attract some of the best names in the business to join our brilliantly creative team and I'm thrilled to be working once again with my friend Toby Jones."
Crook, known for his roles in The Office and Pirates of the Caribbean, previously worked with Jones on Detectorists, the BBC's Bafta-winning comedy he wrote, directed and starred in.
He also starred in Small Prophets, a comedy which made its debut on BBC Two and the BBC iPlayer in February.
The film is expected to be released in 2027.

Transport and other public services across Spain have faced serious disruption in the first general strike for 14 years called by the main unions over housing and the high cost of living.
Demonstrations were also planned later on Wednesday, with the biggest protests expected in Madrid and Barcelona. Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.
The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Ãlvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."
However, the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations said participation was "low and uneven", depending on the areas and sectors involved.
Some of the biggest disruption on Wednesday was seen in the main industrial hubs of Madrid and the north-eastern region of Catalonia where traffic was halted on several main roads.
The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices.
The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later.
Rental prices in the capital have soared in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50m sq apartment in Madrid was an average of â¬1,170 in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about â¬2,460 (Â£2,056).
That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform.
Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes.
And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. SÃ¡nchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing.
"Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcareâ¦ These were collective conquests," he wrote on social media, praising those who took part in previous strikes.
The conservative People's Party (PP), by contrast, has accused the government of attempting to weaponise the strike for electoral gain.
PP leader Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o called the general strike "nonsense", calling the unions "mafia" and "trash". Feijoo's party is leading in the polls and party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed, which looks the most likely outcome of the 29 November election.
SÃ¡nchez told Spanish TV this week: "What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike."
Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Ãlvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid.
Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights.
The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.
Ãlvarez knew the 87-year-old, who had faced a tripling of her rent under new landlords, and says he was deeply upset by her treatment.
He rents a small, one-bedroom flat with his girlfriend, a dental hygienist, in the city's southern Arganzuela disrict. The couple pay â¬1,000 between them, which means each spends about half of their salary on housing, even before other bills.
"It's absolutely crazyâ¦ with the food, with the electricity, with the water, with gas."
He sees no way of getting on the property ladder: "You have to collect an insane amount of money to be able to buy a house. So with these salaries, it's impossible."
With current rent and purchase prices, he believes buying somewhere is "completely impossible".
However, the vice-president of the CEOE, Spanish biggest business association, Miguel Garrido, criticised the strike, complaining that businesses had little to do with the price of housing.
"This is not a strike for labour-related reasons, but rather for political ones, and it is closely linked to the early calling of elections," he said.
Demonstrations were planned for some of Spain's biggest cities later in the day and the scale of support will be widely viewed as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election.
Another reliable indicator of support for strikes is the level of demand for electricity with Spain's industrial sector.
Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red ElÃ©ctrica. During the last general strike 14 years ago, equivalent consumption was down by more than 15%.

Global health officials have been urged to widen the use of an existing Ebola vaccine in DR Congo following reports it may provide protection against a strain it was not designed to target. The Bundibugyo strain â for which there is currently no vaccine â has killed more than 5,300 people in the countryâs largest-ever outbreak. Medical charity Doctors Without Borders said restrictions on using Ervebo, developed by Merck for use against a prior Ebola strain, should be lifted so more people at risk, including young children, can be vaccinated.
The charity said DR Congo requested 500,000 doses of Ervebo, but only 70,000 were released. The World Health Organization recommends limiting its use against Bundibugyo to research studies because its effects remain unproven. Doctors Without Borders said early observations of fewer infections and deaths among previously vaccinated people justified wider use. A larger release from the global stockpile requires backing from the WHOâs vaccine advisers, who meet next week.

A criminal court in Cairo has postponed the retrial of the prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, whose case has drawn international condemnation.
Wednesday's opening hearing was adjourned until 18 November after defence lawyers representing the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr requested a new judge.
The UN has warned of "widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists".
Attalah told the BBC that a recent crackdown was meant to "send a chilling message" to "the very few newsrooms that are left".
She warned: "Everybody should be careful, everybody should be scared, everybody should be wondering if they are next."
Set up 13 years ago, Mada Masr became Egypt's leading independent news site with Attalah as its editor-in-chief and co-founder.
Last month, the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court convicted her of running a website without a licence - which she said she had tried in vain for years to obtain. She was issued a hefty fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds ($56,000; Â£42,000) and Mada Masr was ordered to shut down.
After that trial, Attalah found that a court had previously given her a one-year prison sentence, without her knowledge, for "spreading false news" - a charge often used against journalists and dissidents - as well as operating a website without a licence. It was issued in absentia in 2024, even though she was in the country at the time. Attalah is now being retried in that case by the same judge.
At the opening session, Attalah's defence team requested the judge's recusal, arguing that he had "already formed a conviction in mind against the defendant", Mada Masr cited its lawyer Hassan al-Azhar as saying, external. The judge went into recess before adjourning proceedings for a week to allow the court to consider the defence's request, he added.
Mada Masr also said Attalah's appeal against last month's conviction was scheduled to take place on 25 November.
Egypt has largely stifled freedom of the press, ranking 169th out of 180 countries for press freedom, according to Reporters Without Borders' 2026 analysis. The group says that at least 26 journalists who were arrested in recent years remain in detention.
While most newspapers and television stations now keep to government lines, Mada Masr remained a rare, independent and investigative news source in Egypt. However, since 2017 the site could only be viewed from outside the country.
It had reported on alleged corruption and human rights abuses, and provided deep coverage of politics and economics, as well as regional upheaval and wars in Libya, Sudan and Gaza.
In her BBC interview on Sunday, Attalah insisted that the factual reporting and professional standards of Mada Masr had an important role to play in Egyptian society, which could benefit the government.
"It's much better if you have a little space left to have it open for professional media organisations who do rigorous reporting, because if we disappear, then you make the space for conspiracies and disinformation," she said.
"People need to know, people need to consume information and you're shooting yourself in the foot if you're killing the newsrooms that do it properly."
In September, six journalists with the independent fact-checking platform, Matsda2sh - constituting its entire newsroom - were arrested in home raids by the Egyptian authorities and held incommunicado for nearly a week.
They have since been charged with joining the Muslim Brotherhood and financing terrorism, and their lawyers report that several were beaten and electrocuted in detention. They say that no evidence has been presented linking them to the Brotherhood.
Egypt's former president Mohammed Morsi â who was backed by the Muslim Brotherhood â was removed from power by the military, led by Abdul Fattah al-Sisi, in July 2013 after widespread protests. Under Sisi, who became president the following year, the Islamist movement was classed as a terrorist organisation, leading to a widespread clampdown.
On Tuesday, a spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Thameen Al-Kheetan, called for the Matsda2sh reporters to be released, with all charges dropped.
He also said the case against Attalah "raises fresh concerns regarding due process and fair trial".
"We call on Egypt to end all forms of harassment of journalists and media outlets, and to respect and fulfil the right to freedom of expression, including the right to information," Al-Kheetan said.
"The steps taken to suppress the continued work of both Matsda2sh and Mada Masr must be overturned. The people of Egypt have a right to read and hear views expressed through these fora on issues of legitimate public concern."
Attalah has suggested the authorities might again be trying to silence independent voices at a time of economic strain in Egypt and regional instability.
It has been widely noted that recent legal action against journalists comes after the US State Department waived human rights conditions on $320m (Â£240m) in its foreign military funding for Egypt in September. This allowed the funds to be released as part of Washington's annual $1.3bn military aid package.
The BBC asked US Secretary of State Marco Rubio whether he had raised the recent crackdown on independent journalism with Egypt's Foreign Minister, Badr Abdelatty, at their meeting about regional tensions in Paris on Monday.
"We didn't discuss it today," Rubio said. "Butâ¦ like anything else in foreign policy, there's always a balancing act to further the national interest of the United States. And in the end, Egypt has been a reliable and good defence partner of the United States."
"That doesn't mean you agree with everything another government does," he went on, adding that he was not "opining about their journalists".

Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.
The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.
All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.
"Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.
The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".
He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.
The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.
"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.
"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient - the seventh to recover from the virus - marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation, which now begins a 42-day countdown to officially being declared Ebola-free.
It had confirmed its first ever case of Ebola early in October when a Kenyan businessman died within days of arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
He had contracted the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 5,000 people have died in an ongoing outbreak that began in May. His mother also subsequently died.
Kenya's health minister said 135 identified contacts of the infected patients had also completed their 21 days in isolation.
"Today with the discharge of the last patient we can confirm and tell the world that seven patients have recovered - and all contacts have completed their follow-up monitoring," Aden Duale said.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) described it as an important achievement in the regional response to the outbreak.
"This is an encouraging moment for Kenya and for Africa. We must sustain surveillance and vigilance until the outbreak is officially declared over," Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya posted on X.
Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October.
All the Kenyan cases were linked to the man who had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda, with health officials reporting no evidence of wider community transmission.
Those who have recovered following treatment included four healthcare workers.
Five patients were discharged on 3 November, followed by a sixth three days later, before the final patient was cleared on Wednesday.
Under World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, 42 days must pass after the last patient tests negative and is discharged, or the last Ebola victim is safely buried, before an outbreak can be declared over.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Duale said the government would maintain heightened surveillance at border crossings, airports, health facilities and communities throughout the countdown.
Emergency response teams will remain on alert across the country, while the health authorities will continue monitoring travellers arriving from affected countries.
Kenyans returning from Ebola-affected areas are required to complete electronic health declarations before travelling, undergo screening on arrival and spend 21 days in quarantine under the supervision of health teams.
The minister also urged countries that had imposed travel and visa restrictions to reconsider them - adding that Kenya had no intention of serving as a quarantine centre for another country.
In May, a Kenyan court suspended US plans to open an Ebola quarantine facility for American citizens.
Kenya has maintained that there is no need to restrict domestic travel, trade or public gatherings.
The outbreak has nevertheless disrupted international travel, with some Gulf countries introducing restrictions affecting travellers from Kenya and other African countries.
Saudi Arabia stopped issuing visas to Kenyan nationals in late October, prompting concerns among those seeking employment there.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has announced that it is lifting its suspension on issuing new visas to Ugandan nationals, easing restrictions introduced in June.
But Ugandans will have to spend at least 21 days outside of Uganda before being allowed to travel to the UAE.
The UAE is also allowing certain students, diplomatic passport holders and Ugandan embassy employees to enter under approved health procedures.
Uganda, which shares a long and busy border with DR Congo, was among the countries first affected but declared its own Ebola outbreak over on 27 August.
The current outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

Jensen Huangâs public rhetoric on China became more admiring, and his stance on export controls more critical, after the US restricted Nvidiaâs made-for-China chip in 2025 â and as he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
A Semafor analysis of 42 podcast interviews with Huang since early 2022 shows how Huangâs argument around global chip policy evolved in a series of long-form, unscripted, and often friendly settings: Huang talked up Chinaâs strengths and cast Beijing as a formidable competitor as he argued more forcefully for a careful balance between protecting US interests and making US technology the backbone of global AI development.
Whether the Nvidia CEOâs position was shaped by his affair with an executive at a Singapore-based data center firm with alleged ties to Beijing is now a matter for the companyâs board, which hired Wall Street law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate, and for Congress, who plan hearings on the matter. But his stance on China and chip controls is freshly in the spotlight.
Semafor identified dozens of exchanges about China across the interviews and used a pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI to score each one on Huangâs stance on export restrictions and how he regarded China.
Before Chinaâs DeepSeek burst onto the global stage and Washington put new limits on Nvidiaâs sales to the country in early 2025, Huang spoke on podcasts about export restrictions in a largely neutral tenor, framing them as a matter of compliance, according to our review.
Mentions of China in Huangâs interviews rose roughly sixfold after those 2025 curbs, as the chip CEO argued that the restrictions hurt the US more than China. âIf we leave a market altogether, thereâs no question somebody else would step in,â he told Michael Milken in May 2025.
In 14 interviews since the 2025 curbs, he talked up Chinaâs AI researchers, open-source models, and manufacturing, often as reasons the US canât afford to cut the country off, or rejected the idea of treating it as an enemy.
He invoked the âAmerican tech stackâ 34 times across eight interviews since July 2025, arguing that the worldâs developers should build on US technology. In eight interviews he said that 50% of the worldâs AI researchers are Chinese or in China, suggesting the countryâs tech talent canât be ignored.

The News
A conservative firebrand who helped craft the Trump administrationâs campaign against Ivy League universities has returned to the White House to help chief of staff Stephen Miller build his team, a move that will test the administrationâs efforts to contain the influence of lobbyists within the White House.
May Mailman, who left her post as Trump policy adviser in 2026 to launch her own lobbying firm, will join the White House on a temporary basis as a special government employee, Axios first reported and Semafor confirmed.
In recent months, Mailman had built a healthy stable of corporate clients with active matters before the Trump administration, including Vestis, a uniform supplier which has pushed the FTC to block a rivalâs acquisition, people familiar with the matter said. The FTC is poised to block that deal, Semafor earlier reported.
Other companies sheâs worked for include Netflix, Meta, HPE, Comcast, and KKR, according to the people. Mailman, as well as the firms, either declined to provide a comment for this story or did not return a request for comment.
Mailman served as a policy adviser early in Trumpâs tenure, helping Miller go after Harvard and Columbia for what the administration called indifference to antisemitism on college campuses. She decided to return to the administration in recent days after Miller was named chief of staff, with Miller asking her to help him staff up his team and find ways to optimize relationships between government entities.
Mailman ruled out a policy role when discussing her return to public service, though, in part over concerns that it would fuel a perception of impropriety, one person with knowledge of her thinking said.
Still, the revolving door between the White House and lobbying work raises questions around how much Mailman stands to benefit personally from her new role and about the level of influence that corporations have held over this White House. The White House didnât immediately respond to a request for comment.
Mailman informed clients of her new role within recent days, and has instructed her firm â which she has taken a leave of absence from â to not engage with the White House while she is serving there for the next few weeks, some of the people said.
Rohanâs view
Americans on both sides of the aisle have grown frustrated with the level of influence big corporations have over this administration â with a CNBC survey of voters finding that corruption was the number one issue going into the midterms.
That perception has only been fueled by the list of Trump-connected lobbyists who have gone in and out of the White House, perhaps the only bipartisan move left in DC.
Mailman, perhaps uniquely, has shied away from the kind of publicity that some lobbyists have courted. And her efforts to create a firewall between her clients and her firm, as she returns to government service, stand in contrast to other administration power brokers, who openly tout their relationships with administration officials.

Some 300 schools across Italy have received bomb threats, according to Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara, who described the incidents as probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk".
Valditara told Italian TV that there was a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in Italy and elsewhere in Europe which had targeted flights, supermarkets and even hospitals.
The emails were sent to schools in Rome, Naples, Vicenza, Florence, Pisa, Trieste and many other Italian cities, and a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has called a meeting of top ministers and intelligence chiefs.
Meloni said the government was monitoring closely the "numerous reports of bomb threats at educational institutions" although checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger".
"These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook.
Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption. Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.
Italian reports said 280 school head teachers had received threats in recent days.
Although many schools were initially evacuated on Wednesday, the alarm was quickly lifted, according to reports from a number of regions, and pupils were allowed to return to class.
In a statement, the head of the central Umbria region Stefania Proietti said "checks conducted so far in Umbrian schools have proved negative, and law enforcement is working rapidly and carefully to verify each report".
In a separate incident, more than 300 schools in Northern Ireland were sent emails which police said they were treating as a hoax. Messages sent to number of schools in Scotland were also being treated by police as a hoax. It is unclear whether any of the incidents are connected.

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.
Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.
Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.
To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

Hundreds of transport workers in Chile have blocked roads and highways across the country in protest over high fuel prices.
Drivers of busses and lorries began protesting on Tuesday, gathering in convoys to halt traffic along major routes.
They are demanding a relief from surging diesel prices, which have been driven up by the war in Iran.
Talks between government officials and protest leaders have so far failed to reach a resolution, with another meeting expected to take place on Wednesday.
The protest is being organised by the â Fuerza del Norte trade union, which represents around 80% of Chile's lorry drivers, and the No+TAG civic protest âmovement.
"There is no point of agreement with the government that could offer any perspective to find solutions for everyone," AndrÃ©s AlarcÃ³n, a spokesman for No+TAG, said after talks broke down on Tuesday, adding "the strike continues".
Economy Minister Daniel Mas called for further dialogue, but warned "at some point, we will have to clear the highways".
He stressed the protests were impacting economic activity and exports, saying "we need to get the country moving again".
The government of President JosÃ© Antonio Kast has faced public discontent over fuel prices for months.
The average price of diesel has risen 74% since March, according to industry groups.
Juan Cornejo, the president of the Association of Intercity Bus Owners, which represents 14 mid-sized companies, told AFP that "we've reached our limit".
"We've spent more than a month working with negative numbers," he added.
