"Right now I'm not making any profit. Sometimes you even have to put in your own money to cover the client," AFP quoted the 47-year-old as saying.

8a391298e147.text:
The News
When users in CÃ´te dâIvoire of the popular ride-hailing and food-ordering app, Yango, started experiencing delays booking taxis and deliveries last month, the glitches were not to do with local bandwidth or power outages but the impact of problems elsewhere in the world.
Though temporary, the issue was a reminder of Africaâs vulnerability as a result of being reliant on internet infrastructure beyond the continent.
Yango licenses technology from Russian company Yandex, whose data centers in Russia were hit by Ukrainian drone strikes in October. While rumors spread among Ivorians that this was the cause of Yangoâs issues, a spokesperson for the Dubai-based company told Semafor the disruptions were down to infrastructure changes in the Gulf.
Hadil Elmaki said it had to move operations to a different data center after a partner company said in September that the infrastructure affected by Iranian attacks could no longer support Yangoâs work. âMoving interconnected systems between data centers is a complex process,â Elmaki said, while describing the disruptions as temporary âaffecting certain functions of our services in CÃ´te dâIvoire. These were not widespread outages, but intermittent issues.â
Yango runs some of its operations using Amazonâs cloud-computing infrastructure, including servers in the UAE, according to public records reviewed by Semafor. In mid-September, Amazon said it could not restore access to one of its three data center zones there after Iranian drone strikes in March.
Egyptian news publisher EnterpriseAM, which also used UAE-based servers, is another company that said it was affected as its website went offline for more than a day in March. It restored operations after moving to another hosting location and recovering missing data from its own systems.
Digital infrastructure has now become a target in conflict and with many African businesses leaning on overseas servers and the cables connecting them to the continent, the recent attacks raise questions about the resilience and control over their own data.
The vital internet cables linking Africa and Europe have also been disrupted amid fighting. In 2024 these under-water pipes in the Red Sea were damaged and attacks on commercial ships by Yemenâs Houthi forces complicated repairs. That conflict is also holding back new capacity â Meta has yet to build the southern Red Sea section of 2Africa, a cable designed to ring the continent. âThis is the new line of warfare,â Jane Munga, a technology policy researcher at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told Semafor. âSomething happening across the world can affect Africa.â
âDigital sovereigntyâ
Increasing numbers of African businesses are moving operations to the cloud, but as there is a lack of in-country servers, many are hosted abroad, said Amreesh Phokeer, research director at non-profit advocacy group the Internet Society. For Phokeer, this is now a policy question for the continentâs governments: âDo they invest locally to build more resilience, or do they create even more dependence on the outside?â
Governments and companies want more infrastructure at home. Under the banner of âdigital sovereignty,â they are expanding local data centers and cloud services to gain more control over their data and digital economies. Mauritania launched a national cloud service in June to support public administration, and Gabon inaugurated a data center built by pan-African technology company ST Digital in July to host government and business services.
Africaâs ambitions to build its own AI industry are adding to that demand. About 1,250 companies applied to be part of the first cohort of Askya AI Growth Platform, a program for African AI startups run by Lagos-based venture capital firm Askya Investment Partners, which began in October. âHow are you going to build sovereign cloud or sovereign AI if you donât have local infrastructure?â Phokeer asked.
Rubenâs view
Africaâs growing reliance on digital services demands greater transparency about the infrastructure behind them. On Facebook, Yango reassured users in CÃ´te dâIvoire that it was working to resolve their problems. In response to my questions, the company did not identify the infrastructure partner involved or say where the services had moved.
As African countries put more banking, public services and state records in the cloud, unanswered questions of this kind carry greater weight. Governments and companies should explain what happens when the systems supporting these services fail, who is responsible and how continuity is ensured.
Users should not have to investigate a companyâs infrastructure to know whether they can rely on its services. âThat is the work of government. That is the work of the regulator,â Munga told me. She also argued that journalists, civil society, and elected representatives can help citizens demand answers.
Regulators should require providers to demonstrate how they would keep essential services running through a disruption. Companies should explain significant failures and what they have done to prevent a repeat. That would give the public something more useful than assurances that an app is working again.
Room for Disagreement
Building local data centers alone will not protect African digital services from disruption. Experts argue that governments and businesses should spread their systems across several sites, with backup locations both inside and outside national borders.
âWhat if the war is local?â Munga said. âIt needs to be a strategy that thinks about diversification.â Phokeer pointed to Ukraine, whose internet proved resilient after Russiaâs 2022 invasion because it was not concentrated in a few strategic sites and could route traffic through several neighboring countries. âGood practice says you shouldnât keep your data in just one place,â he said. âYou need to be able to put it in several places.â

8ac11d2c173c.text: Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) hasn't been sworn in yet, but he's making a name for himself on Capitol Hill as one of the most outspoken anti-establishment progressives in the incoming freshman class. Why it matters: That's an unlikely position for a Democrat who represents a rural Ohio district that President Trump carried by 10 percentage points in 2024. Leonard is archetypal of a burgeoning breed of swing-district House Democrats — populist in style, receptive to left-wing policies and unbound by traditional political norms — that will be well-represented in the 120th Congress. "I'm really vibing with my class," he told Axios in a Tuesday interview on Capitol Hill. "These are everyday citizens who heard the same call I heard and stood up." State of play: Leonard, a professor of city planning who defeated Republican Rep. Mike Carey in last Tuesday's midterm elections, was turning heads on Capitol Hill before he even arrived for freshman orientation on Sunday. He told his local CBS affiliate the day after the election he will "be shopping for a new leader" unless House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) changes his pro-Israel positions. He made an even bigger splash on Tuesday with a video he posted to social media saying he met with "senior members" who warned him his life would be a "living hell" and that he would lose reelection if he opposes Jeffries for speaker of the House. The other side: House Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), asked about Leonard's video at a press conference Tuesday afternoon, told reporters, "I don't know what senior Democrats he's talking about." "I think all of us here can attest to the work, the time, the energy that Hakeem Jeffries put into helping us build this majority," Aguilar said. Aguilar predicted Jeffries will be "overwhelmingly selected" as speaker and that he doesn't "lose any sleep over that." "Members could have ideas and interests and they could have asks along the way, but the outcome is not in question," he added. What they're saying: Leonard, in his interview with Axios later on Tuesday afternoon, characterized the conversation described in his video as a "friendly" and "well-intentioned" talk with "folks who have been on the Hill for a really long time." "They let me know that while we all agree on a lot of this stuff ... the leader is going to pursue his message and agenda as he sees fit, and [said], 'Don't be insane. How could you possibly stand in the way?'" In addition to cutting U.S. aid for Israel, Leonard said he wants Jeffries to commit to supporting a Constitutional amendment to ban super PACs. "The time for half-measures is over," he told Axios. "I hear people, even members of the Progressive Caucus, talking about, 'Maybe we just tax super PACs.' Y'all, we need a 28th Amendment." Between the lines: Leonard said he has also found himself irked by House Democrats' seniority system, which makes it difficult for freshman members to get onto some of the most coveted committees. "I'm just a little confused and frustrated right now by why the Democratic caucus is so hierarchical when it comes to these committees," he told Axios. Leonard added: "When we're less democratic than the Republican Party ... that raises questions for me." What's next: The Ohio Democrat said he got a chance to meet Jeffries for the first time on Tuesday and arrange for their staffers to work out a time to sit down and talk. "I shook his and and I asked him for six minutes," he said, telling Axios he wants to "look him in the eye, let him know that [I] respect his capacity as a leader ... but I need something to take back to my district that shows that my party understands the magnitude of the crisis we face." "I'm going to hope that I can persuade him in the six minutes that we don't have to cross that bridge, but my constituents aren't bluffing and neither am I."

Coachella has announced the line-up for its 2027 festival, with Dua Lipa set to be the first solo female British artist to headline.
The Training Season singer is top of Friday's bill for both weekends in April, with psych-rock band Tame Impala headlining the Saturday shows and US singer SZA closing out both Sundays.
The massive festival returns to the California desert on 9 to 11 and 16 to 18 April next year, with more than 100,000 fans expected to attend each day.
Madonna is also set to return to the festival after a surprise appearance alongside this year's headliner Sabrina Carpenter, 20 years on from her first Coachella set.
The Queen of Pop came back with Confessions II, her first album since 2019, earlier this year and had been rumoured to be headlining Glastonbury 2027 before organisers ruled that out.
Swedish pop star Zara Larsson and US singer-songwriter Phoebe Bridgers are also set to perform, as well as Diljit Dosanjh who returns after making history in 2023 by becoming the first Punjabi language singer to perform at the festival.
Blackpink's Jisoo, US star Kehlani, rock band Weezer and Dancing On My Own singer Robyn are also among the artists on the line-up.
The festival will mark a reunion for Dua Lipa and SZA after the pair both headlined Glastonbury in 2024.
During her Pyramid stage set, Dua, who earlier this year married could-be James Bond actor Callum Turner, also brought out Tame Impala frontman Kevin Parker.
She becomes the first British woman to headline Coachella after Charli XCX performed on the main stage in 2025 before Green Day's headline slot.
During the success of her album Brat, the 365 singer made headlines after being pictured wearing a 'Miss Should Be Headliner' sash following her set.
Green Day appeared to respond with frontman Billie Joe Armstrong wearing a Brat baseball cap during their performance the following weekend.
Other UK artists on the 2027 line-up include EsDeeKid, Chase & Status and Jorja Smith.
Coachella is one of the most high-profile music festivals in the world thanks to its line-up and reputation for attracting a celebrity audience.
Tickets go on sale on Friday.

94eb70410daa.text: A week of political upheaval , financial turmoil and salacious scandal delivered one final indignity to the AI industry Tuesday, as Anthropic's staggering IPO target fell short of expectations. Why it matters: The bubble is wobbling. Investors, businesses and governments need a spectacular success from Anthropic to stave off a crisis of confidence that could tear through the broader economy. Facing new political headwinds, the industry can scarcely afford another setback — much less the spectacle of AI's crown jewel losing its luster on Wall Street. Zoom in: Anthropic announced plans Tuesday to raise as much as $64.4 billion in one of the largest IPOs in history, targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion. That's roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago, as slowing revenue growth, soaring infrastructure costs and a punishing market selloff tempered expectations. Anthropic's annualized revenue reached $81 billion in October, but its long-term commitments to chips, data centers and computing infrastructure have also climbed to nearly $901 billion. Zoom out: Anthropic's valuation reset caps a punishing stretch of new challenges that began with last week's stunning midterm results: 🌊 A blue wave of AI-skeptical Democrats will arrive in Congress armed with subpoena power and an appetite for investigating the industry's safety failures and vast political influence. Voters delivered another blow at the local level, favoring restrictions on data-center development in 40 of 41 ballot measures nationwide. 🤖 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the central cog in AI's global gears, was swept up in an espionage scandal after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. His board, the FBI and Congress are investigating. Nvidia has shed more than $1 trillion in market value since the first New York Times revelations on Oct. 29, with shares plunging further Tuesday as the company faces a new shareholder lawsuit. 📉 Wall Street went into a tailspin as investors reckoned with the implications of the Democratic sweep — including in data-center havens like Texas — for AI's sprawling infrastructure ambitions. The Nasdaq lost $2.5 trillion in market value Thursday, its worst session since April 2025, before staging a sharp rebound. ⚠️ Financial warning signs are mounting: OpenAI scaled back its fundraising ambitions, while SoftBank reported a $3.7 billion write-down on U.S. data-center equipment, contributing to a $7 billion quarterly loss. Amid renewed fears of rate hikes , anxiety is also spreading to credit markets , where lenders have grown wary of financing the industry's astronomical infrastructure spending. Reality check: Anthropic is still poised for one of the largest IPOs ever, with Google, Nvidia and other technology giants committing another $26 billion in private investment alongside the public offering. The company could emerge with roughly $85 billion in net new capital — a historic financial windfall for a company founded less than six years ago. Yes, but: Bubbles don't run on "good enough." They demand more, better and faster — indefinitely. Even a $1 trillion or $1.5 trillion valuation of Anthropic may not be enough to reassure investors, who thought just a few weeks ago it'd be worth as much as $2 trillion . What to watch: Whether Anthropic can deliver a spectacular debut and sustain it after trading begins. SpaceX's stock surged after its record June IPO, only to surrender those gains and fall below its offering price within weeks.

9874d6fb6c80.text: House Republicans are turning to one of their fiercest fighters to lead their diminished conference after one of their biggest drubbings in decades. Why it matters : Jim Jordan , 62, a founding member of the hardline House Freedom Caucus, has completed a stunning insurgent-to-establishment turn after spending much of his nearly 20 years in Congress battling Republican leaders from the right. The Ohio Republican's victory over House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) represents a bet by Republicans that they shouldn't move away from President Trump to claw their way back to power. But Republicans are divided over what went wrong in the midterms, and whether a more confrontational approach is the right answer. Driving the news: Republicans emerged from last week's defeat hungry for change , handing Jordan a 106–73 victory over long-time GOP leader Scalise. GOP Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) and Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) survived their elections. Jordan pitched himself as a battle-tested fighter capable of defending Trump against Democratic investigations and winning back the majority. What they're saying: "I think when you take a beating like we took, you need to make some changes, and I also think we're gearing up for war," Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.), who backed Jordan, told Axios. "We need someone who can punch hard, and I think that he'll do that," Fine said. "We just got beat bad. We can't just go in with the same step forward," Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) told Axios. McClain told Axios: "Don't count Jim Jordan out. He's a fighter. He's been able to get stuff done." Yes, but: Not all Republicans are convinced they have the right response to their losses. Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-Fla.), who backed Scalise, argued that Republicans lost too many independent and Hispanic voters, pointing specifically to the Trump administration's immigration enforcement policies. Asked whether Republicans should have examined their losses before electing new leaders, Gimenez said: "Yeah, we probably should have," adding he was "not sure" whether Jordan is the right person to lead Republicans back to the majority, though he pledged to support him. "We've got to do a lot of introspection," Rep. Mark Alford (R-Mo.) told Axios. "It's going to take some really deep thought and really looking at what we did wrong and what we can do to gain back the trust of the American people." Zoom in: Jordan's victory marks a major shift in the relationship between GOP leadership and the hardline House Freedom Caucus, whose members have spent years clashing with party leaders. Rep. Eric Burlison (R-Mo.), who is running to chair the Freedom Caucus, told Axios he hopes the group won't have to push leadership as hard under Jordan, though it will still try to serve as the party's "moral compass." But Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.), a Freedom Caucus member who voted for Jordan, warned that changing the man at the top won't change the conference's ideological divisions. "I still don't expect a ton to change," Crane told Axios. The intrigue: Jordan's elevation could also sharpen tensions with Senate Republicans, whose leader, John Thune (R-S.D.), has frustrated House Republicans over his handling of Trump's legislative priorities . Asked whether Jordan would push back harder on the Senate than Scalise, Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) told Axios: "That's to be seen, but I think he was voted in with that in mind." The bottom line: Jordan inherits a conference eager for a new direction but still deeply divided over what that should look like.

7c4bc592c088.text: Stephen Miller wants to use his new role as White House chief of staff to win back young and minority men who helped elect President Trump in 2024 but swung toward Democrats in the midterms, two people familiar with the administration's plans tell Axios. Why it matters: Miller, named last week to replace Susie Wiles, plans to focus on reviving the populist agenda that helped the president build his 2024 coalition, with an emphasis on working-class voters. Young, working-class and minority men fled the GOP in droves in last week's elections , amid high prices fueled by Trump's tariffs, the war in Iran, and concerns about AI's impact on the job market. Another key factor in last week's voting: Latino men also swung sharply toward Democrats, as the administration's hard-line immigration crackdown became an increasingly contentious political issue. Driving the news: Miller wants to spend more time highlighting administration policies he believes haven't gotten enough attention, and that will appeal to working-class voters concerned about the economy, insiders tell Axios. His priorities will sound familiar to Trump watchers: eliminating what the administration considers "woke" policies from colleges and workplaces, lowering prescription drug prices, and rooting out government and health-care fraud. He also wants to emphasize reducing the federal bureaucracy and push for permitting reform , while highlighting how those efforts could help address affordability. Sources in the business community say Miller's ideological drive makes him mostly impervious to typical Washington lobbying. Yes, but: With Democrats taking control of Congress in January, Miller will have to advance that agenda without the help of Republican majorities in either the House or Senate. Some of his plans could be pursued through executive orders by Trump. Others, including permitting reform, would require bipartisan cooperation. That could be a challenge: Miller, a political fighter who's been called Trump's " wartime consigliere ," isn't popular among Democrats. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who's in line to become House speaker in January, has said he has "zero interest" in working with Miller, whose immigration policies have made him a frequent target of Democratic attacks. Flashback: Trump won men under 30 by 14 points in the 2024 election, according to a Tufts University study of election data. Last week, Democrats won that demographic by 22 points in House races — a 36-point shift. The shift was even more pronounced among young Latino men, who went from backing Trump by 2 points in 2024 to favoring Democrats by 37 points in 2026. Young voters with a high school education or less swung 37 points toward Democrats — from backing Trump by 12 points in 2024 to favoring Democrats by 25 points in the midterms. More than half of voters under 30 cited the economy and jobs as one of the country's three biggest issues, according to the Tufts study. Among young voters who said they were falling behind financially, 73% backed Democratic House candidates. Miller's focus on young men isn't new. He made direct appeals to them during Trump's 2024 campaign. During a Fox News appearance just before the 2024 election, he urged young men to embrace their support for Trump, telling them to "show that you are a real man" and "not a beta." On Election Day 2024, Miller posted on X : "Get every man you know to the polls."

A historic restoration of Florida’s Everglades is proceeding at an unprecedented pace, although more scientific analysis is needed to understand how the fragile watershed is responding to the multi-billion-dollar effort, according to a new report.
The report from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine, published last month, said the river of grass has benefitted recently from better collaboration between the federal and state governments and a record infusion of funding. Now that several projects are complete and the nearly 26-year effort continues to transition from one of planning to operations, a clearer vision also is required of what the restoration can achieve amid constraints and changing conditions, the scientists said.
“We’ve hit our stride in getting projects constructed, to the point where they’re being operated. And also this report points out we’re beginning to see benefits on the ground,” said Steve Davis, chief science officer at the Everglades Foundation, an advocacy group. “This is a big, challenging undertaking, but with the progress that we’ve been seeing of late, we’re starting to see the benefits of Everglades restoration and we know this large-scale infrastructure can do what we intended.”
The mammoth restoration, envisioned as a 30- to 40-year effort, involves dozens of landscape-scale projects spanning central and south Florida, designed to revive the watershed that is responsible for the drinking water of millions of people. A series of historical attempts to drain the Everglades made modern Florida possible but led to a litany of environmental problems, such as harmful algae blooms that have sickened Floridians and left marine life belly-up. The National Academies, a private nonprofit organization, has provided biennial reports on the restoration’s progress since 2004, based on a congressional mandate.
The report said the pace of restoration has increased substantially over the past two years, reflecting the priority given to projects such as a massive reservoir under construction south of Lake Okeechobee that is the centerpiece of Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ environmental agenda. Seven Everglades restoration projects are complete, including reservoirs to the east and west of Lake Okeechobee designed to help address harmful flows of lake water that have contributed to some of the harmful algae blooms. South of the lake, the reservoir in the region called the Everglades Agricultural Area is scheduled for completion in 2029.
Benefits already are apparent, the report said. In Everglades National Park, dry season flows east of Taylor Slough have improved, although effects on salinity in fragile Florida Bay are difficult to discern. In Shark River Slough, flows have increased particularly during the dry season. In the Picayune Strand, the vegetation is transitioning from that of uplands to wetlands.
“We have to hit the water quality mark.”
— Steve Davis, Everglades Foundation
But the report said scientific analysis of these benefits has not been consistent, hindering understanding of the restoration’s progress and opportunities for learning. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and South Florida Water Management District, federal and state agencies, respectively, oversee Everglades restoration. The Army Corps said it was working with state, tribal and institutional partners to review the report. The water management district said it was focused at the moment on a recent rain event that caused flooding in coastal areas in central and southeast Florida.
The National Academies also raised concerns about the loss of federal staff responsible for Endangered Species Act protections. The effort to rehydrate the river of grass threatens, for example, the Cape Sable seaside sparrow, an endangered ground-dwelling bird found in a remote area of Everglades National Park and the Big Cypress National Preserve. During nesting season some water control structures are closed to spare the sparrows, but this inhibits the flow of water and can flood tree islands that are important to the Miccosukee Tribe and a range of animal and plant life. Sea level rise has exacerbated the problem.
“It takes not only funding, but it takes staff to analyze these project reports. It takes staff to communicate to organizations like ours so we can provide stakeholder feedback,” said Casey Darling Kniffin, policy director at Friends of the Everglades, an advocacy group. “That requires staff at the federal level. So despite having record funding, if we don’t have the staff to carry out this work we will see delays going into the future of Everglades restoration.”

The report noted the restoration’s success depends on water quality. A new standard took effect this year called the Water Quality-Based Effluent Limitation, designed to measure nutrient pollution in the Everglades associated with fertilizer use on the sprawling sugar farms south of Lake Okeechobee. Before the EAA reservoir, characterized by DeSantis as the “crown jewel” of Everglades restoration, can operate at full capacity, the WQBEL must be met for at least five years. So far the standard has not been met, based on available data through water year 2025, the report said. (Water years are measured from May 1 to April 30.)
The scientists warned that if existing strategies are not enough to bring the water into compliance then “aggressive and possibly contentious new actions” likely will be necessary. Some Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee are encouraging leaders to scrap the chamberâs Select Committee on China once their party takes over next year.
âFor a lot of what the China committee was doing â weâve already got a Foreign Affairs Committee, weâve already got the Subcommittee on Asia and the Pacific,â Californiaâs Rep. Ami Bera, the top Democrat on that subcommittee, told Semafor. âWe could do a lot of the work; I think Ways and Means [Committee] could do a lot of the trade policy stuff.â
A spokesperson for New Yorkâs Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs committee, told Semafor that âwe will follow the lead of the incoming speaker on how he wants to handle the China select committee, but the Foreign Affairs Committee is well poised to conduct oversight of this administrationâs China policy.â
The committeeâs current chair, Michigan Republican Rep. John Moolenaar, released a statement last week urging Democrats not to dismantle it. Other Democrats are pushing for the committee to broaden its focus beyond China if they opt to keep it next Congress. Still others in the party are worried about the politics of axing the committee for parochial committee leadership reasons, given recent China-related controversies.
âPolitically, theyâre not smart, because they could use this against Trump, whoâs being basically pro-China,â a person familiar with the jockeying told Semafor. âMaybe modify it [or] alter it in terms of scope â but to shut it down or make it part of the Foreign Affairs Committee is honestly dumb.â
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who as speaker would have the final say over the future makeup of select panels, said earlier this week he would discuss the issue with incoming committee leaders this morning. Some of them have also pushed back against the idea of forming a select panel on AI next year as Democratic committee leaders look to reserve their own turf on AI and other high-profile issues.
Other observers have noted that the China panelâs jurisdiction extends across that of others, and it has collaborated with the House Oversight, Financial Services, Energy and Commerce, Homeland Security, Appropriations, and Natural Resources committees. At least five groups have sent letters, shared with Semafor, urging leaders to reauthorize the committee come January: the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, With Honor Action, the Alliance for Trade Enforcement NOW, the American Mold Builders Association, and the Forging Industry Association.

The News
President Donald Trumpâs flirtation with a bipartisan immigration deal is running into a wall of skepticism in Washington.
For one, Democrats scoffed at Trumpâs decision to promote Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration policies, to chief of staff following the departure of Susie Wiles. Thereâs little indication that Miller has softened on immigration whatsoever.
And while Trump acknowledged in a CBS interview that his deportation policy might âbe too toughâ and said a bipartisan deal could be âdoable,â many in the White House agree thereâs simply far too much daylight between Trump and newly-empowered Democrats.
Thereâs âtoo big a marginâ between the two sides âfor it not to be a crazy bill,â one administration official told Semafor.âThe Dems are going to overreach almost immediately, there will be no amnesty,â the official added.
Still, Trump on Monday suggested that Miller would look to work with Democrats, while quickly drawing a clear line on what an immigration deal could include: âWeâre not going to have amnesty or anything,â Trump said.
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement that Trumpâs âstrong immigration policy remains unchanged.â
âThe administration will continue removing the worst of the worst from our country,â Rogers said, blaming former President Joe Bidenâs administration for creating an immigration crisis. âWhat the Democrats did to our country will not be forgotten, and the president is willing to work with anyone to ensure it never happens again.â
The View From democrats
Democrats have no interest in working with Miller given his record. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries dismissed the White House aide on Monday as âa stone-cold racist,â adding that he has âzero interest in working with that kind of individual.â
Jeffries has talked up the âDream and Promise Actâ as a comprehensive immigration bill that Democrats want to move through both chambers, though itâs unlikely to break a filibuster in the Senate next year. Some lawmakers are also looking to the âDignity Actâ as one potential bipartisan compromise on border security and immigration reform, but that bill already fractured Republicans this Congress who balked at its pathways to legal residency for âDreamers.â
âThe three things that Latinos expected Democrats to do is ICE accountability, pathway to citizenship, and to lower costs,â MarÃa Teresa Kumar, president and CEO of Voto Latino, said at a National Partnership for Women and Families Event Tuesday.
Rep. Veronica Escobar, D-Texas, said the âDignity Actâ would be reintroduced next Congress and could be rewritten to include more Democratic priorities now that theyâd be in control of the House and Senate.
She too, conceded that Miller would be âa problemâ but added âthe ultimate decision is Donald Trumpâs, and he said he was open to making a deal. Letâs see if heâs a man of his word or not.â
Room for Disagreement
A Trump adviser echoed the presidentâs dismissal of any sort of deal on broad immigration amnesty, but suggested a longshot plan: âIf [Trump] can get the Democrats on board with increased funding for ICE and law enforcement to specifically target murderers, rapists, drug dealers, and the most hardened criminals, I think thatâd be a great deal for the country.â That adviser emphasized that Trump and Miller will be focused on doing âwhatâs best for the MAGA base.â
Eleanor Mueller contributed to this report.

Senate Republicans spent this week wrestling through divisions, reelecting John Thune as their leader, and pledging to confirm conservative judges while avoiding a government shutdown during their last two months in the majority.
They still havenât figured out how to use their greatest power in the lame duck: another big party-line bill that would send billions to the Pentagon. Such a proposal could contain other GOP priorities; Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, dubbed it the âlast supperâ for the partyâs reign.
Republicans have just a few more weeks to use the blunt power of budget reconciliation, which allows them to evade a filibuster to send President Donald Trump funding viewed as crucial by many in the Republican Party for depleted military reserves and ammunition after nine months of war. Using the tool, which Republicans wielded last year to pass a party line tax bill and this year for immigration enforcement funding, represents a crucial calculation for Thune to make as Democrats weigh blocking a government funding bill if it includes money for the Iran conflict.
But passing a party-line bill is not going to be easy: It requires 50 Senate votes, a majority in the House, and two unlimited Senate vote-a-ramas that defeated or retiring members may have little interest in enduring. And Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who would set the stage for another big party-line bill, said heâs worried the party isnât moving quickly enough.
âRight now, Iâm not getting engagement from the White House, from either Senate or House leadership. So if thatâs going to happen, itâs going to come from the pressure from members here,â Johnson told Semafor on Tuesday.
Republicans are divided over whether they should shovel more money towards the Pentagon with the Iran war is ongoing, particularly since many in the GOP cite the conflict as one of the main reasons for the partyâs brutal losses in this monthâs midterm elections. Republicans are also growing more frustrated over the leadership of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who avoided a House impeachment on Tuesday but is facing sustained questions from congressional Republicans over Iran and his blocking of military promotions.
And Republicans say there still isnât a blueprint on how to move forward.
âI think weâre going to have a plan,â said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., after a day of literally hours of internal GOP meetings. âIf youâre asking me if we have a plan right now, I wouldnât recognize it if it jumped up and yodeled and bit me in the butt.â
When it comes to more Pentagon funding in a party-line bill, there are real divisions emerging behind the scenes already.
On one side is Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., who said âwe need to get reconciliation done.â Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Semafor the party needs to pass a âstrongâ reconciliation bill and that itâs not going to be aimed at Iran: âThat has a lot more to do with funding our military and giving them what they need than it does the war.â
But Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., argued it would be âtone-deafâ to pass such a bill and vowed to oppose it. He said passing anything âto further or enhance the Iran war, I think thatâs not listening to the electorate.â Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said, âI canât imagine why we would do that.â Both Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, are wary of using reconciliation.
Republicans would not brand the effort as an Iran war funding bill, but they would have a difficult argument to make if the conflict continues. Many Republicans have wanted the war to end as soon as it started.
unanswered questions
Thune said repeatedly this week that heâs not sure he or House Speaker Mike Johnson can round up the votes to get another reconciliation bill done. He said Pentagon funding is a âmajor issue that has to be addressedâ but that he doesnât know if he has 50 Republicans ready to pass a budget resolution and endure those prolonged amendment votes.
With a government funding deadline bearing down on Congress next month, putting a party-line funding bill on the table is âthe only way we create some leverage with the Democrats,â argued Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., a close Thune ally.
âIf we just sit and wait for them to come to the table, theyâll figure they have leverage because theyâll have the majority in the new Congress. So the thing they have to recognize is we can put a reconciliation bill together,â Hoeven said.
There are competing priorities among Republicans of what that reconciliation bill would do. While Pentagon funding is the most obvious must for some Republicans, others would push to include measures to address the cost of living, elections, farm aid, and more.
âWhat weâre trying to do is jam 18 things into a four-thing box,â said Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va. âI may be a proponent of it. Because itâs very possible to try to get as much done as you can possibly get done before the other folks take over.â
Room for Disagreement
Justice said even Republican critics of the Iran war would have to come around eventually. âWeâre there, like it or not like it. And if weâve got folks there, and they need bullets and we canât give them the bullets, shame on us,â he said.
âHowever you feel about [the war], really, if we donât fund the military, weâre sending the wrong signal for even the ones who want to settle out sooner,â Hoeven said.
Burgessâs view
Welcome to the first legislative battle after the midterms. Democrats are starting to line up against anything funding the Iran war, which could leave reconciliation as Republicansâ only play. But itâs still a risky one.
There are logistical challenges: The Senate is only scheduled to be in session for four weeks the rest of the year, although Thune said heâs willing to add days and weeks to complete their agenda. In August 2025, Vice President JD Vance and Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin visited cold storage equipment manufacturer Alta Refrigeration to announce plans to roll back regulations the company opposed.
The EPA followed through in May, giving manufacturers of cold storage and other equipment several more years to continue selling devices that use hydrofluorocarbons with high global warming potential as refrigerants. Now, Georgia-based Alta and the Coalition for the Use of Safe and Efficient Refrigerants—an industry group also based in Georgia and chaired by Alta’s president—are suing the EPA and Zeldin, arguing that the agency did not go far enough.
The lawsuit shows how one company sought to push the Trump administration’s deregulatory agenda even further, revealing tensions between an EPA eager to roll back regulations and industry interests seeking yet more.The case is unfolding alongside a series of legal challenges to the agency’s actions, brought by a broad coalition of major industry groups representing air conditioning and equipment manufacturers, attorneys general from nearly two dozen states and an environmental group, all of whom contend the agency went too far.
The rollback and ensuing lawsuits stem from the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act of 2020, bipartisan legislation signed by President Donald Trump during his first term that mandated a gradual phasedown of hydrofluorocarbons. The chemical refrigerants are potent greenhouse gases, trapping heat in the atmosphere hundreds to thousands of times more effectively than carbon dioxide, pound for pound.
National industry groups supported both the legislation and a related international climate agreement, the Kigali Amendment, because the measures would help boost U.S. manufacturing jobs and exports. In 2023, the EPA issued a rule to help facilitate the required phasedown of hydrofluorocarbons.
The EPA’s May action extended the transition timeline, giving Alta and other manufacturers a five-year reprieve from requirements to use more climate-friendly refrigerants in new equipment. The agency said the delay would benefit companies and lower prices for American consumers. However, Alta wants a permanent reprieve, something it said the head of the EPA previously promised.
“Administrator Zeldin stated plainly that he intended to ‘give ALTA what it was asking for,’ the company argued in a document filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in September.
Before filing their lawsuit, Alta and the Coalition for the Use of Safe and Efficient Refrigerants petitioned the EPA to grant cold storage equipment manufacturers a permanent exemption from the hydrofluorocarbon phasedown. When the agency proposed a reprieve instead, Alta sought help to try to persuade the administration.
A declaration submitted by Alta President Eric Brown describes an exchange between Zeldin and a member of Georgia’s congressional delegation. The documents show screenshots of what appears to be Zeldin explaining that an act of Congress would be needed to make the rollback permanent.
The images show the request came from “Rep Buddy C.”, which may be U.S. Rep. Earl “Buddy” Carter (R-Georgia). Carter and Zeldin, a former U.S. representative from New York, served as colleagues and co-sponsored legislation during Zeldin’s tenure in Congress.
Citing the ongoing lawsuit, the EPA and Carter’s office both declined to comment.
Joseph Goffman, an EPA assistant administrator during the Biden administration who is not involved in the lawsuit, said Brown’s declaration “read as much like somebody throwing a tantrum as it did like a legal document” and praised Zeldin for “actually doing his job.”
Alta Refrigeration declined to comment.
Brown’s declaration said the EPA, through a member of Georgia’s congressional delegation, instructed him to withdraw comments Alta submitted to the White House Office of Management and Budget. Brown wrote that he did so “under duress.”
Goffman said he had never heard of the Office of Management and Budget asking for comments to be withdrawn because the White House disagreed with their content. Goffman said Zeldin’s decision not to permanently exempt Alta from the rule does not undo his earlier decision to give Alta and others a five-year reprieve, which Goffman said should never have been granted.
The industry groups that supported the hydrofluorocarbon phasedown and are now suing the EPA over the rule change represent more than 90 percent of residential and commercial heating, ventilation, air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment manufactured and sold in North America, along with more than 60,000 plumbing and heating, ventilation and air-conditioning professionals.
American companies invested heavily to transition to new technology to comply with the phasedown of climate pollutants, and the 2026 revision disrupted that without adequate explanation, the groups noted.
“It’s bad for the environment, bad for the economy, and it’s opposed by the bulk of the industry,” said David Doniger, a senior attorney and strategist for the Natural Resources Defense Council, the environmental organization that sued over the rule change. “It’s hard to think of something you could do that’s less popular or that does more harm and makes fewer friends than this.”

South Africa's most decorated Olympian Tatjana Smith was in tears as she announced that she has switched allegiance to the Netherlands.
The 29-year-old won four Olympic breaststroke medals, including two golds, before retiring after the Paris 2024 Games.
She came out of retirement in September and hopes to compete in the 50m breaststroke as the event makes its Olympic debut at the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.
Smith, whose maiden name was Schoenmaker, wiped away tears as she read a letter addressed to South Africa, saying that "dreams can change as we grow".
Smith has dual citizenship because her father is Dutch.
She said she has "always been Dutch and South African" and that this is an opportunity to "explore another part of my identity and heritage that I've never experienced through sport".
She said it also offers her "greater high-performance support and the potential to build a more sustainable career" because the "financial and practical challenges of swimming were among the reasons my previous career became difficult to sustain".
Smith has previously said that financial worries, which included a dispute with Swimming South Africa over prize money, contributed to her decision to step away from the sport.
Swimming South Africa has been approached for comment.
Smith won four world and Commonwealth gold medals between 2018 and 2023.
She won gold in the 200m breaststroke and 100m silver at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, before adding 100m gold and 200m silver in 2024.
"Representing South Africa was a childhood dream come true, and it's a chapter I will always look back on with immense pride and gratitude," she said on social media., external
"The people, the memories and everything we achieved together will always be part of me. But dreams can change as we grow.
"This next chapter is about embracing another part of who I am, falling in love with the journey and discovering what more I'm capable of.
"I'm excited for what lies ahead, and I truly hope you'll continue to be part of the journey with me."
Smith, who said she will continue to live and train in South Africa, is set to represent the Netherlands for the first time at the short course World Championships from 1-6 December.
She acknowledged that her switch "may disappoint or break the hearts" of some supporters.
The Ministry of Sport, Arts and Culture in South Africa said it was aware of the "problems at Swimming South Africa".
"The country was delighted to see her return to the pool, but South Africa does not own her," a statement read.
"Tatjana's choice belongs to her and it should not be turned into a political weapon."
Gayton McKenzie, Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture, said: "Every medal, every record and every anthem she gave us belongs to our history forever. We now have to share her with the Netherlands."

The US has warned Madagascar against strengthening its ties with Russia, saying similar partnerships with military-led governments in West Africa have failed to improve security.
US Africa Command deputy head Lt Gen John Brennan said Madagascar's strategic location in the Indian Ocean made it important to global trade.
He warned against what he called the "Sahel model", which he said risked fuelling instability across the continent.
Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, all under military rule, have reduced ties with Western partners and turned to Russia to support their fight against jihadist groups.
Russia has expanded its co-operation with Madagascar since the army seized power in 2025, supplying weapons and military instructors.
"We are concerned about Russia wanting to proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent," Brennan told reporters in an online briefing.
"Madagascar sits in a location that is extremely important, as is Mozambique, and we don't want to see those models be applied in those two locations," he said.
The three Sahel countries had blamed their former Western partners for failing to contain jihadist violence before turning to Moscow.
However, Islamist militant attacks have continued despite their closer military ties with Russia.
Brennan also raised concerns about security in the Mozambique Channel, which separates Mozambique and Madagascar from mainland Africa and is an important route for international shipping and trade.
He said it was vital to prevent militants linked to the Islamist State group in northern Mozambique and other hostile actors from threatening maritime activity.
Citing recent piracy-related incidents along the coast, Brennan said they were adapting their tactics, including developing greater maritime capabilities.
He said US partners were "free to partner with whom they wish" but urged them to understand the potential risks.
Madagascar has not publicly responded to Brennan's comments.
However, President MichaÃ«l Randrianirina has recently reiterated his support for stronger ties between Russia and African countries.
During the Russia-Africa summit last month, Madagascar and Russia signed several co-operation agreements covering defence, tourism and trade.
In February, a few months after seizing power, Randrianirina visited to Moscow. It was the first official visit to Russia by a Malagasy leader in nearly 50 years.

Almost Â£6m has been given to a five-year project set up to restore Scotland's rare rainforest.
The award from the National Lottery Heritage Fund will support the creation of three hubs to be located in Torridon, Morvern and mid-Argyll.
Through the Our Rainforest Futures project local people will be given training and work opportunities around habitat restoration, deer management and the removal of invasive species.
About 75,000 acres (30,351ha) of rain-soaked woodlands on the west coast are designated Atlantic rainforest because of the rare oceanic plant life.
The forest has been found to be home to hundreds of species including glow worms, slime moulds and rare lichens.
Overgrazing by deer and livestock, invasive plant species and disease are among the threats to the surviving areas of woodland.
The Torridon hub would involve communities in Kinlochewe, Shieldaig, Lochcarron, Applecross and Gairloch.
In Morvern, the project would include Lochaline, Strontian and Tobermory in Mull.
Mid-Argyll's hub would involve communities Crinan, Tayvallich, Lochgilphead, Ardrishaig and Tarbert.
Our Rainforest Futures is an Alliance for Scotland's Rainforest project led by the Woodland Trust Scotland.
Argyll Countryside Trust, Community Woodlands Association, Plantlife, RSPB Scotland and SRUC are involved.
Caroline Clark, Scotland director of The National Lottery Heritage Fund, said Scotland's rainforest was internationally significant but largely unknown.
She said: "A 2025 survey found fewer than one in three people even know it exists.
"This major investment, using funds raised by National Lottery players, recognises that the future of our rainforest and the future of many west coast communities are closely linked. With the right support, both can thrive."
Julie Stoneman, Saving Scotland's Rainforest Programme manager at the charity Plantlife, said it was hoped the project could create more than 20 jobs and 15 trainee posts.

e7a1df183c14.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-allows-trump-defamation-case-against-bbc-to-proceed-but-tosses-1-claim Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge allows Trump defamation case against BBC to proceed but tosses 1 claim Politics Nov 11, 2026 4:32 PM EST President Donald Trump's $10 billion defamation case against the BBC remains on track, for the moment. A federal judge in Florida ruled on Tuesday that Trump's defamation claim could go forward, though he did not rule on the merits. The publicly funded British broadcaster had sought to dismiss the case. READ MORE: Judge orders Trump to sit for a deposition in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11 Judge Jeffrey Kuntz did dismiss part of the case, tossing out a Trump claim that the BBC's actions violated a Florida law concerning unfair business practices. Trump filed his lawsuit against the BBC in December. The Republican president accused the BBC of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, "Trump: A Second Chance?" READ MORE: Trump sues BBC for $10 billion, accusing it of defamation deceptive practices over editing of his Jan. 6 speech The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021, before the storming of the U.S. Capitol, to make it seem that Trump was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologized over the editing, and that was something the judge made note of in his ruling Wednesday. The head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. The BBC has denied Trump's claims that it defamed him. READ MORE: BBC director resigns after criticism of broadcaster's editing of Trump's Jan. 6 speech In October, a different judge in Florida ordered Trump to sit for a deposition in the case by Dec. 11. Lawyers for the BBC had complained that Trump was delaying his appearance in his own lawsuit. Charles Tobin, an attorney for the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, "we still haven't been able to depose the plaintiff." The deposition deadline could yet be extended. WATCH: BBC under scrutiny over edit of Trump's speech on Jan. 6 Trump called Kuntz's latest ruling a major victory. "A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth, just handed down by highly respected District Court Judge, Jeffrey T. Kuntz, of the Southern District of Florida," Trump posted on his Truth Social platform. "We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!" 60b2d1a8bfd3.text: Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) secured the 218 signatures needed to force another House showdown over the Jeffrey Epstein files Wednesday, just one day after fellow Republicans blocked his attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Why it matters: Congress overwhelmingly voted last year to force the release of the Epstein files, but survivors and lawmakers say the Trump administration has still withheld records. The new bill would give them the power to sue the DOJ and help state prosecutors pursue investigations. Driving the news: Massie announced Wednesday afternoon that his discharge petition for the Epstein Files Transparency Act II had reached the required 218 signatures. Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.) provided the final signature Wednesday, according to the House clerk's records . Just four Republicans signed the petition: Massie, Nancy Mace of South Carolina, Ralph Norman of South Carolina and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania. The other 214 signatures came from Democrats. What he's saying: "I'm working closely with @RepJayapal, @RepTeresaLF and @RepRoKhanna to get this to the floor for a vote soon," Massie wrote on X . The White House and Speaker Mike Johnson's offices have not yet provided comment. The intrigue: President Trump helped drive Massie out of Congress by backing a primary challenger, but the Kentucky Republican is using his final weeks in office to challenge the administration on some of its most politically sensitive topics. This latest effort could force Republicans to revisit a scandal that dogged the Trump administration for more than a year, even after Congress overwhelmingly voted to require the release of Epstein's files. This time, Massie wants to give Epstein survivors, state prosecutors and lawmakers the power to sue the Justice Department over records they believe it has unlawfully withheld. Catch up quick: Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) led the original push to force the release of the Epstein files. Their first bill passed the House 427-1 in November 2025 after they secured enough signatures to bypass Speaker Mike Johnson. Trump ultimately signed it into law. The law required DOJ to release its Epstein-related investigative records by Dec. 19, 2025, with limited exceptions to protect victims, ongoing investigations and other sensitive information. The department missed that deadline but announced in January that it had released nearly 3.5 million pages. The controversy: Epstein survivors and lawmakers have accused DOJ of withholding too much information while simultaneously exposing victims through inadequate redactions. A report released Tuesday by the Republican-led House Oversight Committee faulted the Trump administration's handling of the disclosures, including failures to protect victims and excessive redactions concealing alleged co-conspirators. The committee also said its investigation found no evidence implicating Trump in Epstein's crimes. What's next: Massie's petition is expected to become eligible for a floor vote by early December, with more than enough legislative days remaining under the House's current schedule. But passage is not guaranteed, and Senate Republican leaders could still decline to consider the measure before the new Congress takes office in January.

d6c9f672ffa7.text: By — Will Weissert, Associated Press Will Weissert, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-says-the-towering-arch-he-wants-to-be-build-might-be-dedicated-to-military-veterans Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump says the towering arch he wants to be build might be dedicated to military veterans Politics Nov 11, 2026 4:11 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump observed Veterans Day by suggesting that the towering arch he wants to build in his own honor would also be dedicated to the U.S. military and those who served in its ranks. That's despite three veterans having sued to stop the project — which a federal court has since temporarily blocked. Some military groups have cheered the arch, but many others have opposed it or joined efforts to stop construction. WATCH: News Wrap: Judge blocks construction of Trump's triumphal arch for now Trump has said for months that the 250-foot (76-meter) arch set for construction near Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial would be inspired by the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, and might even be called the "Arc de Trump." He's also insisted that Washington has wanted a similar structure for centuries — even though that's not true. In comments during an annual ceremony at Arlington Cemetery on Wednesday, however, Trump suggested it was actually veterans who had longed for an arch in the capital. "And soon we're going to dedicate a magnificent triumphal arc to our veterans," he said. "And that's in honor of our great veterans and our great militaries." He added: "They've been waiting for it for 200 years." Veterans' legal efforts to stop the arch are ongoing Though the arch received approval from oversight boards stacked with members chosen by Trump, the three veterans are among several entities suing to block the arch's construction. Nine family members of the Kennedy political dynasty are also seeking to stop the project, arguing that the arch would cast a shadow over their relatives' gravesites at Arlington National Cemetery. Last week, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order, prohibiting work for 14 days. WATCH: Retired general calls Trump's proposed arch near Arlington a 'sacrilege' With Democrats soon taking control of Congress after big wins all over the country in last week's midterm elections, Trump's renovation projects will encounter far more scrutiny and roadblocks — from his effort to put his own name on the Kennedy Center to remaking a public golf course and building his massive White House ballroom and the arch. Despite the midterm defeats by his party and the potential legal and legislative hurdles, the White House has continued to promote the arch project. That includes a slick website unveiled last week which proclaimed that it'd be known as the United States Military Triumphal Arch and was "long overdue, and has been sought for many years, especially by the Military." READ MORE: Trump's triumphal arch is blocked for now, but a new website highlights the plans The website prominently displays a picture of and quote from Trump. It also features the word "Triumph" in gold cursive script recalling the typeface used at the president's Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida and similar flourishes that have been affixed to the White House as part of his overhaul of the Oval Office and West Wing. The arch's plans call for its columns to store munitions and areas on the pedestal and observation deck to be set aside for a sniper's nest. Its base would be designed to launch drones, and the site says that the overall monument "will be Highly Secretive but, at the same time, a Top Level and Lethal structure, the likes of which has not been seen in this Country before." The website does not say how much the project will cost or how it will be paid for, although some estimates have reached as high as $100 million. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The locally-focused media startup City Cast has named Andi McDaniel, the companyâs Chief Creative Officer, its new CEO, replacing David Plotz.
City Cast launched in 2021 as a local podcast and newsletter venture aimed at serving cities where local news was shifting from old newspapers and radio to screens. The company has since expanded to 13 cities, including Austin, Las Vegas, and Philadelphia, among others.
âThis next chapter for us is about expanding audiences. Itâs about adapting to AI, and itâs about making the business successful,â McDaniel, a veteran public radio executive and co-founder of City Cast, told Semafor.
City Cast has gained greater visibility in recent months, primarily for its expansion in its hometown. As Semafor first noted last year, in response to what the company saw as an opportunity created by the turbulence at the Washington Post, City Cast scaled up its newsroom and business in Washington. City Cast is backed by Graham Holdings, which owned the Washington Post before selling to Jeff Bezos. City Cast DC now has 20 people on staff, and said it has found some success attracting a younger audience to its content, tripling the size of people it reaches regularly from roughly 100,000 at the beginning of the year to around 300,000.
Not every bet has paid off. The company shuttered two arms, in Boise and Houston. In a telephone interview, Plotz said Houston was too large a sprawling area to cover with the companyâs resources â most cities operate with a staff of just 5 or 6 employees â while he said the company didnât understand Boise enough when City Cast launched there. The company learned that their podcasts were not a replacement for radio, and that the City Cast model seemed to resonate best within midsized cities with a concentrated downtown that orient residentsâ perspective of the city. Plotz said that revenue was up 40% this year, but the company was still not profitable.
In the six years since the companyâs launch, the companyâs founder told Semafor heâd grown to better understand habits in the local media landscape. He noted that many people under the age of 60 largely got their information from social media, neighborhood listservs, local newsletters, and Reddit.
âPeople do not want local news,â Plotz said. âThey want to know about things to do in their city. They want to know whatâs going on in their city. But if you ask them about local news, they do not express an interest.
âLocal news as a concept does not really have a lot of valence. Itâs more like learning about my city.â
He also noted that national media narratives and big political fights were not as animating to local audiences, who seek out information to be connected to their local communities.
âThe need that people are finding met in local media has almost nothing to do with the highly partisan, cortisol-driven conversations that drive national media and national news media,â he said.
