US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports.
CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal.
Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade.
While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials.
"After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.
Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents.
Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area.
In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans.
The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".
Other US officials reportedly on Iran's list of potential targets include former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Advisor John Bolton and Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Milley and Bolton's security teams were taken away by the Trump administration shortly after he returned to office last year.
Bessent is one of a number of administration officials that live on military bases. The White House's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, was moved to a base in late 2025 - before the conflict with Iran began.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both live on military bases, as did former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard.
The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.
In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a blockade targeting Iranian ports.

Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.
It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.
The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.
Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.
Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.
Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.
It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.
Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.
On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.
Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.
Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.
His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.
Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.
Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.
Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.
All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.
On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

1e0caadefc7b.text: By — Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-weighs-lawsuit-brought-by-peltola-campaign-over-absentee-ballots-in-alaskas-us-senate-race Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge weighs lawsuit brought by Peltola campaign over absentee ballots in Alaska's Senate race Politics Nov 11, 2026 11:01 AM EST JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — A state judge said Tuesday that he expects to issue a swift decision in a lawsuit filed by the campaign of Alaska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola, which is seeking a list of absentee voters whose ballots have been rejected in one of the most closely watched races of the midterm elections. LIVE RESULTS: Alaska Senate midterm election Peltola's campaign also said it wants to know the reasons for the rejections and said its intent is to ensure that all qualified voters have their ballots counted. Attorneys for the state say the information requested would violate voter privacy. The campaign sued Friday, three days after the ranked choice election in which Peltola and two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan are the main contenders. Absentee, early in-person and other ballots are still being tallied. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Alaska's is one of two U.S. Senate races, along with Mississippi's, that remain too early to call. In arguments before state Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews, Peltola attorney Abha Khanna said the campaign isn't seeking to disrupt the ongoing ballot counting process and it has seen no cause for concerns. READ MORE: Alaskans are waiting for more votes in Senate and governor's races. Both could go to ranked tabulations "As far as we can tell, the absentee ballot review process is going incredibly smoothly and we plan to keep it that way," she said. But Khanna argued the information the campaign seeks is a matter of public record and is in line with what campaign observers have access to in locations where absentee review boards are meeting. The campaign wants access to that information in a more centralized way, she said. Absentee review boards meet at the state Division of Elections' regional offices, and campaigns and parties can have observers on hand to watch the process. State law includes provisions for challenging absentee ballots if there is "good reason to suspect" that a challenged voter is ineligible to cast a ballot. In a court filing, attorneys for the state said daily reports generated by the division with lists of absentee ballots to be reviewed are not public records because they contain confidential information and are "ephemeral working documents that are not meant for preservation." The final word on whether to accept or reject an absentee ballot comes from the state review board, which goes over the work of the regional absentee review boards. The version of the report that observers, such as those affiliated with the campaigns, receive does not include as much confidential information but does include home addresses that many voters seek to keep private, said Michaela Thompson, who manages absentee ballot review boards for the elections division. The state's "old, inflexible" voter database cannot produce a report that excludes confidential addresses, she said. The observers must sign confidentiality agreements and cannot keep, copy or record information in the report, she said. No absentee ballot is rejected until after the state review board process finishes and the results are certified, she said. Assistant Attorney General Margaret Paton Walsh told the judge that state law sets out timelines for notifying voters if their absentee ballot is rejected. Voters can check the status of their ballot through an online system, but the information isn't posted until at least 10 days after certification, she said. It doesn't make sense that a campaign would have access to that information before a voter does, she said. Alaska does not have a process that allows voters to fix problems on absentee ballots that can cause them to be rejected, such as forgetting to sign the envelope. The state accepts ballots up to 15 days after general elections from overseas voters, making Nov. 18 the final day to receive them. That also is the target for the Division of Elections to conduct ranked vote tabulations if no candidate wins more than 50% of the first-choice votes. The division has announced vote counts for Tuesday and Friday this week, with the potential for additional days, as well as the Nov. 18 count. An attorney for Sullivan's campaign, Stacey Stone, filed a motion in support of the state. But the campaign said that if the judge ordered any production of data or documents, it's asking that such information be made "equally and simultaneously available to all candidates in the affected race." Matthews said he planned to issue a written ruling within a day of Tuesday's hearing. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.
Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be elected to the US Senate in more than 140 years.
Fewer than five thousand votes out of nearly a million counted separated him from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The result means the Democrats will hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.
Colom, 43, won with 49.2% of the vote, while Hyde-Smith received 48.7% and an independent candidate got 2.1%, according to figures from CBS.
Hyde-Smith congratulated Colom in a video posted on X on Wednesday evening and wished him well.
"While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said.
Dozens of people were gathered at the Mississippi HQ of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in Jackson on Wednesday when Colom's victory was announced.
The room burst into deafening applause and cheers.
"This is an amazing result," said Leon Russell, chairman of the NAACP board.
"This is purely the work of particularly the black community," he continued. "There was not a whole lot of money, but there was a whole lot of organising.
"This is a historic election."
Across the room, filled with people embracing, Amber Thomas sat, revelling in the victory.
"When you fight, you win," Thomas said. "Right now, I am overwhelmed with joy."
The result wipes away a Republican winning streak in the Magnolia State that dates back to 1982.
The contest was never expected to be this close, with Hyde-Smith running for re-election in a state that President Donald Trump won in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.
But Democrats have scored a series of major wins in these midterm elections, taking control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
The party flipped Senate seats in Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa.
Polls suggest this was due in large part to voter frustrations with the economy and the Iran war under President Trump.
Colom appeared to a ride a national wave of resentment against Republicans.
Voter backlash against Trump's Republican party has been driven in large part by economic woes, blamed on his administration's tariffs and war with Iran, according to exit polls.
Colom, a local prosecutor, used the national mood to his advantage, highlighting his opponent's support for Trump's tariffs and giving her the nickname "Cindy High Prices".
The Democrat campaigned aggressively, visiting all of Mississippi's 82 counties.
Hyde-Smith's campaign assailed Colom as a puppet of billionaire liberal donor George Soros, whose family has helped fund the Democrat's political campaigns.
The 67-year-old Republican was criticised for a lack of public appearances.

Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.
The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.
Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.
Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.
The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.
Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms in Africa's largest oil producer.
"That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.
The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians.
"Fuel prices went up, and everything that Nigerians consume skyrocketed," Osiyemi told the BBC.
"Most Nigerian families are saying they cannot survive on 10,000 naira [$7.40; Â£5.50] a day," he said, referring to a survey conducted by his organisation.
Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including beans, garri (cassava flour) and bread, also recorded substantial increases.
In a sign that the reforms might be starting to pay off, SBM Intelligence, a security risk consulting firm, found that the cost of preparing a pot of jollof rice fell by 11.5% between June and September 2026, the sharpest decline it had recorded in the 10 years it has been running its Jollof Index.
However, this has not translated into significant relief for most households.
"Nigerians spend more and more of their income on basics," said Ikenna Okonkwo, head of research at SBM Intelligence.
The reforms were praised by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for their effectiveness.
Nigeria's headline inflation stood at 14% in September 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, down from a high of 34% in 2024. The gap between the official and parallel exchange rates has also narrowed.
Tinubu has said the removal of fuel subsidies freed up more than one trillion ($740m; Â£550m) naira in government resources in just the first two months.
However, he has recently said he will work to reduce fuel cost.
His administration subsequently announced a 125bn naira intervention package for small businesses, including grants for smaller enterprises and loans for manufacturers.
Atiku has criticised Tinubu's decision to remove the fuel subsidy.
"My position stands! I will restore subsidy to make life easier and affordable for Nigerians," Atiku wrote on X.
However, restoring the fuel subsidy could prove challenging given Nigeria's economic realities.
"The current budget for Nigeria in 2026 is about 68.32tn naira, with 15.8tn going towards debt servicing. So, we are not fiscally strong enough to say that we want to return to the subsidy," Osiyemi said.
While Tinubu's reforms are lauded for restoring some stability at the macroeconomic level, they have also created instability in households.
Two months away from elections, the cost of living and economic hardship are the major issues for many voters.
"These kinds of things can get punished in polls," said Okonkwo of SBM Intelligence.
To address this, Tinubu promised to lower the cost of living, grow the economy by 6% and halve youth unemployment if he wins re-election. Achieving these targets will require increased oil and agricultural production.
But much of Nigeria's agricultural production is concentrated in the north, where insecurity has made farming increasingly difficult.
Osiyemi says many farmers are reluctant to return to their fields.
"They're not sure whether when they go to their farms, they have the chances of also coming back home, to meet with their family."
To address insecurity, Tinubu proposes recruiting an additional 28,000 military personnel and 50,000 police officers.
"The security situation, especially in the north, is more complex than a matter of just recruiting more soldiers," Okonkwo said.
The threats include jihadists, kidnap gangs and conflict between herders and farmers in central Nigeria.
Insecurity is also a major priority for Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, who came third in the 2023 presidential election and attracted significant support from young Nigerians.
He unveiled his 2027 Governance Agenda on 10 November, under the campaign slogan "A New Nigeria is Possible", placing national unity at the top of his priorities, followed by security.
"Nobody will kidnap school children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you," he said.
Further, delivering on those ambitions will also depend on improving electricity supply, particularly for businesses and industries. Tinubu promises to increase available electricity generation towards 10,000MW.
"There is nothing in the manifesto about where that investment is going to come from because it will cost a lot of money," said Okonkwo.

Levels of the two most toxic "forever" chemicals in England's rivers have dropped by nearly a third over the last decade, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA).
The decline in the chemicals, PFOS and PFOA, has been put down to stricter restrictions on their use in products after increasing evidence emerged of their damaging impact on human health and the environment.
One expert studying the impact of the chemicals said it was "brilliant" to see how far the UK has come on this issue.
Thousands of other forever chemicals, known officially as PFAS, remain in use but the regulator said its report showed the need for them all to be better monitored and regulated.
PFAS were first developed in the 1930s in the US and became popular with companies making products like frying pans and firefighting foam because of their useful, oil-resistant, water-resistant and electrical properties.
They are called forever chemicals because their natural resistance means they take a very long time to break down naturally.
The earliest types of these chemicals were called PFOS and PFOA. But two decades ago researchers started to find that they were linked to tissue damage in animals and increased rates of certain serious health conditions such as testicular cancer., external
As a result, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010 and PFOA in 2020.
The latest data from the regulator, published on Thursday, shows that the concentrations in English rivers of PFOS and PFOA over the last ten years have now fallen by 30% and 29% respectively.
Levels in fresh-water fish have fallen 49%.
"It's brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years," said Dr David Megson, reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University.
There are thought to be around 15,000 other PFAS, although only around 200 are frequently used.
The EA said that despite increasing research into these compounds, "uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS". It said its findings "reinforces the need" for regulating all PFAS rather than one by one.
The chemicals industry has long opposed such an approach, arguing that there is currently no, or limited, evidence to suggest that other PFAS are toxic and that some have vital uses such as in life-saving medical equipment.
The regulator is now regularly testing for 60 other PFAS to build a picture of contamination across the country, and earlier this month the government announced it would begin monitoring levels in people's bodies.
The EA report acknowledged that while concentration levels have fallen, because the chemicals take so long to break down, the overall amount still in the environment is likely to have remained unchanged - they have simply been diluted and been washed into the sea.
"There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused," said Megson.
One of the few ways to permanently destroy PFAS is by high-temperature incineration - there are just two such suitable sites in the country currently.

d432a054b7d5.text: Iran's top national security official warned that it would strike American bases beyond the Gulf, including in Europe, if the United States resumes air strikes against the Islamic Republic. The warning comes one day after indictments in New York against three men who allegedly conspired to attack U.S. Air Force planes at a base in England. Nick Schifrin reports. Amna Nawaz: Iran's top national security official today warned the U.S. that it would strike American bases beyond the Gulf, including in Europe, if the United States resumes airstrikes. Geoff Bennett: The warning comes a day after three men were indicted in New York for allegedly plotting to attack U.S. Air Force planes at a base in England. One of the suspects with deep ties to Iran allegedly directed the plot from a federal detention center in New York. The threat prompted the U.S. to relocate bombers from the British base back in September. Nick Schifrin has more. Nick Schifrin: The attack was livestreamed and set to propaganda music, a man throwing a Molotov cocktail at a media company critical of the Iranian regime, as, 1,500 miles away, one of the organizers watched and recorded. It was one of multiple terrorist attacks across Europe in March and April, including the stabbing of two Jewish Londoners and another arson attack on a Jewish-owned charity that the U.S. now says was orchestrated remotely by this man, Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, seen here in 2024 with machine guns behind him. The U.S. accuses Al-Saadi of working on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iranian proxy group Kataib Hezbollah based in Iraq. Earlier this year, the U.S. alleges he planned or promoted 18 terrorist attacks in Europe, as well as a plot against a New York synagogue. He was then arrested in August by Turkey and extradited to the United States. But that didn't stop his plots. The U.S. alleges that, while behind bars in Brooklyn, he directed and paid fellow militants in the United Kingdom to drive these white vans to a British air base. The vans pretended to be from a gas delivery and swimming pool supply business, but were actually surveilling the Royal Air Force base at Fairford. The U.S. alleges the plotters had bought shrapnel and chemicals that could be used for a bomb. The plot forced the U.S. to evacuate B-1s that had been used to bomb Iran. And the U.S. alleges Al-Saadi initiated the attack while he was in the Brooklyn prison while speaking to his immediate family using code words. Colin Clarke, The Soufan Center: This is something that really hearkens back more to things like gangs or the mafia, right? So, allowing mafia members or gang leaders to have conversations that are then monitored, surveilled, and acted upon. Nick Schifrin: Colin Clarke is the executive director of The Soufan Center, which focuses on terrorism. He says the plot against Fairford highlights Iran's willingness to use terrorism and other asymmetric attacks to fight what it considers a decades-old war against the U.S. and Israel. Colin Clarke: It just shows that the Iranians are going to continue to be relentless in their pursuit of what they see as revenge, even if we were to reach a deal tomorrow, which, by the way, is highly unlikely. Nick Schifrin: And in response to the 2020 U.S. strike that killed powerful Iranian commander Qasem Soleimani, the U.S. has long accused Iran of trying to assassinate senior American officials. Colin Clarke: The United States killed Qasem Soleimani in January 2020 and helped the Israelis find and kill the supreme leader of Iran. And so all bets are off when it comes to Iranian vengeance. This is something we're going to see for the foreseeable future. Nick Schifrin: And this week's indictment shows, to seek that vengeance, Iran will increasingly turn to proxies, including the Iraq-based Kataib Hezbollah. Omar Al-Nidawi, Atlantic Council: Most of the Kataib Hezbollah operations in the past have been crude military operations, lobbing rockets, short-range rockets against American bases. Nick Schifrin: Omar Al-Nidawi is with the Atlantic Council's Iraq Initiative. Omar Al-Nidawi: This is the first foray of -- by Kataib Hezbollah into attacks, terror-style attacks, sophisticated-style -- sophisticated attacks on European soil. Nick Schifrin: And why is that significant? Omar Al-Nidawi: It definitely pulls Iraq closer into the conflict. It also highlights Iran's increasing reliance on these factions. Nick Schifrin: A plot thwarted this time that American officials fear Iran could try to repeat. For the "PBS News Hour."

c7b7da7d21f0.text: Shares in Nvidia sank Wednesday night after the New York Times reported CEO Jensen Huang had a second affair with a senior executive who reports to him. Why it matters: The report adds to mounting scrutiny of Huang, already under investigation over an affair with a purported Chinese spy. The potential impact goes beyond one man and one business, though. Huang is arguably the world's most powerful CEO at the moment, his company serving as the beating heart of the AI revolution. He also has no obvious successor . Driving the news: Huang, 63, had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, 48, Nvidia's vice president of health care, according to the Times. Both are married to other people. The two were reportedly seen being affectionate at a hotel during Nvidia's annual developer conference in San Jose in March. A bystander recorded the interaction, and Huang's security team made an offer to the person to sign a nondisclosure agreement, per the Times. The paper reported that Nvidia declined to issue a statement, and Powell did not respond to a request for comment. By the numbers: Nvidia shares fell nearly 8% in after-hours trading as of 6 p.m. ET Wednesday. The company's lost about $1 trillion in market cap since the Times first reported on Oct. 29 that Huang had a "close relationship" with a suspected spy. On the prediction market Kalshi, the odds of Huang being out as CEO as soon as this weekend skyrocketed. Zoom out: This new report comes after Huang confirmed in a company email that he had been unfaithful in his marriage. Nvidia has an independent panel investigating, and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to handle the probe. Between the lines: Peter Jaworski, a business ethics professor at Georgetown University, said it will be hard for Huang to keep his job after this. "You can't have a relationship like this with a direct report," Jaworski tells Axios. "Does the CEO get fired? In this situation that's probably the move to make." Jaworski said the situation could also raise questions about what the board knew and when it knew it. At a minimum, he says Nvidia's board needs to place Huang on administrative leave immediately while it conducts an investigation into both relationships. What we're watching: How Nvidia handles the growing scandal could have effects far beyond just its walls. Editor's note: This story has been updated with new details.

a3c60a1e62db.text: In our news wrap Wednesday, Democrat Scott Colom has defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, a group that included Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was admonished by an Army sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and peace talks between Ukraine, Russia and the U.S. ended with an agreement to exchange prisoners, but no breakthrough on ending the war. Happy Veterans Day. Meantime, in Copenhagen ... Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President: Europe must be at the table. Hundreds of schools were evacuated, and police conducted searches classroom by classroom. Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says the e-mails were aimed at generating alarm and concern, and that an investigation is under way. Scotland and Ireland reported similar incidents, though no evacuations were ordered. It follows a series of hoaxes across Europe targeting airlines and broadcasters. Police clashed with the protesters and made three arrests, though the crowd soon dispersed. The former president was attending a ceremony at Trinity College honoring his son Hunter. Footage from the scene shows a large emergency response in the Flatbush neighborhood. Fire officials say the collapse occurred this afternoon in an area where construction had been taking place. United States is being intentionally sunk off the Florida Panhandle coast. It's part of a multimillion-dollar project to lure divers and fishing enthusiasts to the area and to create a habitat for Marine life. In 1952, the ship set a speed record on its maiden voyage. It went on to cross the Atlantic more than 800 times, carrying presidents, Hollywood stars, and even royalty. But a rise in air travel hurt demand and it ended up mothballed at a Philadelphia pier. 37e339ac5774.text: Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a stunning Mississippi upset , becoming the first Democrat elected to the state's Senate delegation since 1982, AP projects. Why it matters: Colom's victory marks another extraordinary breakthrough for Democrats in the Deep South, extending the historic blue wave that handed the party control of both chambers of Congress. Colom also becomes Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction. Hiram Rhodes Revels became the nation's first Black senator in 1870. Mississippi's last Black senator, Blanche K. Bruce, served until 1881. Catch up quick: Colom's victory expands Democrats' 55–44 advantage over Republicans in the Senate. Worries of a recount — which requires a court order, as Mississippi has no recount law — seemed moot as Hyde-Smith posted a video message to X shortly after AP called the race, appearing to concede to Colom. "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Cologne and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state," she said. Hyde-Smith also addressed another worry from Mississippi voters following a significant purge of the state's voter rolls, saying that her campaign "has worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election." "I am proud of what we have accomplished together, but I want to make one thing very clear: an election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will," she said. The big picture: Colom's victory followed a late surge of Democratic spending and organizing in a state Trump carried by 23 points in 2024. Hyde-Smith faced warning signs in the campaign's closing months, when Colom raised twice as much as the GOP senator despite her overall cash advantage. She was also outspent on TV advertising , with a flood of ads from left-leaning PACs and super PACs pushing support for Colom and attacking the senator for her vote not to release files related to the convicted human trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. Hyde-Smith's campaign also faced criticism over an interview she gave to WLOX-TV in Biloxi, Mississippi, where she fumbled an answer about the price of beef, saying that Mississippians had "so many other proteins to choose from." Colom's campaign capitalized on her blunder, creating a viral campaign ad urging voters to "choose another senator." The GOP made a late push to help Hyde-Smith, including President Trump speaking at a rally for her in Alcorn County, where he won by 68% in 2024. But it wasn't enough. Hyde-Smith's term will end after eight years. She was appointed to the Senate in 2018 by then-Mississippi Gov. Phil Bryant, and ran for a full term in 2020, where she bested her Democratic challenger Mike Espy by 10 points. Zoom in: Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney from Columbus, campaigned on lowering the cost of living, raising wages and protecting rural hospitals. His campaign also drew in heavy Democratic hitters to stump for him, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock. The bottom line: Colom's win adds Mississippi to a growing list of Republican strongholds where Democrats broke through in the midterms, including Texas and South Carolina. It also reinforces the role of Black voters in the Democratic comeback, after the party rebuilt support among a crucial voting bloc that showed signs of shifting toward Trump in 2024. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated. This story has been corrected to show that Hyde-Smith's interview was conducted in Biloxi (not Jackson, Mississippi).

4565df3c4c84.text: With Democrats set to take control of Congress, the White House is threatening them over investigations into the Trump administration. The top White House lawyer warned that aggressive oversight of the administration “may cross the line into blatant criminality.” It comes amid a wave of resignations within the Justice Department. Amna Nawaz discussed more with Devlin Barrett of The New York Times. Amna Nawaz: As Democrats gear up to take control of Congress, the White House is threatening them over planned investigations into the Trump administration. In a letter this week, the top White House lawyer warned the likely incoming House Oversight chair, Robert Garcia, that aggressive oversight of the administration -- quote -- "may cross the line into blatant criminality." It comes amid a wave of high-profile resignations within the Justice Department following last week's Democratic wins and reporting that there are more to come. Here to discuss this is Devlin Barrett. He's a New York Times reporter who covers federal law enforcement. Welcome back. Good to see you. Devlin Barrett: Thanks for having me. Amna Nawaz: Let's start with this letter. Is there any basis for the White House to be threatening members of Congress for their oversight? Devlin Barrett: Look, as a legal document, it doesn't mean very much. As a political document, it's quite important, because it's sending the message about how much the White House plans to fight these investigations. We have already seen the administration fight even judicial inquiries about what the administration has done. So I take this letter to basically mean, we intend to fight every subpoena you send us. Amna Nawaz: Related to that, we saw the attorney general, Todd Blanche, over the weekend say that Democrats' talk about investigating some of the administration was akin to outright threats and that some of those could be considered a crime. Do you see the attorney general launching probes into Democratic lawmakers who are engaged in oversight? Devlin Barrett: Well, we have already seen them launch probes into Democratic lawmakers for very shaky premises. For example, there was an attempt to get an indictment on lawmakers who made a video talking to military officers about not following illegal orders. I don't think there's any reason to expect they will stop launching investigations of Democratic lawmakers. But I think, when it comes to this particular fight over investigations, they're going to be very hard-pressed to craft a sort of criminal theory of why a congressional investigation is in any way a crime. They haven't articulated that certainly. The letter really doesn't, nor does Blanche in his comments. Amna Nawaz: Devlin, let's talk about some of those resignations, several high-profile folks leaving their jobs in the last week, and some were very strong enforcers of the president's agenda, among them Harmeet Dhillon, who was the president's former personal lawyer and led the Civil Rights Division to DOJ, Jason Quinones, who oversaw investigations into the president's opponents. Brett Shumate was central in attacking DEI programs, and John Eisenberg oversaw national security at the Department of Justice. What do we know about why they're leaving and why now? Devlin Barrett: First of all, it's not completely out of the ordinary for senior DOJ officials to leave after an election, to leave after two years. But, obviously, this is a very different type of Department of Justice in the Trump administration. And I think what you're seeing here in a lot of these cases is senior officials who, for very different reasons, each sort of unique to their own jobs, did not live up to some of the expectations that the White House set for them or even that Todd Blanche set for them, particularly when you look at the U.S. attorney in Miami, who's in charge of this grand conspiracy investigation of former officials. There's been a lot of disappointment by the White House that that hasn't produced more in the way of criminal charges or accusations. Amna Nawaz: You think that they were forced out of these rules or asked to leave? Devlin Barrett: Our reporting shows that there is a significant amount of displeasure from senior officials with the U.S. attorney in Miami who just left. And there were significant disagreements in some of these other issues like national security, like civil rights. Amna Nawaz: Permanent replacements for those roles would require Senate confirmation. With the incoming Democratic majority, how do you see that playing out? Devlin Barrett: Well, that's why these departures are categorically different than many other administrations, because it's going to be extremely hard to confirm someone in these top jobs that the president would like to have in these top jobs. So it may be that, for the people who stay in the Trump Justice Department, they may be in a sense locked in for a long -- for the rest of the ride. Amna Nawaz: There's also this reporting that the DOJ warned its field office leaders in a meeting earlier this week to prepare to be on -- quote -- "wartime footing" when Democrats take over or to leave if they couldn't do that. When you hear that, combined with these resignations, what do you think we should expect to see from the Department of Justice? Devlin Barrett: So one thing is, this happened in the type of call where the person -- the senior official doing these calls does a lot of this sort of rhetoric. Like, to many of the career staff, it comes across as wild rhetoric. But this kind of rhetoric is not that unusual for this senior official. But what's really interesting here is, the elections had consequences for the Justice Department. And one of those consequences is states like Texas are now going to be run by Democratic officials. Until now, states like Texas have been very cooperative with the Trump administration on issues related to ICE and immigration. You have already seen local officials in Texas say they ar

e17267fb1039.text: As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, Delaware Sen. Chris Coons is poised to become chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, succeeding retiring Democrat Jeanne Shaheen. A staunch supporter of Ukraine and a critic of President Trump’s war with Iran, Coons would take the helm at a consequential moment for American foreign policy. Coons joined Geoff Bennett to discuss more. Geoff Bennett: As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, Delaware Senator Chris Coons is poised to become chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. A staunch supporter of Ukraine and a critic of President Trump's war with Iran, Coons comes to the role at a consequential moment for American foreign policy. And Senator Coons joins us now. Welcome back to the program. Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE): Thank you, Geoff. Great to be on with you again. Geoff Bennett: So, as we said, you are set to chair Senate Foreign Relations with the U.S. at war with Iran, with Russia's war in Ukraine continuing. There is growing national concern over artificial intelligence. As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, what are your top foreign policy priorities? And where do you most want to change the administration's course? Sen. Chris Coons: So, Geoff, as I was campaigning up and down the state of Delaware in the last few months, I heard over and over that folks' top concern was their costs. And when I asked, why do you think your costs have gone too high, they would say Trump's tariff war with Canada and Trump's illegal or immoral war against Iran. I heard that over and over from voters. So finding a way that we can deliver on that to lower their costs by repealing Trump's tariffs, by ending the war in Iran, by improving wages and the way that wages are growing and rebuilding our alliances globally will be among the top priorities for me. As has recently been covered, there is an intersection between corruption in the Trump White House and this latest scandal involving AI. The Trump White House was in bed with Nvidia, the largest, most important chip manufacturing company that makes advanced AI chips, and the CEO of Nvidia was in bed with a Chinese spy. Despite hearing that months ago, leaders in the Trump administration failed to warn that this was an urgent national security issue. So, to me, we need to both have some oversight and investigations about recent developments in Nvidia and China and AI, actions by Elon Musk to control whether or not Ukraine can defend itself using his Starlink system, and we have to knock down the tariffs that have raised people's costs. Geoff Bennett: On Nvidia, The Wall Street Journal is reporting exclusively tonight that Nvidia's board is preparing to oust the CEO, Jensen Huang, over what are now two reported affairs, one with an employee and the one that you mentioned with the suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia, as you know, the it's central to the AI economy. Huang is practically synonymous with that company. Given how much is riding on Nvidia's success, how concerned are you about the fallout and the disruption to the broader economy? Sen. Chris Coons: I'm concerned. Frankly, the reason we have continued to have a strong stock market and, to the extent there's been a strong economy, it's all rested on huge investments in AI data centers and in the future of the AI economy. The underlying American economy has been quite weak. In fact, some have argued it's in a recession, except for the investments in AI.So the central role that Nvidia and Nvidia designed and manufactured chips play is a core concern for me, in particular the urgency of putting limits on exporting Nvidia's chips to China. I have a bipartisan bill with Senator Ricketts that would put guardrails on those exports. It is called the SAFE Chips Act. And part of what is so concerning to me about these recent allegations about Nvidia -- look, I'm not that interested in the salacious details of the private life of the CEO of Nvidia. I'm very interested in why credible reports of a national security threat were not acted on, and Jensen Huang was allowed to continue advocating for the export to China of some of his most advanced chips, in particular to the company represented by the Chinese spy. Geoff Bennett: I want to ask you about this effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which failed yesterday in the House. Should Democrats revive that effort when you take control of both chambers next year? Sen. Chris Coons: Look, Geoff, my hope is that President Trump will read the tea leaves, recognize that Secretary Hegseth, more than anyone, is responsible for giving him bad advice about the war in Iran and the current situation we find ourselves in, with no easy or positive way to get out of the war with Iran, and fire him and replace him. I do think that there will be another effort in the House to impeach and remove Secretary Hegseth. But, frankly, what would be best for our country is to just move on to new leadership. Secretary Hegseth has fired dozens of senior flag-rank officers across the Pentagon with no justification or explanation in a way that has demoralized and weakened the senior ranks of the American military at exactly the moment when we can least afford that. I think it's time for those firings to move to the secretary level and for Trump to find a next secretary of defense who can be confirmed by the Senate. Geoff Bennett: Speaking of new leadership, I want to ask you about your party's own leadership. The midterms delivered this overwhelming vote for change, and you have senators as far apart ideologically as Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin Democrats, obviously, both calling for Chuck Schumer to step aside a Senate Democratic leader. Our audience is seeing a press conference they held yesterday over in the Senate. Do you believe that Senator Schumer is the right person to lead your caucus in the next Congress? Sen. Chris Coons: So, we're in the middle of vigorous caucus discussions a

96a38d2caf96.text: Companies have always tried to maximize profits, but now there are a host of sophisticated tools to determine the prices of the goods and services they sell. At a time when so many Americans are frustrated with rising costs, those tools are under greater scrutiny. Economics correspondent Paul Solman explains how that technology is transforming the prices we pay. Amna Nawaz: Companies have always tried to maximize profits, but now there are a host of sophisticated tools to adjust the price of goods and services. But at a time when so many Americans are frustrated with rising costs, those tools are under greater scrutiny. Our economics correspondent, Paul Solman, explains how that technology is transforming the prices we pay. Paul Solman: A simple experiment; 400 shoppers across the U.S. logged in to Instacart and bought the same 20 items from the same stores, then took screenshots of their carts. The result? Lindsay Owens: Seventy-five percent of items in the cart were offered at different price points to different shoppers in the exact same pickup location at the exact same time. Paul Solman: Lindsay Owens, who heads Groundwork Collaborative, in conjunction with researchers at Consumer Reports and More Perfect Union, had discovered an experiment Instacart was running on shoppers. Lindsay Owens: To test how much they could charge them for every item in their carts without their knowledge. The price point differences were as much as 23 percent. Paul Solman: Soon after it became public, Instacart halted the experiment and explained -- quote -- "Those tests raised concerns, leaving some people questioning the prices they see on Instacart. That's not OK." But Owens says plenty of firms are OK with variable pricing, and not just to experiment. Lindsay Owens: Age-old impulses to nickel-and-dime you or squeeze you or turn a profit have been supercharged by new technologies. Paul Solman: Instead of one price for a good or service, companies can now use algorithms to jiggle their prices based on your personal data. Lindsay Owens: They might be able to collect your location from where you log on, your I.P. address, if you're shopping online. They may have detailed information about your purchase history because you shop there regularly, you use a loyalty card, or you log in to an app before you make a purchase. They may be able to ascertain or try to guess demographic information about you. Paul Solman: Owens' new book, "Gouged," expands on her work at Groundwork Collaborative, a consumer advocacy group. Elizabeth Pancotti, Groundwork Collaborative: We did a dive into 315 patents. Paul Solman: Walmart patent applications for customer tracking tech, for instance. Elizabeth Pancotti: We found evidence of Walmart creating the technology that can connect to your Apple Watch or other kind of wearable device and look at things like your heart rate, what your blood sugar is, and they talk about using that in the ice cream aisle. And so when you open the freezer door, you grab your favorite pint of Ben and Jerry's. They know which one makes your blood sugar spike or drop or your heart rate responds. Paul Solman: Walmart plans to install digital price tags in all U.S. stores by the end of the year, which could allow them to change prices in a heartbeat. But in an open letter, Walmart executive Dan Bartlett said -- quote -- "Walmart does not and will not use an individual customer's personal information, income, shopping history, urgency, or willingness to pay to set an individualized price." And so a reasonable question, will they or won't they? Owens says so-called personalized pricing technology is everywhere these days. Lindsay Owens: Data gathering, cloud computing, machine learning, such that, when they gather all that information, they can try to figure out what it means about you. Paul Solman: To prove the point: Elizabeth Pancotti: So everyone's going to add a Big Mac meal with a medium Coke. Paul Solman: Owens, her staff, and I ordered the same meal on Uber Eats from the same location to the same delivery address at the same time. I have got my total? Yours. Woman: Yes, mine is $19.25. Paul Solman: Nineteen twenty-five. Woman: Eighteen seventy-eight. Elizabeth Pancotti: Twenty sixty-nine. Lindsay Owens: Whew. Woman: Twenty-two thirty-five. Woman: Eighteen thirty-five. Paul Solman: And I have got $22.55. What could possibly explain? Lindsay Owens: For most of us, it looks like they're varying the fees. And this is Uber's cut, right? Paul Solman: All of us were charged $13.59 for the meal. It was Uber Eats' delivery fees that varied. Lindsay Owens: I have $2.49 for the delivery fee. Paul Solman: I'm $3.49 here. Elizabeth Pancotti: I'm $4.49 for -- this is the exact same location. Paul Solman: So the algorithm is all over the place because it's so many variables that it can make this kind of discrimination? Lindsay Owens: Yes, look, it could be random. Like we could all be subject to what is effectively a pricing experiment. It's a little hard for us to know. We can't get entirely under the hood of their process. Paul Solman: Uber did not respond to our request for comment. But how to explain these? Lindsay Owens: Expedia was shown to be charging individuals who logged on from the San Francisco Bay Area more for the exact same Manhattan hotel room than individuals who logged on from what they viewed to be less affluent areas of the country. Another example, Target changing the price in the app as you approach the store. They think you're getting closer to the store, you're probably going to spring for the purchase. You're in the parking lot, you're definitely going to spring for the purchase. Paul Solman: Now, look, I had a question out of economics 101. Why shouldn't a company charge me as much as I'm willing to pay? Lindsay Owens: I don't want to be charged the maximum amount I can pay for every single ingredient when I make a lunch sandwich, right, like, the maximum I could fork over for the mustar

268503dc7391.text: Over the last 250 years, the United States military has helped shape the nation's history – from the fight for independence to its emergence as the world's leading military power. But as the military's reach has grown, fewer Americans are serving in uniform. Judy Woodruff explores what that means for the country in her series, Crossroads: America at 250. Geoff Bennett: Over the last 250 years, the U.S. military has helped shape the nation's history from the fight for independence to its emergence as the world's leading military power. But, as our military reach has grown, fewer Americans are serving in uniform. This Veterans Day, Judy Woodruff explores what that means for the country in her series Crossroads: America at 250. Judy Woodruff: So this is your first deployment. Former Cpl. Jeremy Villanueva, U.S. Marine Corps: My wife had made these nice illustrations, and she listed right here all the things that I had missed. Daniel being born was a big one. Judy Woodruff: Jeremy Villanueva had been a U.S. Marine for just a year when the 9/11 attacks happened. Former Cpl. Jeremy Villanueva: The idea of being in the United States Marine Corps as an infantryman suddenly became very, very real. Judy Woodruff: He was newly married with a baby on the way. Former Cpl. Jeremy Villanueva: They put us on a boat and we sailed out December 1, and my son was born December 17. And I didn't get to see him until he was 6 months old. Ensign Daniel Villanueva, U.S. Navy: I always wanted to join the Amphib Navy, so Marines would be on board, and I could feel a little bit closer to my dad and what he went through when he was on board a Navy ship. Judy Woodruff: Today, that son is a Navy officer and has served aboard the same kind of ship that once carried his father overseas to fight the war on terror. From the Revolutionary War, when Americans took up arms to fight for freedom to today's war with Iran, military service has helped shape what it means to be an American. But today's military looks dramatically different. From small localized forces that relied heavily on volunteers, it has grown into six branches with more than two million uniformed personnel. Col. Greg Daddis (Ret.): We're moving from a regional power to a global power. Judy Woodruff: At the National Guard Memorial Museum in Washington, we talked about that history with retired Army Colonel Greg Daddis of Texas A&M University and Katherine Kuzminski of the Center For a New American Security. Katherine Kuzminski: While there was a U.S. military, the concept was much more localized at the state level. We shifted from a mixed force of conscripts and volunteers to the all-volunteer force. Judy Woodruff: But as the country expanded, so did its military reach. Col. Greg Daddis (Ret.): I think, from a historical standpoint of thinking of Native Americans as being national threats, but, in fact, we were invading other nations, and that impulse continues after the late 1890s as we move into Spanish colonies and Cuba and the Philippines, and then just continue that outward expansion, especially with the two World Wars. Judy Woodruff: Fighting wars on a much larger scale required more troops. The draft brought millions of American men into military service. Katherine Kuzminski: The beginning of World War I, we saw the first real melting pot of the entire U.S. Army specifically thinking about the United States as a fighting force in the world. We, of course, had to induce a draft to make that happen in World War I and then again in World War II. We saw that draft take us through the Vietnam War. Judy Woodruff: But, eventually, it went away. Katherine Kuzminski: It wasn't politically tenable to the American population that we are sending our sons, because the draft was only for men, to fight the nation's wars without the broader public say in the use of those forces. Judy Woodruff: But after the war in Vietnam, there was a big shift. The military became a smaller, all-volunteer professional force. Katherine Kuzminski: We're able to have a smaller force because we rely on a number of factors of national power, to include our economy, our ability to raise and develop ambassadors and diplomats, and we lean on all of those measures of national power, and then we can leverage this professional military. Judy Woodruff: And the backbone of that military is increasingly made up of families like the Villanuevas, who pass down the tradition of service from one generation to the next. According to Pentagon data, more than three in four new Army recruits had a family member who also served. Col. Greg Daddis (Ret.): Serving in the military itself has become a family business. When I'm teaching at West Point and the cadets that I have in class, their mothers have gone to West Point, their fathers have gone to West Point, and there's just now a very strong tradition of those who are serving, that their sons and daughters will follow in their footsteps. Former Cpl. Jeremy Villanueva: My dad worked until the day he died in a factory, so that I could go and I could serve my country, and I didn't have to worry about the same things that they had to worry about. And I went and enlisted in the military so that my son could go ahead and commission into the military. Ensign Daniel Villanueva: Family service was encouraged throughout my childhood, both from my father and my uncles and my cousins. So joining the military wasn't that big of a question when I was a kid. Judy Woodruff: But that tradition may be weakening. A 2025 Blue Star Families survey found just 37 percent of active duty family respondents would recommend service to a young relative, down from 55 percent in 2016. Former Cpl. Jeremy Villanueva: Unless you have lived through it, you can't fully appreciate what that sacrifice actually is. The hardest thing for that parent is that we know exactly what that person is going to have to sacrifice. And to see your own child make that same sacrifice, it's hard. Judy Woodruf

1ed0c2185a36.text: The themes of service to country and reflection on humanity are at the center of the new film "The Mosquito Bowl." Special correspondent Mike Cerre caught up with some of the forces behind the film and the real historical event. It's part of our arts and culture series, CANVAS. Geoff Bennett: Also on this Veterans Day, the themes of service to country and reflection on humanity are at the center of a new film. Amna Nawaz: Special correspondent Mike Cerre caught up with some of the forces behind the film "Mosquito Bowl" and the real historical event on which it's based for our arts and culture series, Canvas. Mike Cerre: Purdue's "Touchdown Tony" Butkovich was the country's leading rusher in 1943, and a first-round NFL draft choice. He is portrayed in the film by Ray Nicholson. Ray Nicholson, Actor: I want to play for the New York Giants. I want to live the hell out of my life. Ultimately, that's what this movie's about. It's about this invincibility of youth, feeling like you're on top of the world, the world's at your fingertips. Mike Cerre: World War II forever changed the world for many college football stars like Tony Butkovich, who put their promising careers on hold to serve their country. Pat McAfee, Actor: I have heard some of you have vacated your football dreams to chase a higher glory and serve in the United States Marine Corps. Is that accurate? Ray Nicholson: Sir, it is this recruit' desire to protect and defend my country, sir! Mike Cerre: The Mosquito Bowl was an actual football game played on Guadalcanal on Christmas Day, 1944, between two Marine regiments loaded with top college and pro football players. The film is based on the bestselling book by Buzz Bissinger, the celebrated author of "Friday Night Lights." Buzz Bissinger: I'd like to think that "Friday Night Lights," when I wrote it, and also "Mosquito Bowl," it was never about football as football. It was about football as a vehicle for something else. Actor: Gentlemen, the hopes and dreams of an entire town are riding on your shoulders. Mike Cerre: Like their previous "Friday Night Lights" collaboration, Bissinger and director Peter Berg use football in this film as a microcosm of American life and the times. Peter Berg, Director: It's a reflection on humanity, on life, on love, on death that has combat in it, that has football in it. Mike Cerre: The film refers to their new Marine teammates as the greatest American offensive line in history for the Marines' island-hopping campaign in the Pacific, starting with their terrifying landing on Tarawa, and eventually reuniting his former college teammates and opponents on Guadalcanal for that Christmas Day football game to boost morale. Brent Comer, Actor: I think there's a time in everybody's life, hopefully, where someone feels called to lend themselves to something that's bigger than themselves. Mike Cerre: Brent Comer plays George Murphy, the tight end and captain of Notre Dame's 1942 team and captain of the 29th Marines Team on Guadalcanal. Cpl. Neal McCallum (RET.), U.S. Marine Corps: In my company, we had five football standouts. Mike Cerre: Former Corporal Neal McCallum was only 18 when he was on Guadalcanal. (AP) — Democratic nominee Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, and it will echo through the country as well. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom's favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi. The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43 year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state's large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith's missteps as she sought a second full term. "They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through," Colom said in the campaign's closing stretch. Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society. "It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better, and we don't come up with excuses as to why we can't do it," he said. A race Washington once viewed as a longshot The contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, drawing attention from Democrats who belatedly infused cash into Colom's candidacy. The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith's vulnerabilities crystallized. Colom attracted particular notice for some of the year's most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith, 67, seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they'd "pick another senator instead." WATCH: Mississippi voters reflect on surprising Senate race as count continues When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities. Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: "Is this not the best president in our lifetime?" Then she stepped away. Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. "I love that," Trump replied when he continued his 80-plus minutes at the microphone. "Sometimes they get up and they talk for 10 minutes." The appearance tracked Colom's tactic of criticizing Trump's policies — especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a non-entity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state that has been accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi. There is some irony to Hyde-Smith finding herself flat-footed against Colom. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi's senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination. Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom's confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president's choices for federal judicial positions in their home state. Colom said his Senate bid was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith. Colom called on Mississippi's history The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family. "In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection," Colom said, telling the story of Evers' military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction. Hopes had been low for any significant development in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped POWs but have remained far apart in their demands for accepting a peace settlement. READ MORE: Russia and Ukraine hold nearly 4 hours of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi U.S. officials say they are determined to revive Washington's peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results. Along with postwar security guarantees for both countries, other key hurdles are the fate of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory and what role European countries will play in an eventual settlement. U.S. envoys to meet with Putin and Zelenskyy The sides last met in February on Russia's invasion, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians. The talks lasted just under two hours Wednesday, after a four-hour session the previous day. "One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalize the numbers tomorrow," said Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, after the Abu Dhabi talks ended. READ MORE: Russia-Ukraine peace talks led by U.S. will look at security guarantees for both sides Vladimir Medinsky, head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Kyiv's contingent, confirmed the planned POW exchange, although Medinsky noted the agreement was "in principle." Alexander Zorin, a deputy chief of the General Staff's information department who attended the talks, told Russian state TV it would be one of the biggest such swaps since 1,000 soldiers from each side returned home last year. The latest exchange could take place in the next two or three weeks, he said. WATCH: Zelenskyy on his 'emotional' relationship with Trump and fighting Russia Kushner said he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin, Ireland, to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Ukrainian leader gave a muted welcome to the outcome of the talks, saying a proposed prisoner exchange was a positive step. But he said Ukraine will not give in to demands that it cede its territory that has been occupied by Russia in exchange for peace. Medinsky said he felt the talks helped Moscow and Kyiv edge closer to peace, while Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov described them as "substantive and quite useful." Russia opposed European officials in the talks Umerov said Kyiv's delegation was expected to meet later Wednesday with representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO who were in the capital of the United Arab Emirates but did not attend the three-way talks. Moscow doesn't want European countries, which are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. Kushner said one of the goals of the Moscow meeting is to try to get Europeans added to the talks. In Dublin, Zelenskyy said it was positive that security advisers and senior officials from European governments, the EU and NATO were in Abu Dhabi, even though they were not a part of the talks. Despite that. he said there had been a "change in temperature," with Washington warming to the idea of a European role. "Ending this war without Europe's participation would be unjust, and it would be impossible," Zelenskyy said through an interpreter. READ MORE: Zelenskyy pushes for 'clear' postwar security guarantees in Ukraine Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said European representatives could eventually join peace talks but added their current statements "don't indicate any desire on their part to contribute to movement along the path toward peace." Moscow complains that Europe is financing and supplying weaponry to Ukraine. Kushner said both Ukraine and Russia needed clarity on postwar security arrangements. He said European countries, the EU and NATO have to be involved in those discussions to build consensus on next steps. Ukraine wants to ensure that Moscow doesn't invade again, and EU officials say any discussions on Europe's security arrangements could only start after a ceasefire. Many in Europe see the inclusion of Russia in those plans as a concession to Putin, who has described NATO's eastward expansion as a top security threat to his country. Moscow has demanded that the alliance's troops be pulled back its troops from Russia's borders. Russia's security concerns were discussed at the talks, Kushner said, adding that Moscow was told it needs to provide different de-escalation proposals acceptable to Europe. "The reality is, is there's no trust right now between the sides. And that's to be expected after a conflict like this," he said. But he posted on X later that the POW exchange "will reunite families, build trust and create momentum toward peace." The talks were held in a new political atmosphere The context of the negotiations has changed since the February meeting in Geneva. The Trump administration now must reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections, and they could demand more support for Ukraine. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and members of his team were admonished by an Army guard at the Arlington National Cemetery after he and his entourage appeared to violate the solemn war memorial's rules for decorum.
A video of the Veterans Day observance event shows Hegseth, his wife and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
The Army sentinel on duty then steps towards Hegseth and his group and yells: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
Rules on etiquette at the cemetery dictate that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.
The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.
A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the Tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.
"While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum," Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement.
"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoredâand will always honorâthe sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."
Earlier, President Donald Trump, Vice-President JD Vance and other top officials attended the annual wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery.
During his speech at the ceremony, Trump offered his gratitude to uniformed service members who have fought for the country. He also touted what he sees as his administration's success in the Iran war.
"Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back. All of us fought back," he said.
"And we won," Trump said of the Iran war. "It's just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory."
Trump also pointed out Hegseth during the ceremony, saying he's done a "fantastic job" as defence secretary.
Trump has repeatedly defended Hegseth amid Democratic lawmakers' push to impeach him. On Tuesday, an effort to impeach the defence secretary under accusations that he waged war on Iran without congressional authorisation failed on Capitol Hill.
Hegseth has called the impeachment efforts a "farce" and a "stunt".

Cacti are among the toughest plants on the planet, withstanding scorching temperatures and parched conditions that would wilt a more sensitive sprout. But climate change may threaten these hardy plants more than previously thought, a new study suggests.
Scientists in recent years have raised some concerns over the effects of rising temperatures on cactus species, which span nearly every type of ecosystem on the planet—from tree-hanging Christmas cacti in tropical rainforests to the mighty saguaros standing tall in the harsh Sonoran Desert. However, few studies have incorporated the potential risk of another climate-change side effect: extreme drought events.
It turns out these combined factors aggressively crank up the threat level, according to a study published Wednesday in the journal Nature. Integrating new spatial data on severe drought with climate models, the researchers tracked how future conditions could affect the suitable climatic area for nearly 1,000 species of cacti. They found that more than a quarter of the analyzed cactus species could lose most of their suitable habitat by the end of the century, more than 80 percent in all. That’s far more than when only rising temperatures and projected average precipitation were considered.
The habitat declines identified in the paper are associated with substantial losses in cactus diversity in some regions.
These findings challenge a long-standing assumption for cacti that “in a warming world, they’ll likely be winners,” said study co-author Brian Enquist, a professor at the University of Arizona. “Even in these really hot, dry environments where you see cactus species, the climate now is shifting into a new climate regime that these species haven’t encountered in their evolutionary history.”
The study analyzed nearly 650,000 records of cacti around the world, including community science data from the app iNaturalist, which more than doubled the number of species analyzed. Models showed that droughts and heat are poised to have the worst impacts on species in some of the world’s most concentrated cactus hotspots, including Chile, Argentina, Peru, Ecuador and countries in Central America.
Some regions, such as the Mexican Pacific coast, saw modest gains in cactus species diversity, but these were offset by large losses in neighboring areas.
Cacti are already some of the world’s most imperiled plants, with more than 30 percent of species considered threatened. That’s largely due to habitat loss and illegal trade, which has helped supply the collector and houseplant industry as cactus popularity spikes around the world.
On top of this, unprecedented droughts in recent years have fueled widespread die-offs of species such as Copiapoa cacti in Chile’s Atacama Desert and saguaros around Phoenix and Tucson. That’s a precursor of what’s to come if climate change continues to fuel longer, more intense periods of heat and dryness, said study co-author Michiel Pillet, a postdoctoral researcher at University of South Florida.
“We were extremely surprised by how intense our results were,” Pillet said. He added that the impacts are likely an underestimate due to insufficient data on rare species—and the disproportionate impacts they face from climate change. “Think about a cactus species that only lives right at the coast in a single spot, and a hurricane comes in and wipes out that entire population.”
The study’s authors say their modeling approach could be applied to other plant species.
That was echoed by David Williams, a botany professor at the University of Wyoming who was not involved in the study.
“The findings extend well beyond our understanding of the climate vulnerability of cacti,” he said over email. “The work will guide future studies that uncover species-specific ecological, demographic and physiological processes that shape persistence across shifting climatic conditions.”
